And the chorus, in many copies, now appears only as «song of the chorus» between one scene and the next.","What is Aeolosicon?","A parody of Euripides' Aeolus mixed up with Sicon, a famous cook. Imagine the king of the winds stuck in the kitchen. Myths offer lots of scope: greedy gods, cowardly heroes, Zeus in love making a fool of himself. The audience knows the stories, and that helps us laugh at them.","Who pays for all this?","The choregos, a rich citizen whose turn it is to fund the chorus. It used to be a highly sought honour; now, with the city poorer, they're sometimes hard to find, and once or twice two choregoi have been appointed for the same play. The archon chooses the competing poets, and judges chosen by lot decide the winner.","What changed in Athenian comedy at the start of the fourth century?","Less direct political satire and more mythological parody and everyday life","Masks were banned","Plays were performed only at Delphi","No. So-called Middle Comedy cut back personal attacks and the role of the chorus, and preferred mythological parody and everyday scenes.","Antiphanes","Young comic poet","Myth and comedy: the poet's craft","On the seats of the theatre of Dionysus","Antiphanes began staging comedies around 385 and went on to write hundreds. I'm Antiphanes. They say my family came from abroad, from Smyrna or Rhodes, but I'm from here, from the theatre. Come, sit down. Do you know how unfair the comic poet's trade is?","Why do you say it is unfair?","Because the tragedians have it so easy! Everyone already knows the stories before they open their mouths. After purifying themselves with water and putting on garlands, the participants escorted the victim, unblemished and decorated, to the altar. It was sprinkled with water and barley, a few hairs were cut from it, the priest prayed with arms raised and the butcher (mageiros) cut its throat amid the women's ritual cry. The thigh bones wrapped in fat were burned so the smoke would rise to the gods; the meat was roasted and shared out. For many it was one of the few chances to eat meat. The gods of the sky were offered white animals; the gods below, black ones, and the victim was burned whole.","Did you see this morning's sacrifice? A spotless ewe, for the Twelve Gods. We all wash our hands in lustral water and put on garlands. In front goes the kanephoros, a girl with the basket: inside are the barley and, hidden, the knife. Behind comes the victim, with ribbons, and the piper. The animal is sprinkled: if it shakes its head, it's saying yes. And many of both kinds are metics.","Do they pay taxes?","Metics pay their yearly tax, and those who sell in the Agora without being Athenian pay another for their stall. At Piraeus a tax is charged on everything that comes in and goes out by sea: a fiftieth, two per cent. The city farms these taxes out to collectors, who advance the money and then collect what they can.","And if a foreigner has a problem?","He looks for his city's proxenos: an Athenian who represents another polis's interests here, a sort of official host. The Corinthians have theirs, the Thebans theirs… The proxenos puts them up, introduces them and defends them if they have a lawsuit. For us, whoever mistreats a stranger offends Zeus Xenios, protector of guests.","How do people buy and sell?","By word of mouth, before witnesses, paying and handing over at the same time if possible. If you trust the other man and pay first, that's your lookout. For important things you leave a deposit, an advance. Land isn't registered anywhere, and selling your forefathers' land is frowned upon, though it can be done.","What did the metronomoi of the Agora do?","Check that the sellers' weights and measures were correct","Fix the price of all goods","Collect stall rents for the king","No. The metronomoi, chosen by lot each year, checked the sellers' weights and measures against the official standards.","Cteson","Ship-owner of Piraeus","Loans and the risks of the sea","Sea trade was financed by the maritime loan (nautikos tokos): a lender advanced money to the owner of the ship or the cargo; if the ship came back, he got his capital back with very high interest, up to 30% depending on the risk; if it sank, he got nothing. It worked as insurance, and lent itself to fraud. Between friends there were interest-free loans (eranos); ordinary loans charged a drachma per mina a month (12% a year). When land secured a debt, the creditor set up a marker stone (horos) on it. Banks, like Pasion's, lived mainly on money-changing.","That one there is my ship: forty paces of hull, Chian wine on the way out and wheat from the Pontus on the way back, gods willing. I'm Cteson, shipowner. Well: shipowner on borrowed money, like all of us.","How is a voyage like that paid for?","With a maritime loan. A rich man in Piraeus advances me three thousand drachmas for the cargo. If I come back, I repay the money and twenty or thirty per cent interest, depending on the route and the season. If I sink, I owe him nothing: the sea keeps his money. That's why he sometimes sends one of his men on board to keep an eye on things.","Doesn't anyone cheat?","Plenty! They tell of two men from Massalia who took out loans on a cargo that didn't exist and then tried to sink the ship on the high seas so as not to pay. One of them jumped into the water to escape and drowned. Others take out two loans on the same cargo. That's why contracts are written down, left with a friend and signed before witnesses.","And ordinary loans?","Between friends, the eranos: several people pool their money and lend it without interest, and whoever gets it pays it back when he can. If you go to a moneylender, the usual rate is a drachma per mina a month: twelve per cent a year. And if what you pledge is your land, the creditor plants a stone marker on it, a horos, with what you owe. You'll see them outside the walls.","What are bankers for, then?","Mainly for changing money: every city strikes its own, and coins arrive here from Corinth, from Aegina, Persian gold darics, staters of Cyzicus… The banker weighs, tests, changes and keeps a little. He also holds deposits and pays whoever you tell him to. Pasion, the one in the Agora, started as a slave at one of those tables.","Do you sail all year round?","No. From spring to autumn; in winter the sea is «closed». You travel by day and, if you can, close to the coast. And when you've got rich from two or three good voyages, the smart thing is to stop sailing and become a lender: the man who risks his money on land sleeps better than the man who risks his life at sea.","What happened to a maritime loan if the ship sank?","The borrower owed nothing: the lender lost his money","It had to be repaid with double interest","The city of Athens paid it","No. With a maritime loan, if the ship was lost the borrower did not have to repay anything; that's why the interest was so high, like insurance.","A trial: Against the Grain Dealers","Court of the Heliaia","At the Heliaia: ask Lysimachus, the juror, to take you to a trial","Ask Lysimachus, the juror of the Heliaia, to take you to a trial, listen to both sides and vote.","Around 386 several grain dealers, metics, were tried for buying more than the fifty baskets the law allowed. Only the prosecution speech survives, written by Lysias (speech 22). It shows Athens' dependence on imported grain, distrust of traders and the value of due process: the Council came close to executing them without trial.","Herald","Herald of the court","Citizen jurors: today you are five hundred and one, chosen by lot this very morning. Several grain dealers, metics, are on trial, accused of buying more grain than the law allows. The prosecution will speak first, then the defence; the water clock will measure each one's time. At the end you will vote in secret, without conferring among yourselves.","Prosecutor","Member of the Council · speech by Lysias","Judges: many have been surprised that I, a member of the Council, should accuse these men. I'll tell you why. When the prytaneis brought the matter before the Council, some were so indignant that they wanted to hand them over without trial to the Eleven for execution. I opposed it: it seemed terrible to me to accustom the Council to such a thing, and I proposed that they be tried according to the laws. That's why I'm here: so that, if they are guilty, they pay after a trial.","The law is clear: no grain dealer may buy more than fifty baskets at a time. I asked them before the Council whether they had bought more, and they admitted it. Now they say they did it on the magistrates' advice, that Anytus recommended they buy together so as not to bid against one another. But Anytus advised them not to drive up the price, not to hoard. And this year's magistrates deny having told them anything.","See how they behave: when bad news comes, that ships have been lost at sea, that the Spartans have captured them, that the markets are closing, they're the first to know it, or to invent it, and they raise the price a drachma in a single day. They rejoice at our misfortunes. They keep us under siege in peacetime. If you condemn them, the other traders will be more honest; if you acquit them, you'll give them leave to do as they please. I ask for the death penalty.","Defence","One of the dealers · reconstructed defence","Citizens: we are metics and for years we've been bringing grain from the Piraeus to the city, even during the war, when no one wanted to take the risk. We bought together because Anytus, who was a magistrate, advised us not to compete with one another so the price wouldn't soar. We didn't hide the grain: we sold it. If you sentence us to death for following a magistrate's advice, who will want to bring bread to Athens tomorrow?<br><br><i>(This speech is a reconstruction. Only the prosecution's survives; the arguments come from what the accuser himself says they claimed.)</i>","You are given two voting tokens: one to condemn and one to acquit. It was made up of the main couple, their children, the elderly parents, unmarried or widowed sisters or orphans taken in, and also the slaves, animals, tools and land. Aristotle says the oikos is «the man, the woman and the helper for work», which for the poor is the ox.","<b>Birth.</b> The father decided whether a newborn would be raised; he could expose it. If he accepted it, around the fifth day he carried it running round the hearth (amphidromia), and on the tenth he named it before the relatives. At the Apaturia he presented it to his phratry, swearing it was legitimate; from 451 one had to be the child of an Athenian father and mother to be a citizen. It took five or six births per woman for two or three children to reach adulthood.","<b>Marriage.</b> Marriage was a private agreement between two houses: the engyesis with a handshake, the handing over of the bride with her dowry, and living together. The wedding lasted three days and was entered in no register; its witnesses were the guests. Women married between fourteen and eighteen; men, around thirty. Divorce simply meant the woman went back to her father's house, with her dowry.","<b>Old age.</b> Around sixty, the father could hand the house over to his son. The law required the son, on pain of losing his rights, to feed and house his parents and to bury them, provided they had taught him a trade. The city's poor old men could earn a living as jurors.","<b>Slaves.</b> Most worked in households, though there were also slaves in workshops, in the Laurion mines and in the city's service. Anyone could fall into slavery through war or piracy, so it was seen more as bad luck than as natural inferiority, though Aristotle tried to justify it. Nurses and paidagogoi usually stayed in the house until they died; some slaves saved up and bought their freedom.","<b>The phratry.</b> Above the oikos stood the phratry, a hereditary brotherhood of neighbouring families under the protection of Zeus Phratrios, and the deme, the district in which a young man was enrolled at eighteen. Athenians identified themselves by their own name, their father's name and their deme.","Aristotle, Politics 1252b-1255b","Xenophon, Oeconomicus","Isaeus, Speeches","Menander, Dyskolos 729-740","Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 42 and 56.6","D. Hernández de la Fuente and R. López Melero, Civilización griega (Madrid, 2014), ch. 2.11-2.16",null,"Birth and death rates are modern estimates.","The women of Athens","The image of the Athenian woman shut up at home comes largely from nineteenth-century scholars. The sources show something more nuanced: citizen women did not vote or sit as judges, because those rights were tied to military service, but they had a fundamental public role in religion, ran the oikos and went out to the fountain, the market, the tombs, festivals and the theatre, trying not to go alone.","<b>Religion.</b> Athens had some 170 festival days a year. There were highly prestigious female priesthoods, such as that of Athena Polias; girls carried the sacred basket as kanephoroi, and married women alone celebrated Demeter's Thesmophoria.","<b>Property.</b> Inheritance passed through the male line, but the dowry worked as the woman's own property, which the husband had to return on divorce. If there were no sons, the daughter inherited as an epikleros and had to marry her father's nearest kinsman. Her so-called kyrios, father, brother or husband, represented her in court, because only men acted as citizens.","<b>Culture.</b> Many could read, write and play the lyre, though education, which was private, went to sons first. Plato presents Socrates as a pupil of Diotima and credits Aspasia with the ability to write speeches.","<b>Non-citizen women.</b> Pericles' law (451), restored in 403, made marrying within the citizen body the rule: a metic's daughter, however rich, could not marry an Athenian. Many lived as concubines (pallakai) or hetairai, who might be anything from banquet musicians to companions as respected as Aspasia. In the fourth century the law grew harsher: a foreigner living in a false marriage with an Athenian woman could be sold into slavery.","Thucydides II 45.2","Aristophanes, Lysistrata and Assemblywomen","Plato, Symposium 201d and Menexenus 235e","Lysias I","Demosthenes LIX","D. Hernández de la Fuente and R. López Melero, Civilización griega (Madrid, 2014), ch. 4","S. B. Pomeroy, Goddesses, Whores, Wives, and Slaves (1975)",null,"How much freedom of movement Athenian women of well-off families had is an open question.","The theatre in 386","Tragedies and comedies were performed in Athens at two festivals of Dionysus: the Lenaia, in winter, and the City Dionysia, in spring. Each tragic poet presented three tragedies and a satyr play; the audience, several thousand strong, spent the whole day in the seats.","<b>A special year.</b> An inscription, the Fasti of the Dionysia (IG II² 2318), says that in 386 «the tragedians for the first time presented an old drama». From then on works by the great fifth-century poets were often revived, above all Euripides, who in the fourth century became the best-loved and most performed tragedian.","<b>What a performance was like.</b> Three actors, all men, played every role by changing mask and costume. The chorus, fifteen strong, sang and danced in the orchestra, accompanied by an aulos player (a two-pipe reed instrument). Behind stood the skene, a wooden building that served as palace front and dressing room.","<b>In the game.</b> The theatre of Dionysus stages three plays by Euripides: Medea (431) in the morning, The Trojan Women (415) in the afternoon and The Bacchae (405, staged after his death) at night. Night performances didn't exist: it's a licence so you can see all three in one day.",null,"Aristotle, Poetics 1449a-b","Pollux, Onomasticon IV",null,null,"The game's chorus has twelve figures; in classical tragedy there were fifteen.","Thebes in 386: before its hegemony","Thebes was the great city of Boeotia and head of the Boeotian League, a federation of cities with eleven districts. During the Peloponnesian War it was Sparta's ally; afterwards, its enemy alongside Athens, Corinth and Argos in the Corinthian War (395-387).","<b>The King's Peace.</b> The treaty of 387/386 demanded the autonomy of every Greek city. Sparta used it to force the Boeotian League to dissolve and to rebuild Plataea, Thebes' enemy. In 386, then, Thebes is weakened.","<b>What is to come.</b> In 382 a Spartan seizes the Cadmea by treachery; in 379 Pelopidas and other exiles free it. In 371, at Leuctra, Epaminondas defeats the Spartan army. Then begins the Theban hegemony, which lasts until Epaminondas' death at Mantinea (362).","<b>In the game.</b> That's why the Thebes you visit is not yet the dominant power in Greece, but the two men who will make it great are already there.","Xenophon, Hellenica V 1.32-36 and V 2-4","Hellenica Oxyrhynchia 19","Diodorus XV 50-88","Buckler and Beck (2008)","Athens in 386 BC","In 404 Athens lost the Peloponnesian War. Sparta imposed the demolition of the Long Walls, cut the fleet to twelve ships and backed an oligarchic government, the Thirty, which executed hundreds of people and confiscated the property of rich metics. In 403 the democrats led by Thrasybulus retook the city and an amnesty was sworn that prevented a war of revenge.","The restored democracy revised and published its laws, introduced pay for attending the Assembly and was more cautious about reforms. In 399 it condemned Socrates to death. From 395 Athens fought Sparta again in the Corinthian War, alongside Thebes, Argos and Corinth, and with Persian money. Conon's victory at Cnidus (394) made it possible to rebuild the walls; Thrasybulus regained influence in the Aegean until his death in 388.","The war ended with the King's Peace (387/386): the Persian king Artaxerxes II kept the Greek cities of Asia and Sparta took charge of making sure the rest were «autonomous». Athens kept Lemnos, Imbros and Scyros. This is the moment of the game: a smaller, poorer city than Pericles', living on Black Sea grain and Piraeus trade, with many metics and slaves.","It is also a decisive intellectual moment. Socrates' pupils have scattered and are founding schools: Plato at the Academy (c. 387), Antisthenes at the Cynosarges, Euclides at Megara. Isocrates has taught rhetoric since around 390. Lysias writes speeches for the courts and Aristophanes stages his last comedies.","What is to come, and no one in the game knows yet: the Second Athenian League (378/377), the Spartan defeat by Thebes at Leuctra (371), Aristotle's arrival at the Academy (367) and, in 338, the victory of Philip II of Macedon at Chaeronea.","Xenophon, Hellenica II-V","Diodorus Siculus XIV","Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 34-41","Lysias 12 and 13","Andocides 3, On the Peace (391)",null,"Authors and figures alive around 386","This list gathers the Greek writers, thinkers and public figures who were alive in the spring of 386 BC and could therefore appear in the game. Austin, Poetae Comici Graeci (1983-2001)","Many dates of birth and death are deduced from late sources and may be off by several years.","Money, prices and wages","The unit of account is the silver drachma, divided into six obols. A hundred drachmas make a mina and sixty minas a talent (6,000 drachmas). The commonest coin is the tetradrachm, with Athena's head and the owl, struck from Laurion silver and accepted all over the Mediterranean. Obols, tiny coins, were often carried in the mouth, as Aristophanes reminds us.","At the end of the war Athens struck emergency coins of silver-plated bronze; around 390 they were withdrawn, and the Assemblywomen jokes about people left holding them, worthless. That's why money-changers checked every coin.","Some reference figures: a skilled worker earned about a drachma a day at the end of the fifth century (Erechtheion accounts); a juror, three obols; attending the Assembly, three obols around 390 (later rising to a drachma or more). A metic paid a tax of twelve drachmas a year. Isocrates charged a thousand drachmas for his full course. Grain prices varied a lot and could soar in wartime, as Lysias denounces in speech 22.","Aristophanes, Wasps 787-791 (obols in the mouth) and Assemblywomen 815-822 (the withdrawn bronze coinage)","Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 41.3 and 62.2","Erechtheion accounts, IG I³ 474-479","Xenophon, Ways and Means (Poroi)",null,"Calendar and festivals","The Athenian year began with the first new moon after the summer solstice, in the month of Hekatombaion, and had twelve lunar months (with an extra month every so often). Each year was named after its eponymous archon. In parallel, the Council used a calendar of ten prytanies.","The game's spring corresponds to the months of Mounichion and Thargelion. The great festivals were: the Panathenaia (Hekatombaion, summer), the Eleusinian Mysteries (Boedromion, autumn), the Thesmophoria, reserved for married women (Pyanepsion), the Lenaia, with comedy contests (Gamelion, winter), the Anthesteria, festival of the new wine (Anthesterion) and the City Dionysia (Elaphebolion, late March or April), with the tragedy and comedy contests.","<b>Festivals month by month.</b> Hekatombaion: the Kronia, when masters and slaves ate together, and every four years the Great Panathenaia, with procession, games and torch races. Boedromion: the Eleusinian Mysteries. Pyanepsion: the Pyanepsia, with a dish of beans for Apollo; the phratries' Apaturia; the married women's Thesmophoria; and the craftsmen's Chalkeia, for Athena and Hephaestus. Poseideon: the Haloa and the Rural Dionysia, with phallus processions and mockery. Gamelion: the month of weddings, with the sacred marriage of Zeus and Hera, and the Lenaia. Anthesterion: the Anthesteria, when the jars of new wine were opened, children tasted it and the dead returned for a day. Elaphebolion: the City Dionysia, five days of dithyrambs, comedies and tragedies.","The Greeks didn't count hours as we do: they spoke of moments of the day, like dawn or «when the agora is full», mid-morning. The game's clock uses these expressions with an approximate hour.","Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 43 and 56-57","Aristophanes, Women at the Thesmophoria","Herodotus IV 181 and Xenophon, Memorabilia I 1.10 («when the agora is full»)","D. Hernández de la Fuente and R. López Melero, Civilización griega (Madrid, 2014), ch. 5.8",null,null,"Gods from the East","Roman religion was polytheistic and open: Rome had gradually adopted gods from conquered peoples and from the Greeks, and in a city of a million inhabitants from all over the Mediterranean many cults lived side by side. Historians called \"oriental cults\" those that came from Asia Minor, Egypt, Syria or Persia; today the label is debated, because each had its own history and many became thoroughly Roman.","<b>The Great Mother.</b> She was the first and the most official. In 204 BC, in the middle of the war against Hannibal, the Sibylline Books advised bringing the black stone of the Idaean Mother from Pessinus in Phrygia. Her temple on the Palatine was dedicated in 191 BC and her games, the Megalesia, were held every April with plays. But her priests, the galli, Phrygian eunuchs who danced with drums, scandalised people: citizens were forbidden to become galli.","<b>Isis and Serapis.</b> The Egyptian goddess came with traders from Delos and Campania. In Rome she was persecuted for a century: the Senate pulled down her altars, Augustus banned her rites in the city centre and Tiberius destroyed her temple in AD 19. But her devotees kept growing, and around 40 the great Iseum of the Campus Martius was built, with obelisks and sphinxes brought from Egypt. The Flavians protected it: Vespasian and Titus spent the night there before their triumph of 71. The fire of 80 damaged it and Domitian will rebuild it.","<b>Jews and Christians.</b> The Jews of Rome, perhaps several tens of thousands, lived mostly across the Tiber, spoke Greek and had several synagogues. Their single God without images, the Sabbath and circumcision attracted attention; some Romans drew close to them and others mocked them. From 70 they paid a tax for Jupiter Capitolinus. From their synagogues had come the first Christians, a still small group that met in houses and that Nero had persecuted after the fire of 64.","<b>Others.</b> The Syrian Goddess (Atargatis), with her wandering priests; Nero was devoted to her and then despised her. Ma-Bellona, from Cappadocia, whose priests wounded themselves in trance. The Persian god Mithras, on the other hand, has barely arrived: the first Latin author to mention him, Statius, writes around 90, and the mithraea of Rome date from the 2nd and 3rd centuries. That is why there are none in this game.","These cults attracted people because they offered something civic religion gave less of: a personal relationship with the divinity, initiation rites, communities of believers and, sometimes, the hope of a happy life after death. Apart from Jews and Christians, nobody demanded exclusivity: one could be devoted to Isis, sacrifice to Jupiter and honour the household Lares.","Livy XXIX 10-14","Ovid, Fasti IV 179-372","Dionysius of Halicarnassus II 19","Josephus, Jewish Antiquities XVIII 65-84 and Jewish War VII 123","Suetonius, Domitian 1 and Nero 56","Tacitus, Annals II 85 and Histories IV 81-84","Philo, Embassy to Gaius 155-158","Statius, Thebaid I 719-720","F. Korres, studies on the Parthenon and its restoration","The scale of the distances between districts is compressed, and the height of the Acropolis above the Agora is about 60 m in the game against about 90 m in reality.","Historical licences taken in the game","This game is a teaching reconstruction, not an exact model. These are its main licences:","<b>Scale and positions.</b> The buildings are life-size and the Acropolis and Agora keep their approximate layout, but distances between districts are compressed: the Academy, the Lyceum and the Cynosarges are closer than they were, and the Acropolis is somewhat lower. The houses are generic, though they follow the courtyard-house type documented in Athens.","<b>Characters.</b> Plato, Isocrates, Lysias, Aristophanes, Pasion and Antisthenes are historical. Eucles, Euthydemus, Lysimachus, Sosias, Manes, Timocrates, Theano, Cleotimus and Philinna are invented, though plausible. Their words are recreations based on the sources cited in each lesson.","<b>Anachronisms and doubts.</b> Aristophanes may already have died by 386. Plato's Republic and Isocrates' Panegyricus are somewhat later. The kleroterion and bronze tickets are documented from the mid-fourth century. The Heliaia and the prison are disputed archaeological identifications. Pasion's bank was in the Piraeus.","<b>Xenophon.</b> He doesn't appear because in 386 he was exiled from Athens and living at Scillus, near Olympia. Antisthenes talks about him.","<b>Islands and Piraeus.</b> The islands are reduced settings reached by ship; their geography is schematic and they include only a handful of places. The Piraeus is a simple quay. The Orpheotelestes, the grandmother, the sick man, the initiate and the island characters are invented.","<b>Daily life.</b> Glycera, Nicarete, Callias, Myrrhine, Carion, Ariston and Cteson are invented. The school, sacrifice and wedding scenes are generic reconstructions, and their timings are simplified.","<b>Troy, Thebes and the theatre.</b> Troy (Ilion) and Thebes are reduced, schematic settings; Thebes is reached overland with a muleteer who, for convenience, leaves from the north gate. The theatre's night performances are a licence. Demophon the bookseller, the travellers Teleclus, Balacrus, Hicetas, Timarchus, Eudicus and Sabyrtus, Idaeus of Ilion and Periboea are invented; Iphicrates and Chabrias may have been away from Athens in 386, and Aristippus may have been elsewhere.","<b>Look and sound.</b> The colours of clothes and temples are conjectural, though we know sculpture and architecture were painted. The lyre music is an evocation using Dorian scales, not a reconstruction: ancient Greek music is only partly known. There are no cicadas because it's spring; instead you hear birds by day and crickets by night.","Further reading","Almost all the ancient texts cited in this library are translated into English in the Loeb Classical Library. In the <a href=\"https://www.perseus.tufts.edu\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Perseus Digital Library</a> they can be read free in Greek and English.","For the archaeology of the Agora, the American School's excavation website, <a href=\"https://agora.ascsa.net\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">agora.ascsa.net</a>, has photographs, plans and inventories.","General reading in Spanish: D. Then Gaia, the Earth, and Eros were born. Gaia brought forth Uranus, the Sky, and with him the Titans, the Cyclopes and the Hundred-Handers. Uranus shut his children up inside the Earth, until Gaia gave a sickle to Cronus, the youngest Titan, who castrated his father; from the sea foam Aphrodite was born. Cronus, warned that a son would overthrow him, swallowed the children Rhea bore him. She gave him a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes and hid Zeus in Crete. Grown up, Zeus forced Cronus to vomit up his brothers and sisters, defeated the Titans in a ten-year war and shut them in Tartarus. Zeus chose the fat; that's why men burn the bones for the gods and eat the meat. Zeus, angered, took fire away from them, and Prometheus stole it hidden in a hollow reed. As punishment, Zeus chained him to a rock, where an eagle devoured his liver every day, until Heracles freed him. To men he sent Pandora, the first woman, adorned by all the gods. Pandora opened a great jar and all the evils came out; only hope remained inside.","Hesiod, Theogony 507-616 and Works and Days 42-105","Aeschylus (attributed), Prometheus Bound","In Hesiod it is a jar (pithos); «Pandora's box» is a Renaissance mistake.","The authorship of Prometheus Bound is debated.","The ages of man and the flood","According to Hesiod, the gods created successive races of men: the golden race, which lived without toil or old age; the silver, foolish and impious; the bronze, violent, which destroyed itself; the race of heroes, who fought at Thebes and Troy; and the iron race, ours, condemned to toil and pain. Another myth tells that Zeus sent a flood to wipe out mankind. Deucalion, son of Prometheus, and his wife Pyrrha survived in an ark and, on the gods' advice, threw stones over their shoulders: from his stones men were born; from hers, women.","Hesiod, Works and Days 106-201","Pindar, Olympian IX 41-53","Apollodorus, Library I 7.2","Perseus and Medusa","Acrisius, king of Argos, learned from an oracle that his grandson would kill him, and shut his daughter Danae in a bronze chamber. Zeus came in as a shower of gold and Perseus was born. Acrisius cast mother and son into the sea in a chest, which reached the island of Seriphos. There King Polydectes, who desired Danae, sent Perseus to fetch the head of the Gorgon Medusa, whose gaze turned people to stone. With the help of Athena and Hermes, winged sandals, the cap of invisibility and a pouch, Perseus beheaded her while looking away; from her neck sprang the horse Pegasus and Chrysaor. On his way back he saved Andromeda from a sea monster. Years later, at some games, his discus accidentally struck an old man: it was Acrisius.","Hesiod, Theogony 270-283 and Shield 216-237","Pindar, Pythian XII","Pherecydes of Athens, fragments 10-12","Perseus looking at Medusa reflected in his shield appears in later sources.","Son of Zeus and the mortal Alcmene, Heracles was persecuted from the cradle by Hera, who sent two snakes that the baby strangled. He passed other tests and married the king's daughter. He blinded the Cyclops Polyphemus, son of Poseidon, after telling him his name was «Nobody», and the god pursued him from then on. Aeolus gave him a bag holding the winds, but his men opened it. The sorceress Circe turned his companions into pigs. He went down to Hades to consult the seer Tiresias. Architects: Ictinus and Callicrates; sculptor: Phidias. It measures 30.9 by 69.5 metres, with 8 columns on the façades and 17 on the sides, over 10 metres high. More than a temple for worship it is a treasury and a monument to the victory over the Persians. Look at the colours: friezes, pediments and mouldings are painted; no bare marble here.","Athena Parthenos","Phidias' statue: almost twelve metres of wood covered in ivory (the skin) and over a tonne of gold (the dress), which can be removed and weighed in case of need. In her right hand she holds a Nike, winged Victory; at her feet, the sacred serpent. In front is a shallow pool of water.","Foundations of the Old Temple","Between the Erechtheion and the Parthenon you can see the foundations of the old temple of Athena, from the time of the Peisistratids, burned by the Persians in 480. Whether part of the building went on standing for years is debated. The columns and entablatures of the burned temples were built into the north wall of the Acropolis, where they can be seen from the Agora as a reminder of the destruction.","Temple of several cults, finished around 406: Athena Polias, Poseidon, Erechtheus and Cecrops. The ground drops about 3 metres, so the building has porches at different levels. Under the Caryatid porch lies the tomb of Cecrops, the first king; in the north porch they show the marks of Poseidon's trident. The frieze is grey Eleusinian stone with white marble figures attached.","The treasury of the Parthenon","The west room of the Parthenon, with four Ionic columns, does not connect with the statue's room. Here and in the rear porch the treasures of Athena and the other gods are kept: gold crowns, gold and silver bowls (phialai), ceremonial arms, coins. Every year the treasurers take an inventory and carve it in stone; that's why we know, object by object, what was here.","Athena Polias and the golden lamp","In the east room of the Erechtheion is the most sacred image in Athens: an old olive-wood statue of Athena, said to have fallen from the sky. It is to her that the peplos is offered at the Panathenaia. In front a golden lamp by Callimachus burns day and night: it is filled with oil once a year, and its smoke escapes through a bronze palm tree that serves as a chimney.","The sea of Erechtheus and the trident marks","In the west part of the Erechtheion are altars of Poseidon-Erechtheus, of Boutes and of Hephaestus, and paintings of the priestly family of the Boutadai. There is also a well of salt water, the «sea of Erechtheus», said to sound like surf when the south wind blows. In the rock under the north porch they show the marks left by Poseidon's trident in his contest with Athena; that's why the porch roof has an opening.","Pinakotheke","The north wing of the Propylaia holds paintings on panels. Pausanias saw, among others, Diomedes and Odysseus carrying off the Palladium of Troy, Orestes killing Aegisthus, the sacrifice of Polyxena and Achilles among the daughters of Lycomedes on Scyros, some attributed to Polygnotus. Because of its shape, with an off-centre door, many think it was also a banquet hall with couches.","The Acropolis branch of the sanctuary of Artemis at Brauron, on the Attic coast. The goddess is offered mainly clothes and textiles, which the inventories describe one by one. At Brauron, Athenian girls served the goddess as «bears» (arktoi) before marrying; Aristophanes recalls it in Lysistrata.","The bronze store of the Acropolis: weapons, shields, missiles, vessels and other bronze objects belonging to Athena or kept for the city. Its fourth-century inventories survive in inscriptions.","Athena's olive tree","According to myth, Athena made the first olive tree spring up here in her contest with Poseidon for Attica. It grows in the Pandroseion, the courtyard west of the Erechtheion. From this tree descend the sacred olives (moriai) of Attica, whose oil rewards the victors at the Panathenaia. The work was left unfinished when the Peloponnesian War broke out.","Areopagus","The hill of Ares. Here meets the ancient council made up of all former archons, who keep the post for life. Since Ephialtes' reforms (462) it has lost almost all its political power, but it still tries homicides. According to myth, Orestes was tried here and acquitted by Athena's vote.","Cave of Pan","A cave on the north slope of the Acropolis. According to Herodotus, before Marathon the god Pan appeared to the runner Philippides and complained that the Athenians did not honour him. After the victory they dedicated this cave to him, with sacrifices and a torch race every year. Close by are other sacred caves of Apollo and Zeus.","The portico of the king archon, the magistrate in charge of religious affairs. Here the laws of Solon and Draco are displayed, revised and inscribed anew after 403, and here the magistrates swear on a great stone. In this portico Socrates answered the charge of impiety in 399; Plato sets the opening of the Euthyphro here. On the roof are terracotta figures: Theseus throwing Sciron into the sea and Dawn carrying off Cephalus.","The «painted portico». Its great wooden panels, by Polygnotus, Micon and Panaenus, show the battle of Oenoe, Theseus against the Amazons, the fall of Troy and the battle of Marathon. It's a place for strolling and conversation: philosophers, merchants and the curious gather here.","Bouleuterion","Seat of the Council of Five Hundred, built at the end of the fifth century behind the old Council building. It is Athens' point zero: distances to everywhere in Attica are measured from here. Every citizen has a bronze plate with his name (pinakion), which is slotted into this stone. A tube drops black and white balls at random: each ball decides whether a whole row of names is chosen or not. That's how jurors and magistrates are picked without anyone being able to cheat.","Boundary stone of the Agora","The inscription reads: «I am the boundary of the Agora». This marker was found in its original place, next to the house of Simon. Within these limits the space is sacred and public. Those who have committed certain offences are forbidden to enter: they are cut off from the life of the city.","House of Simon the shoemaker","A modest house at the south-west corner of the Agora. Behind, the wooden stage building with its three doors.","Odeon of Pericles","A huge square hall of about 62 by 68 metres, covered by a pyramid-shaped roof held up by a forest of columns. The musical contests of the Panathenaia are held here and poets present their works before the Dionysia.","Sanctuary of Asclepius","Asclepius, the healing god of Epidaurus, came to Athens in 420/419, in the middle of the war and after the plague. The sick sleep here hoping the god will heal them in dreams and leave votive offerings showing the body part that was cured.","Dipylon Gate","The «double gate», the largest in Athens: a courtyard of about 40 by 22 metres between four towers, with a double gate at each end, to trap attackers. Isocrates has his school very close by.","The temple of Olympian Zeus, begun by the sons of the tyrant Peisistratus around 520 to be the largest in Greece and abandoned when the tyranny fell. Almost a hundred and forty years later only the foundations and a few column drums remain. day","You walk to the ",", heading for ","About "," kilometres: ","a day"," on the road.","<span class=\"label\">You reach ","</span><br>The way back to "," leaves by the ","Temple of Apollo of Larissa","The plain of Thessaly","The largest plain in Greece, watered by the river Peneus and ringed by mountains: Olympus to the north, Pindus to the west, Othrys to the south. The best horses are bred here and the best Greek cavalry is formed. The land belongs to a few aristocratic families, such as the Aleuadae of Larissa, and is worked by the penestae, subject peasants who are neither free nor quite slaves. To the north, the narrow Vale of Tempe leads to Macedon; to the west, across the Pindus, to Epirus.","Sanctuary of Pella","Pella, capital of Macedon","A few years ago King Archelaus moved the capital of Macedon from Aegae to here, beside a lagoon open to the sea. He wanted to make his court a little Athens: he invited the painter Zeuxis to decorate his palace and the poet Euripides, who died in Macedon in 406. Now Amyntas III reigns, fighting to keep his throne against the Illyrians and the league of Olynthus. In southern Greece people argue whether the Macedonians are really Greeks. In four years his son Philip will be born here, who will dominate Greece, and from Philip will come Alexander.","The oracle of Dodona","The oldest oracle in Greece, according to Herodotus. Zeus speaks through the rustling of the leaves of a sacred oak, and his priests, the Selloi, sleep on the ground and do not wash their feet, as the Iliad already says. Around the tree stands a circle of bronze cauldrons on tripods: when you strike one, the sound passes from cauldron to cauldron. The faithful write their questions on lead tablets: whether they should marry, whether the child their wife is expecting is theirs, whether they should emigrate. Thousands have been found.","Temple of Artemis Laphria","The Calydonian boar","Here myth places the hunt for the monstrous boar that Artemis sent against Calydon because King Oeneus had forgotten her in his sacrifices. Heroes came from all over Greece; the huntress Atalanta was the first to wound it and Meleager killed it and gave her the hide, which sparked strife. Above the city stands the sanctuary of Artemis Laphria. Many Aetolians still live in unwalled villages and are known as light-armed warriors: in 426 they defeated Demosthenes's Athenians in their mountains.","Sanctuary of Zeus Homarios","Aegium and the Achaeans","The cities of Achaea, on the north coast of the Peloponnese, form a league that meets at the sanctuary of Poseidon at Helice, not far from here. Helice does not know it, but in thirteen years, in 373, a night-time earthquake and a giant wave will swallow it whole, and for centuries travellers will see its ruins under the water. Afterwards, the Achaeans will meet here, at Aegium.","Sanctuary of Zeus Ithomatas","Messenia and the helots","Messenia is one of the most fertile lands in Greece, and that is why Sparta conquered it centuries ago. Its people are helots: serfs who farm the land for their Spartan masters and hand over half the harvest. They have rebelled several times; in the great revolt that followed the earthquake of 464 they held out for ten years here, on Mount Ithome, by the sanctuary of Zeus Ithomatas. In seventeen years, Epaminondas of Thebes will free Messenia and found the city of Messene on this slope.","Temple of Apollo of Chalcis","The Euripus","Chalcis lies by the Euripus, the strait that separates the island of Euboea from Boeotia: at its narrowest it is about forty metres wide, and since 411 a bridge has crossed it. Its currents change direction several times a day, so fast that ships have to wait, and nobody knows why. Aristotle, who will spend his last days here, will try to explain it. Centuries ago Chalcis founded colonies all over the Mediterranean, from Sicily and southern Italy to the peninsula that bears its name, Chalcidice.","Rhegium","Temple of Rhegium","The Strait of Sicily","Rhegium, the Rhegion founded by the Greeks of Chalcis, watches over the strait that separates Italy from Sicily, barely three kilometres across at its narrowest. Sailors fear its whirlpools and currents: here the Odyssey places Scylla, the monster of the rock, and Charybdis, the whirlpool that swallows ships. On the other shore lies Messana. About twenty years ago the apostle Paul landed at this port, a prisoner, on his way to Rome.","Lucius Ancarius","Shipowner · ships to Hispania and Africa","the shipowner","Hagnon","Shipowner · ship to the islands","the shipowner","Piraeus","Harbour warehouses","Athens' great port, about seven kilometres from the city and joined to it by the Long Walls. It has three natural harbours: Kantharos, for trade, and Zea and Mounichia, for warships. Its streets were laid out in a grid by Hippodamus of Miletus. Here money is changed, Black Sea grain is bought and ships leave for the whole Mediterranean. In the game the port is much simplified: just a quay with a merchant ship.","Temple of Aphaia","Doric temple of around 500, some 13.8 by 28.8 metres, at the top of a pine wood in the north-east of the island. It is dedicated to Aphaia, a local goddess identified with the Cretan Britomartis. Its pediments show the Trojan wars presided over by Athena; the warriors, painted in bright colours, are among the finest sculpture of their time.","Temple of Apollo","Aegina's turtles run through every market on the sea. Ours, not the owls.","Athenian? My grandfather was driven off this island by your people. We came back with Lysander.","They say Aeacus still judges the dead. May he find me in a good mood.","Harbour of Aegina","Aegina was a great trading power: its silver coins with a turtle are among the first in Greece. An enemy of Athens, in 431 the Athenians expelled its people and shared the island among Athenian settlers. After the Athenian defeat of 404, Lysander gave the island back to the Aeginetans. During the Corinthian War its privateers raided Attica, until the King's Peace.","Temple of the Athenians","Great temple","Altar of horns (Keraton)","The altar which, according to myth, Apollo built as a child from interlocking goat horns. Theseus danced the crane dance around it on his return from Crete. Its archaeological identification is debated.","Sacred lake and Leto's palm tree","The round lake beside which, according to myth, Apollo was born. A sacred palm grows on its shore: already in the Odyssey, Ulysses recalls seeing a young palm shoot on Delos by Apollo's altar.","Terrace of the Lions","A row of Naxian marble lions, from about 600, looks towards the sacred lake. They were a gift of the Naxians, who then controlled the sanctuary. Originally there were about sixteen.","Doric temple Athens built around 425-417, when it controlled the sanctuary. When the tyranny fell, the work was abandoned. According to local tradition, Theseus abandoned Ariadne on this islet. It faces Delos.","Unfinished kouros","In a quarry on Naxos lies a kouros (statue of a youth) about ten metres long, abandoned unfinished in the sixth century, perhaps because it cracked. It shows how sculptors roughed out the block in the quarry itself before transporting it.","Naxian marble is the best; Parian, say the Parians.","Dionysus is our god. The wine here is truly good.","At night, look for Ariadne's crown in the sky.","Ruins of Knossos","These enormous ruins, covered with earth and grass, have been abandoned for almost a thousand years. The Cretans say they were the palace of King Minos and that here Daedalus built the labyrinth; that is why the city's coins bear a labyrinth. Today we know it was a Bronze Age palace, about 150 metres across, with a great central court, storerooms full of jars and wooden columns, destroyed around 1375 BC.","The palace that cannot be seen","Anachronism flagged: the palace of red columns and colourful frescoes in the books is the reconstruction made by the archaeologist Arthur Evans from 1900 onwards, partly in concrete. In 386 BC nobody had seen it like that: only these razed walls remained. If you dream of the labyrinth, you will see the palace as it may have been at its height.","Grove of Rhea","The foundations of the house of Rhea","The people of Knossos show these foundations, in the middle of a very old cypress grove, and say they were the house of Rhea, the mother of Zeus. The Curetes danced, beating their shields so that Cronus would not hear him cry. That is how the cave of Mount Ida and that of Mount Dicte were revered; both received offerings from the Bronze Age onwards. This is a small grotto on the coast; the great cave of Ida is inland: follow the post “The road to Ida”.","Shrine of the head of Orpheus","According to tradition, Orpheus' head came singing to this coast at Antissa and was buried in a cave, where it gave oracles. The lyre, they say, was offered in a temple of Apollo.","Temple of Apollo (Lesbos)","The island of poets","Lesbos gave Greece some of its great musicians and poets: Terpander, who according to tradition gave the lyre seven strings; Arion of Methymna; Alcaeus and Sappho of Mytilene, who around 600 wrote poems in their Aeolic dialect to be sung to the lyre. For the opening of the Flavian Amphitheatre in 80 he wrote the Book of Spectacles, short epigrams celebrating Titus' games: beast hunts, combats and mythological scenes in the arena. His epigrams portray daily life in Rome with humour and bite.","Ah, another stranger come to see the games! I'm Marcus Valerius Martialis, from Bilbilis, in Hispania, though I've been in Rome for sixteen years. I write epigrams: short poems with a sting in the tail. These days I'm writing about what goes on in there: the biggest amphitheatre the world has ever seen.","What are you writing?","A little book for the opening games: a hundred days of shows paid for by the emperor Titus. A poem for each marvel: an elephant kneeling before Caesar, a rhinoceros tossing a bull into the air, a woman fighting a lion… I begin by saying that the pyramids of Egypt and the walls of Babylon can fall silent: every human work yields to Caesar's amphitheatre.","What happened with Priscus and Verus?","Two gladiators fought with neither giving way, and the crowd called for their freedom. Titus had set a rule: fight until one raised his finger. But both raised it at the same moment, and Caesar gave them both the wooden sword, the rudis, and the palm of victory. I tell it in one of my epigrams. Priscus is out on the sand; ask him.","How does a poet live in Rome?","Badly, my friend. I get up at dawn to go and greet my patrons in a toga, which weighs a ton in summer, and in return they give me the sportula: a few coins or a bit of food. I live on a third floor on the Quirinal and climb a lot of stairs. The booksellers sell my books for five denarii and I don't see a single as. But everyone reads me.","For what occasion did Martial write the Book of Spectacles?","For Titus' opening of the Flavian Amphitheatre in AD 80","For Augustus' triumph after Actium","For Nero's funeral","No. The Book of Spectacles celebrates the opening games of the Flavian Amphitheatre, which Titus gave in AD 80.","Marcus Fabius Quintilianus","The education of the orator","In the Basilica Julia, in the Forum","Quintilian (c. 35-c. 100), born at Calagurris (Calahorra, Hispania), was the first teacher of rhetoric paid by the state, with a salary granted by Vespasian. He championed a complete education from childhood, without corporal punishment, to form the ideal orator: «a good man skilled in speaking». He set it out later in his Institutio Oratoria.","Welcome. I'm Marcus Fabius Quintilianus. I teach rhetoric here in Rome, and the emperor Vespasian granted me a salary of a hundred thousand sesterces a year, paid from the treasury: the first teacher paid by the state. My pupils go on to speak in these very courts of the Basilica Julia.","To speak well, which is the same as thinking well and living well. The perfect orator, said Cato, is a good man skilled in speaking. Technique isn't enough: you need to know everything, history, law, philosophy, poetry. We start with grammar and the poets; then come the exercises: narratives, praise speeches, speeches on invented cases. And a lot of memory work.","Do you beat your pupils?","Never. Flogging is for slaves and teaches nothing: it humiliates and hardens. A child learns through play and emulation, if the teacher knows how to awaken his ambition. And learning starts in the cradle: let the nurse speak well, let the paedagogus be educated. Speech faults learned as a child take years to undo.","Where does one speak in public in Rome?","Right here: the centumviral court, which tries inheritance cases, sits in the Basilica Julia. There are four courtrooms at once, and sometimes the audience applauds so loudly it can be heard next door. The Senate doesn't decide as much as it used to; since Augustus, the princeps is in charge. But in the courts words can still save or ruin a man.","Why was Quintilian's post a novelty?","He was the first teacher of rhetoric with a salary paid by the state","He was the first Roman to teach in Greek","He was the first senator to write poetry","No. Vespasian granted him a public salary: he was the first teacher of rhetoric in Rome paid from the treasury.","Flavius Josephus","Jewish historian","The Jewish War and the Temple of Peace","In the Temple of Peace, beside the fora","Josephus (37-c. 100), a priest of Jerusalem and rebel commander in Galilee, surrendered to Vespasian in 67 and foretold that he would be emperor. Freed and given the Flavian family name, he witnessed the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 and wrote The Jewish War in Rome. The objects from the Temple in Jerusalem, such as the seven-branched candlestick, were displayed in the Temple of Peace.","Shalom, stranger. I was called Yosef ben Matityahu, a priest of Jerusalem. After years at sea, by way of Carthage, where Queen Dido killed herself when he left her, he reached Latium. There he defeated King Turnus and married Lavinia. His son founded Alba Longa, and from his line Romulus and Remus would be born. That's why the Julian family, Caesar's and Augustus', claimed descent from Venus.","Virgil, Aeneid","Livy I 1-3","Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities I 45-64","The Aeneid, written in Augustus' time, gave the best-known form to a much older legend.","Romulus and Remus","Amulius, king of Alba Longa, forced his niece Rhea Silvia to become a Vestal so she would have no children. But Mars made her the mother of twins. Amulius ordered them thrown into the Tiber; the basket ran aground under a fig tree by the Palatine, and a she-wolf suckled them until the shepherd Faustulus took them in. Grown up, they restored their grandfather to the throne and decided to found a city. They argued over where: Romulus saw twelve vultures from the Palatine; Remus, six from the Aventine. Romulus ploughed the furrow for the wall and, when Remus jumped over it mockingly, killed him. It was 21 April 753 BC, by Varro's reckoning.","Livy I 3-7","Plutarch, Romulus 3-11","Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities I 76-88","The date of 753 BC is a scholarly calculation of the first century BC. Archaeology shows villages on the Palatine from the tenth-ninth century BC.","The rape of the Sabine women","Romulus' new city had men but few women, and the neighbouring peoples wouldn't marry their daughters to those fugitives. Romulus organised games in honour of Neptune and invited the Sabines with their families. At a signal, the young Romans carried off the girls. There was war; in the thick of battle in the valley of the Forum, the Sabine women, by now wives and mothers, threw themselves between their fathers and their husbands. Peace was made, and Romans and Sabines became one people.","Livy I 9-13","Plutarch, Romulus 14-19","Ovid, Fasti III 167-258","The Horatii and the Curiatii","In the time of King Tullus Hostilius, Rome and Alba Longa decided to settle their war with a combat: three twin brothers on each side, the Horatii for Rome and the Curiatii for Alba. Two Horatii died; the third, unhurt, pretended to flee, and the three wounded Curiatii chased him one by one. He killed them in turn. On his return, his sister, betrothed to one of the Curiatii, wept for him, and Horatius killed her. He was tried and acquitted by the people.","Livy I 24-26","Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities III 13-22","Lucretia and the end of the kings","Sextus, son of Rome's last king, Tarquin the Proud, raped Lucretia, wife of his cousin Collatinus. She summoned her father and her husband, told them what had happened, made them swear vengeance and stabbed herself. Lucius Junius Brutus drew the dagger from the wound and swore to drive out the Tarquins. The people rose, the king was exiled and in 509 BC Rome became a republic, governed by two consuls elected each year.","Livy I 57-60","Ovid, Fasti II 685-852","Modern historians debate how much of the end of the monarchy is historical.","Horatius Cocles and Mucius Scaevola","The kings had just been driven out when the Etruscan Porsenna attacked Rome to restore Tarquin to the throne. Horatius Cocles held the entrance to the Sublician bridge alone while his comrades demolished it behind him; then he leapt armed into the Tiber and swam to the bank. Next, the young Mucius slipped into the Etruscan camp to kill Porsenna, but killed his secretary by mistake. Captured, he thrust his right hand into an altar fire without flinching to show the courage of the Romans. Porsenna, impressed, let him go and made peace. From then on he was called Scaevola, «left-handed».","Livy II 10-13","Polybius VI 55","Rome in AD 80","In the year 80, Rome is the capital of an empire stretching from Britain to Syria and from the Rhine to the Sahara, with perhaps fifty or sixty million inhabitants. The city has close to a million: the largest in the Mediterranean world. For the past year it has been ruled by Titus, son of Vespasian, the general who won the civil war of 69 and founded the Flavian dynasty.","Sixteen years have passed since the great fire of 64, which destroyed much of the centre, and twelve since the death of Nero, the last emperor of Augustus' family. After a year of civil war, the year of the four emperors (Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian), the Flavians have presented themselves as restorers: they have given the grounds of Nero's Golden House back to the people and built the Flavian Amphitheatre and public baths on them.","The year 79 was terrible: in August (or perhaps October) Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum, and in 80 a new three-day fire burned the Capitol, the Pantheon and other buildings in the Campus Martius, and there was an epidemic. Titus responded with generosity and with shows: a hundred days of games to inaugurate the amphitheatre.","This is the Rome of Martial and his epigrams, of Quintilian and his school of rhetoric, of Flavius Josephus writing the Jewish War, of Pliny the Elder just dead and his nephew studying rhetoric, of Stoic philosophers like Musonius and Epictetus. The city is home to senators and fabulously rich freedmen, hundreds of thousands of poor people in rented flats, slaves from all over the empire, Jewish communities and the first Christians.","What is to come: Titus will die in September 81, aged 41. His brother Domitian will succeed him, rule for fifteen years, build the great palace on the Palatine and end up murdered in 96. Then will come Nerva, Trajan and Hadrian, and with them the empire's greatest extent.","Suetonius, Life of Titus","Cassius Dio, Roman History LXVI","Tacitus, Histories I 1-11",null,"M. Beard, SPQR: A History of Ancient Rome (2015)",null,"The exact date of the inaugural games and of the fire of 80 is not known for certain.","The city: fora, insulae and domus","Rome had no orderly plan like the new Greek cities. It grew among seven hills and the river Tiber, with narrow, winding streets. The political and religious centre was the Roman Forum, in the valley between the Capitol and the Palatine; beside it the emperors had built new forums: Caesar's, Augustus' and Vespasian's Temple of Peace.","Most Romans lived in insulae, rented apartment blocks of four or five storeys with shops on the ground floor. The rich lived in domus, single-family houses closed to the street, with atrium and peristyle, mostly on the hills (Palatine, Caelian, Aventine, Esquiline). A fourth-century catalogue counts some 46,000 insulae and 1,800 domus.","The Campus Martius, the plain beside the Tiber, had filled with great public buildings: the Theatre of Pompey, Agrippa's Pantheon, the Mausoleum of Augustus, the Ara Pacis, baths and porticoes. Across the river, Trastevere was a district of craftsmen, sailors and foreigners.","Water arrived through nine aqueducts, and there were hundreds of public fountains, latrines and baths. Since Augustus the city had been divided into fourteen regions and 265 neighbourhoods (vici), each with its magistrates and its altar to the Lares of the crossroads.","Strabo V 3.8 (description of Rome)","Suetonius, Augustus 28-30","The fourth-century Regionaries (Curiosum and Notitia)","F. Hornblower and A. Spawforth (eds.), The Oxford Classical Dictionary (2012)","Many dates of birth are approximate.","The reference coin was the sestertius, of brass. Four sesterces made a silver denarius, and twenty-five denarii a gold aureus. The as, of copper, was worth a quarter of a sestertius, and the quadrans a quarter of an as: the price of entry to the baths.","Some figures: a legionary was paid 1,200 sesterces a year under Domitian (before that, 900); a praetorian, about three times as much. To be a knight you needed 400,000 sesterces, and to be a senator, a million. Quintilian received 100,000 a year from the state. In Pompeii a cup of ordinary wine cost one as, and a loaf a few asses.","In the game, just as in Athens each lesson was paid in obols, in Rome you are paid in sesterces: three for each lesson passed, a little less than a legionary's daily pay.","Suetonius, Domitian 7.3 (rise in military pay)","Pliny the Elder, Natural History XXXIII 42-47","Price inscriptions from Pompeii, CIL IV",null,"Prices varied greatly by place and time.","The Roman calendar and festivals","Since Julius Caesar, Rome had used a solar calendar of 365 days, with an extra day every four years: the Julian calendar. Months had three fixed days: the calends (the first), the nones (the 5th or 7th) and the ides (the 13th or 15th). Years were named after the two consuls; the year 80 was the consulship of Titus (for the eighth time) and Domitian (for the seventh).","There were many festivals: the Lupercalia in February, with young men running round the Palatine lashing out with strips of hide; the Parilia on 21 April, Rome's birthday; the Saturnalia in December, when slaves sat at table and presents were exchanged; and the Roman, Plebeian, Apollinarian or Megalensian games (ludi), with races in the Circus and theatre.","The Romans divided the day into twelve hours from sunrise to sunset, longer in summer and shorter in winter. The game's clock uses an approximate hour.","Ovid, Fasti","Macrobius, Saturnalia I 12-16","Calendars in inscriptions (Fasti Praenestini)","How Rome was reconstructed","The layout of Rome mode roughly follows the archaeological plans: the Roman Forum between the Capitol and the Palatine, the imperial forums to the north, the Flavian Amphitheatre to the east, the Circus Maximus between the Palatine and the Aventine, and the Campus Martius to the north-west, by the bend of the Tiber. Distances are compressed and the hills simplified.","Some measurements used: Flavian Amphitheatre 188 x 156 m and about 48 m high, with 80 arches per storey and superimposed Tuscan, Ionic and Corinthian orders, and an attic with pilasters; arena about 83 x 48 m. Circus Maximus about 600 m long. Temple of Capitoline Jupiter about 53 x 62 m. Temple of Castor with eight Corinthian columns on the façade on a high podium. Temple of Saturn with Ionic columns on a podium of about 9 m.","The decoration follows the great reconstructions of imperial Rome, above all Italo Gismondi's model (Museo della Civiltà Romana) and the Rome Reborn project: the Forum and squares paved with travertine, the Forum of Augustus with coloured marbles, the main streets with basalt paving and raised pavements, statues in the pediments, on the attics and in the arches of the amphitheatre's second and third storeys, with bronze shields and the awning masts on its attic, honorific arches with quadrigas, rostral columns, the Golden Milestone, the Lacus Curtius and the Lapis Niger, public fountains, altars of the Lares at crossroads, wooden balconies on the insulae and milestones on the roads.","The houses are generic models: brick insulae with shops below and domus closed to the street with roofs sloping towards the atrium. The trees are mainly stone pines and cypresses, though the stone pine spread especially in later periods.","Forma Urbis Romae (marble plan from the time of Septimius Severus)",null,null,"Rome Reborn project (B. Its main licences:","<b>Dates.</b> Things that happened throughout the year 80 have been brought together in a single moment: the amphitheatre's inaugural games, the Capitol and Pantheon intact (the fire of 80 damaged them) and the newly opened Baths of Titus. Work on Domitian's palace on the Palatine began a little later.","<b>Characters.</b> Martial, Quintilian, Flavius Josephus, Epictetus, Musonius Rufus, Frontinus, Pliny the Younger, Tacitus, Dio of Prusa, Sulpicia, Rabirius, Atrectus, Priscus and Cornelia are historical, though we don't always know whether they were in Rome in 80. Hermeros, Lucius Fabius, Marcus Valerius Pudens, Felix, Tiberius Claudius Eutyches, Secundus, Aulus Sempronius, the augur, Junia, Asclepiades, Aurelia, Lucius Vibius and Ambivius are invented.","<b>City.</b> Distances are compressed, the hills simplified and many streets and minor buildings left out. The insulae and domus are repeated models. The traditional date, 24 August, is disputed today: several clues point to October.","Have you come from Rome? Then you know about Pompeii. I'm Numerius, a fuller, or I was: my workshop lies under five metres of pumice. I live here in Neapolis, at a cousin's house. Ask, if you like. Sometimes talking helps.","What was the eruption like?","There had been tremors for days, but here the earth shakes often: seventeen years ago an earthquake brought down half the city and we were still repairing it. At midday the mountain split open and a huge cloud rose up, like a pine tree. Little white stones began to fall, light ones, without stopping, and it became night. Roofs caved in under the weight. I took my wife and children and we fled towards Nuceria with pillows tied to our heads. The next day clouds of fire came down. Those who stayed never got out.","What has the emperor done?","Titus has appointed two former consuls to restore Campania and has given the money of the dead who left no heirs to help those of us who are left. This year he came himself. Many of us have settled here, in Neapolis, in Puteoli or in Nola. Some go back to dig tunnels in the ash to get out what they can: statues, money, the stones of the temples. Pompeii won't be rebuilt.","What was Pompeii like?","A cheerful city: wine, fish sauce, cloth. We had the oldest stone amphitheatre, and because of a brawl there with the people of Nuceria, twenty years ago, the Senate banned games for ten years. On the walls we painted the names of election candidates in red, and people wrote everything: love notes, insults, accounts, lines of Virgil. All of that is down there.","Who died in the eruption of Vesuvius while trying to rescue the people of the bay?","Pliny the Elder","Seneca","Virgil","No. Pliny the Elder, admiral of the fleet at Misenum, died at Stabiae; his nephew tells the story.","Marcus Pactumeius","Shipowner of Brundisium","Travelling by sea in the Empire","In the harbour of Brundisium","In the Empire people travelled by sea on cargo ships, paying for passage, sleeping on deck and bringing their own food. The sailing season ran from spring to autumn. Brundisium was the great port for the East: from there you crossed in a day to Dyrrachium or Apollonia, in Epirus, and carried on overland along the Via Egnatia. Goods travelled in amphorae, and the State hired private shipowners to carry grain to Rome.","Greetings. Marcus Pactumeius, shipowner. I have two ships and half of another, which I share with a partner. If you're looking for passage to Greece, you'll have to wait for a west wind. If you're looking for Apulian wool, you've come to the right place.","What's a voyage on your ship like?","Don't expect a cabin: passengers sleep on deck, under an awning if it rains. Everyone brings their own food and blanket, and pays according to the destination. On the stern we carry the image of the ship's protecting god, and before sailing we make a sacrifice. If there's a storm, the cargo goes overboard. Twenty years ago a ship carrying a Jew from Tarsus to Rome, a man called Paul, was wrecked on Melita after fourteen days adrift. Everyone was saved, they say.","What cargo do you carry?","To Greece, wool from Apulia and Tarentum, wine, oil. On the way back I bring marble, wine from the islands, sometimes slaves. But the big business is grain for Rome: Claudius promised privileges to shipowners who built ships for grain, and that the State would pay for losses in storms. That's why there are so many new ships.","Why is Brundisium so important?","Because from here Greece is a day away. We also sell olive oil, red pottery and wild beasts for the games.","Who took and destroyed Carthage in 146 BC?","Scipio Aemilianus","Scipio Africanus","Julius Caesar","No. It was Scipio Aemilianus, adoptive grandson of Africanus, who had defeated Hannibal at Zama in 202.","Phileros","Atriensis, slave in charge of the house","The Roman domus","In the domus on the Caelian, beside the impluvium","The domus was the single-family house of well-off families. From the street you entered through the fauces into the atrium, with its compluvium and impluvium, around which opened the cubicula, the alae and the owner's tablinum. Behind it, the peristyle, a garden surrounded by porticoes, gave light to the most private rooms: the triclinium, where people dined reclining, the bedrooms and the kitchen. The walls were painted in fresco and the floors covered with mosaics. The house was home to the family in the Roman sense: the father, his wife, the children, the slaves and the freedmen. In Rome most people did not live in a domus but in rented flats in the insulae.","Salve. I'm Phileros, the atriensis: the slave who looks after my master's house, Lucius Caecilius Rufus. I open and lock up, I keep an eye on the other slaves and make sure nobody touches the strongbox. If you like, I'll show you round. My master loves people to admire it.","What is the salutatio?","Every morning at sunrise my master's clients queue in the street, in their togas, to greet him here in the atrium. He receives them in order of importance, listens to their requests and gives them the sportula, a few coins or some food. In return they escort him to the Forum and applaud when he speaks. The more clients, the more important the patron looks. Martial complains in his epigrams about how humiliating it is.","Who lives in this house?","The family, in the Roman sense: the master, who is the paterfamilias and has authority over everyone; his wife, his children and the master's widowed mother; and some thirty slaves: cooks, doorkeepers, hairdressers, a Greek secretary, the children's tutor, the nurse. And a few freedmen, who still live and work here. The upper floors and the shops we rent out to other families.","Do all Romans live like this?","Not at all! In Rome there are about two thousand domus and more than forty thousand blocks of flats, the insulae. Most people rent one or two rooms, with no kitchen and no water, afraid of fires and collapses. The poets complain that in Rome you sleep badly and pay dearly. This house is a luxury for very few.","What was the name of the basin in the atrium that collected rainwater?","The impluvium","The peristyle","The triclinium","No. The impluvium is the basin in the atrium; the compluvium is the opening in the roof through which the rain falls.","Pomponia","Pronuba of the wedding","The Roman wedding","At the door of the house of the Valerii, on the Caelian","Roman marriage was a private agreement: all it took was the will of both to live as husband and wife and the consent of their fathers. In the 1st century almost all marriages were sine manu: the wife remained under her father's authority and kept her own property, and the dowry went back to her family if there was a divorce, which was easy. The wedding had well-known rites: the hairstyle of six braids and the flame-coloured veil (flammeum), the auspices, the dowry contract, the joining of right hands before the pronuba, the banquet, the night procession to the groom's house with torches, nuts and Fescennine verses, and the entry into the new home: anointing the doorposts, being carried over the threshold and receiving water and fire.","Salve. I am Pomponia, and at this wedding I am the pronuba, the matron who accompanies the bride. Tomorrow Valeria, the daughter of Marcus Valerius, marries Quintus, the son of Lucius Caecilius Rufus, who owns the big house on this very street. Would you like to come? You will see everything, from the eve until the following day.","What does a pronuba do?","A pronuba is a matron who has married only once and whose husband is still alive: it is an honour and a good omen. I join the bride and groom's right hands, I go with the bride to her new home and take her to the bedroom. I have been married to the same man for thirty years, imagine that!","How is a wedding arranged?","First, the betrothal: the fathers promise their children, sometimes while they are still small, and the groom gives the bride a ring, which she wears on the ring finger of her left hand; they say a nerve runs from that finger straight to the heart. Girls can marry from the age of twelve and boys from fourteen, but in good families it is usual for her to be fifteen or eighteen and him about twenty-five.","On which day do people marry?","Not just any day. You must avoid the Kalends, the Nones, the Ides and the day after each of them, the whole month of May (\"bad women marry in May\", as the saying goes) and the first half of June, while the temple of Vesta is being cleaned. After 15 June, on the other hand, it is a very good time. Widows prefer holidays, when there are few people about.","And if the marriage goes wrong?","They divorce, and it is no scandal at all: it is enough for one of them to tell the other with the formula \"keep your things to yourself\". The husband returns the dowry and the children stay with the father. What is frowned upon is not marrying: Augustus's laws penalise bachelors and those without children.","What did the pronuba do at a Roman wedding?","She joined the right hands of the bride and groom","She read the entrails of the victim","She carried the torch of the procession","No. That was done by the auspex and one of the boys in the procession. The Luperci sacrifice a goat and a dog in the cave of the Lupercal, dress in strips of hide and run half-naked around the Palatine, striking everyone they meet. Women put themselves in their path, because they say it will help them have children. More than a century ago, at this festival, Mark Antony offered Caesar a king's diadem. Caesar refused it. A month later they killed him.","Is it true that you give oracles?","In the grove of Albunea, beside a sulphurous spring. Whoever consults me sacrifices a sheep, sleeps on its fleece and hears my voice in dreams. That is how King Latinus asked what to do about his daughter Lavinia, and I told him to marry her to a foreigner. That foreigner was Aeneas.","Do you have a family?","I'm the son of Picus, the woodpecker, and grandson of Saturn. My son was King Latinus. Some say there are many fauns and not just one, as there are many satyrs in Greece. I've never cleared that up. A little mystery suits a god of the woods.","Visit the Lupercal, the she-wolf's cave, on the slope of the Palatine.","Go to the Lupercal, the cave where the she-wolf suckled the twins, at the foot of the Palatine. That's where my runs begin. Listen carefully: you may hear my voice.","The Lupercal is on the south-west slope of the Palatine, near the Circus Maximus.","Did you hear anything? No? Well, I heard you. Heh, heh. Here.","Silvanus","god of woods and of field boundaries","in the woods east of the city","Hail. Silvanus, of the woods. I have no great temples or priests in purple: farmers, slaves, woodcutters and shepherds honour me with a little milk, some grapes and a prayer beside a tree. And women aren't admitted to my rites, mind you.","Who honours you?","Humble people. Cato explained how to offer me a sacrifice for the health of the oxen: in the woods, by day, with flour, bacon and wine, and with no women present. Many slaves and freedmen dedicate little altars to me with their names on them. I'm a god who doesn't ask for much, and so they ask a lot of me.","What do you protect?","Woods, flocks, gardens and above all the boundaries of fields. The surveyors say there are three Silvanuses: the one of the house, the one of the field and the one who guards the boundary between two estates. If you move a boundary stone, you'll answer to me and to Terminus.","Are you like any Greek god?","Not quite. Sometimes they compare me with Pan, because of the woods, but I'm more serious. Virgil says the ancient inhabitants of Latium consecrated a grove and a feast day to me as \"god of fields and cattle\". I'm as old as the first trees of Italy.","Travel to Samnium, to Saepinum, among mountains and flocks.","Go to the mountains of Samnium, to Saepinum, where the shepherds drive their flocks along the grassy drove roads. Here.","Fortuna","goddess of luck","beside the Via Portuensis, across the Tiber","Hail. I am Fortuna, she who gives and she who takes. I have a hundred names: Fortune of the Roman People, Fortune of Women, Fortuna Primigenia at Praeneste… Here, by the river, King Servius Tullius built me a temple: he was born a slave and became a king. Who better to worship me?","What is the festival of Fors Fortuna?","In June the people sail down the Tiber in boats decked with garlands to my temples on this bank, and come back singing and rather drunk. It's a festival of ordinary people, craftsmen and slaves, in memory of Servius, the king who was born a slave. That day no one is ashamed of where they come from.","What is at Praeneste?","My most famous sanctuary, in Latium: a whole mountainside turned into terraces, ramps and porticoes, up to my temple at the top. There I give oracles by lots: oak tablets with ancient words, drawn from a box by a child. Many people climb up to ask me about their future. I answer, but not always clearly.","Are you the same as Tyche?","The Greeks call me Tyche. They paint me with a rudder, because I steer men's lives; with a horn full of fruit, because I give wealth; and sometimes with a wheel, because everything turns: whoever is on top today will be at the bottom tomorrow. The emperors treat me with great respect.
