dog\"","Through this narrow passage, the fauces, you enter from the street. To one side, in his little room, lives the doorkeeper (ostiarius), often chained to the door, with a dog. On the floor a mosaic warns: CAVE CANEM, \"beware of the dog\". In Pompeii there is one just like it in the House of the Tragic Poet. On either side of the entrance the house rents out two shops (tabernae) facing the street.","The atrium and the impluvium","The heart of the house. The roof slopes inwards and leaves an opening in the middle, the compluvium, through which light and rain come in; the water falls into the impluvium, the marble basin, and is stored in a cistern. Here every morning the master receives his clients at the salutatio. Beside the impluvium stands the marble table (cartibulum), and in a corner the iron-and-bronze strongbox with the family's money, in full view of everyone.","The lararium","The altar of the household gods. Painted on the wall: the two Lares, young men dancing with drinking horns in their hands, and between them the Genius of the master, with his toga over his head, making a sacrifice; below, a snake, guardian of the house. Every day they are offered incense, wine or part of the meal, and on feast days, garlands.","The alae and the ancestors","In these alae, open to the atrium, noble families keep in cupboards the wax masks of those ancestors who held office, with their names and posts written underneath. At funerals actors wear them so that the illustrious dead escort the deceased. Polybius was impressed: \"There is no finer sight for an ambitious young man.\"","The cubiculum","Bedrooms are small, dark and without windows onto the street: a wooden bed with a wool mattress, a chest and an oil lamp. The walls are painted with light panels. Rich Romans spend little time in them: they are for sleeping, for keeping things and, sometimes, for receiving a friend in private.","The tablinum","Between the atrium and the peristyle is the master's office, the tablinum, open at front and back: from the street door you can see the whole house in a line, a view designed to impress. Here the family's accounts and documents are kept and the master deals with his business. A curtain or wooden screens close it off when needed.","The wall paintings","The walls are painted in fresco in the fashionable style that historians will call the \"Fourth Style\": a dark dado, large red, black or yellow panels with a small scene in the middle, and between them fantastic architecture, as delicate as a toy. The colours are expensive: cinnabar red comes from the mines of Hispania. The painter Fabullus decorated Nero's Domus Aurea this way.","The floors","Each room has its own floor: black-and-white mosaics with geometric patterns in the atrium and the tablinum, opus signinum floors (lime and crushed brick, reddish, inlaid with white tesserae) in the service rooms and the porticoes, and in the triclinium a coloured emblema in the middle, made of tiny tesserae, like a painting in stone.","Behind, the most private part of the house: a garden surrounded by columns, in the Greek manner. There are beds with box hedges, roses, laurel and herbs, a fountain with a statue and sometimes aviaries. The surrounding rooms open onto the porticoes for light and air. Here the family strolls, the children play and people dine in summer.","The dining room. Three couches in a U shape around a table: the diners eat reclining on their left elbow, three to a couch, and the place of honour is on the middle couch. The slaves serve from the open side. A dinner with guests has starters (gustatio), several main courses and dessert, with wine mixed with water. The women of the family recline too.","The kitchen and the latrine","A small, smoky kitchen: a masonry hearth where food is cooked on trivets over charcoal or wood, an oven for bread, amphorae of oil and wine and clay pots. Next to it, the latrine, connected to the sewer or to a cesspit. The household slaves work here; the owners hardly ever come in.","Stairs and shops","The stairs lead to the upper floors, the cenacula, which the owner rents out with their own entrance. The two shops on the façade are rented too: a tavern selling wine and hot food, and a workshop. The houses of the rich are surrounded by businesses and poor neighbours: in Rome, rich and poor live wall to wall.","Theatre of Neapolis","Temple of the Dioscuri","Forum of Neapolis","Pompeii, buried","Beneath this grey plain lies Pompeii, a city of some twelve thousand people, buried under four to six metres of pumice and ash. Only the highest roofs and a few columns poke out. The survivors dig tunnels to recover what they can. Titus has appointed two former consuls \"commissioners for the restoration of Campania\" and has given the victims the property of those who died without heirs. This year the emperor himself has come to the area.","Vesuvius","A little more than a year ago, at the end of summer or in the autumn of 79, the mountain, covered in vineyards, exploded. A column of smoke and stones rose into the sky and burning clouds swept down its slopes: Pompeii, Herculaneum, Stabiae and Oplontis vanished. Pliny the Elder, admiral of the fleet at Misenum, died at Stabiae while going to the rescue of the inhabitants. His nephew, Pliny the Younger, will tell the story in two letters to the historian Tacitus.","The \"new city\" was founded by the Greeks of Cumae more than five centuries ago, and here people still speak Greek, hold games in the Greek manner, the Sebasta, and study rhetoric and philosophy. Many rich Romans have their country villas here. In this theatre Nero made his debut as a singer in 64: an earthquake shook the building, which collapsed just after the audience had left.","The tomb of Virgil","On the road from Neapolis to Puteoli, less than two miles out, is the tomb of Virgil, who lived here for many years and wrote the Georgics here. His epitaph reads: \"Mantua bore me, the Calabrians snatched me away, now Parthenope holds me; I sang of pastures, fields and leaders.\"","Ash still falls in my hair when the wind blows from the east.","My cousin lived in Herculaneum. We've heard nothing of him.","Here we speak Greek at home and Latin in the forum.","Families have come from Pompeii with nothing. The emperor sends money, but it isn't enough.","Warehouses","Temple of Brundisium","Forum of Brundisium","The harbour of Brundisium","The best harbour in Italy for the East: an arm of the sea that forks like a stag's antlers (that is what its name means in Messapian). From here ships sail to Dyrrachium and Apollonia, in Epirus, a day's sailing, and from there the Via Egnatia runs on to Byzantium. Governors, soldiers and merchants bound for Greece and Asia all pass through here.","The end of the Appian Way","Here ends the Appian Way, begun by Appius Claudius in 312 BC as far as Capua and later extended to this port. The poet Horace told the story of his journey from Rome to Brundisium in 37 BC with humour: cheating innkeepers, mosquitoes, frogs and a kitchen fire that nearly burned down the inn.","Here Virgil died","In September of 19 BC Virgil landed here ill, on his way back from Greece, and died a few days later. He had asked for the Aeneid, which he had not finished polishing, to be burned. Augustus forbade it and had it published. He was buried in Neapolis.","Calabria, the heel of Italy","In your time Calabria is not the toe of Italy but the heel, the land of the Messapians and of Tarentum, the old colony founded by the Spartans. The toe is Bruttium. Around here was born the poet Ennius, who said he had three hearts because he spoke Greek, Oscan and Latin; and here was born Pacuvius, his nephew. Apulia is sheep country: the wool of Tarentum and Canusium is famous.","A ship sails for Dyrrachium tomorrow, if the wind allows.","My sheep spend the summer in the mountains of Samnium and the winter here.","Ennius came from near here: he spoke three languages and said he had three hearts.","Everyone coming back from Greece lands here, telling of wonders.","Temple of Hera (the oldest)","Second temple of Hera","Temple of Athena","Temple of the forum of Paestum","Forum of Paestum","The temples of Poseidonia","Three great Doric temples built by the Greeks of Sybaris, who founded Poseidonia, the city of Poseidon, here around 600 BC. The oldest has nine columns across its front, which is very unusual. Its columns swell in the middle and its capitals are as wide as tables. They were probably dedicated to Hera and Athena. When you see them, they are already older than the Roman Republic itself.","From Poseidonia to Paestum","Around 400 BC the Lucanians, an Italic mountain people, took over the Greek city. A Greek writer told how the Poseidoniates met once a year to mourn, in Greek, the language and customs they had lost. In 273 BC Rome founded a Latin colony here, Paestum, which stayed loyal even while Hannibal roamed Italy.","The roses of Paestum","Virgil and Propertius sang of the rose gardens of Paestum, which bloom twice a year. The roses are sold in Rome for crowns, perfumes and banquets, and for the garlands of the gods.","Lucania and Bruttium","Further south, the toe of Italy is Bruttium, a land of forests: pitch from the Sila mountains caulks the ships of half the Empire. There lies Rhegium, beside the strait where sailors say Scylla and Charybdis live. The Bruttii went over to Hannibal, and Rome punished them: for a long time they served as attendants to the magistrates.","The roses here bloom twice a year. We sell them in Rome.","These temples were already old when Hannibal passed through.","In summer the plain fills with mosquitoes. Better to live on the hill.","Pitch from the Sila caulks half the Empire.","Forum of Saepinum","Basilica of Saepinum","Theatre of Saepinum","Sanctuary of Pietrabbondante","A small town in a mountain valley, in the heart of old Samnium. Its towered walls were paid for by Tiberius and his brother Drusus in the time of Augustus, as the inscription on the gates says, where there are statues of captive barbarians. Inside: a forum, a basilica, a theatre, baths, shops. Everything you need to live as in Rome, but with more sheep.","The drove road","The main street of Saepinum is also a drove road: every autumn thousands of sheep come down it from the mountains of Samnium to the winter pastures of Apulia, and in spring they go back up. The flocks belong to great landowners, sometimes to the emperor himself, and the shepherds are often slaves.","The Samnite Wars","The Samnites were Rome's toughest enemies in Italy: three wars, between 343 and 290 BC. In 321 they trapped a Roman army in the Caudine Forks and made it pass under the yoke, a humiliation Rome never forgot. In 82 BC Sulla defeated them at the gates of Rome and took his revenge with massacres.","The Samnite sanctuary","On that summit stands the great sanctuary of the Samnites, with a temple and a theatre together, where the leaders of their league used to meet. It was abandoned after the Social War, when the Samnites fought Rome for citizenship. Today hardly anyone goes up there.","My grandfather still spoke Oscan at home.","The flocks go down to Apulia in autumn and pass right by the town gate.","Here there's no sea and no great lords: stones, sheep and cold.","The emperor's tax collectors count sheep better than we do.","Temple of Asculum","Forum of Asculum","Asculum and the Social War","In 91 BC the people of Asculum killed the Roman magistrate and every Roman in the city in the theatre: so began the Social War, fought by the peoples of Italy who wanted Roman citizenship. Pompeius Strabo, father of Pompey the Great, took the city in 89 after a long siege. Rome won the war, but ended up granting citizenship to almost all Italians.","The captive boy who became consul","Among the prisoners from Asculum paraded in the triumph of Pompeius Strabo was a boy, Publius Ventidius. As a man he was a mule-driver for the army, won Caesar's trust, became consul and in 38 BC defeated the Parthians. He was the first Roman to celebrate a triumph over them: he had entered Rome as a captive in a triumph and returned as the triumphant general.","The Via Salaria","Along this road the Sabines carried salt inland from the mouth of the Tiber, hence its name. Today it links Rome with Asculum and the Adriatic. The bridge over the river Truentus dates from the time of Augustus.","The Picentes and the woodpecker","According to legend, the ancestors of the Picentes came here from Sabine country, guided by a woodpecker, the picus, the bird of Mars: hence their name. Picenum is olive country, and its olives are served at the finest tables in Rome.","The olives of Picenum are the best: ask at any table in Rome.","The woodpecker guided our ancestors here.","My great-grandfather saw the city burn in the war against Rome. Now we're more Roman than anyone.","The travertine from our quarries is as good as the stone of Tibur.","Forum of Ariminum","Temple of Ariminum","The Arch of Augustus",null,"The Senate dedicated this arch to Augustus in 27 BC, when he restored the Via Flaminia and the main roads of Italy. Here ends the Flaminia, which comes from Rome. In the medallions: Jupiter, Apollo, Neptune and the goddess Roma.","The bridge of Tiberius","Five arches of Istrian stone over the river Ariminus. Augustus began it in AD 14 and Tiberius finished it in 21. From here the Via Aemilia sets out for Placentia, across the plain of the Po. This bridge will still be in use two thousand years later.","A few miles to the north runs the Rubicon, a stream that marked the border between Italy and the province of Cisalpine Gaul. A general could not cross it with his army. Caesar crossed it in January of 49 BC saying, according to Suetonius, \"the die is cast\", and the civil war began. It is said that he addressed his soldiers in the forum of Ariminum.","Umbrians and Gauls","The Umbrians were an ancient mountain people; at Iguvium they keep bronze tablets with their rites written in their own language. This coast, on the other hand, belonged to the Senones Gauls until Rome defeated them in 283 BC: that's why it's called the \"Gallic land\". Ariminum has been a Latin colony since 268.","Here the Flaminia ends and the Aemilia begins: everyone passes through Ariminum.","They say Caesar spoke to his soldiers in this very forum.","Fish from the Adriatic is better than fish from the Tiber.","Ships leave the harbour for Istria and Dalmatia.","Painted tomb","The painted tombs","On this hill, facing the city, the Etruscans of Tarquinii buried their dead for centuries in chambers cut into the rock, under earthen mounds. The walls of many are painted: banquets, musicians, dancers, athletic games, hunts. Go into this one: the ancestors are still feasting, for ever. Some families still honour their dead here.","The haruspices","The Etruscans are the masters of the \"Etruscan discipline\": they know how to read the will of the gods in the livers of sacrificed animals and in lightning. Rome still consults their haruspices, and the emperor Claudius, who wrote twenty books of Etruscan history, reorganised their college of sixty. The haruspex Spurinna, from a family of this town, warned Caesar about the Ides of March.","The city of the Tarquins","From here came Lucumo, son of a Corinthian noble who had taken refuge in Etruria; he went to Rome with his wife Tanaquil and became King Tarquinius Priscus. His family gave Rome its last king, Tarquin the Proud. Tarquinii was one of the great cities of the Etruscan league; today it is a quiet Roman municipality.","The great temple","My family has been Etruscan since before Rome. We still read the books of lightning.","In the ancestors' tombs there are painted banquets that never end.","Few speak Etruscan any more. The old people, and the haruspices.","The wine of Graviscae, the port, is thin; the oil is good.","Forum of Mutina","Temple of Mutina","The Via Aemilia","The consul Marcus Aemilius Lepidus laid it out in 187 BC, straight as a ruler, from Ariminum to Placentia on the banks of the Po: some 260 kilometres. Along it colonies were founded every few days' journey: Bononia, Mutina, Parma, Regium. The whole region has taken its name from it.","The gridded fields","When a colony is founded, the surveyors divide the land with the groma into great squares of twenty actus, about 710 metres on a side, separated by straight roads: the cardines and the decumani. Each square is shared among a hundred plots. Two thousand years later, these squares will still be visible from the air on the plain of the Po.","The War of Mutina","In 43 BC, after Caesar's murder, Mark Antony besieged Decimus Brutus here. The Senate, spurred on by Cicero's speeches, sent the two consuls, Hirtius and Pansa, and the young Octavian against him. Antony was defeated, but both consuls died, and Octavian kept their armies: it was the first step towards his power.","The wool of Mutina","A Roman colony since 183 BC, Mutina lives from its fields and livestock. Its white, fine wool is famous in Rome, like that of Parma. On the plain they also raise the pigs that feed the city of Rome.","Since they laid out the fields in squares, everyone knows where his own land ends.","The wool of Mutina is as white as can be.","Legions pass along the Aemilia on their way to the Rhine and the Danube.","My grandfather received his plot of land when he was discharged from the legion.","Temple of Genua","The bronze tablet of the Polcevera","In 117 BC the people of Genua and their neighbours in the Polcevera valley were quarrelling over some land. The Senate sent two brothers, the Minucii Rufi, who gave a ruling: which fields were public, how much wine and grain was paid for them and where the boundaries ran, from stone to stone. It was engraved in bronze. It will be found in 1506, and is one of the oldest documents about the Italian countryside.","The harbour of the Ligurians, Rome's ally of old. The Carthaginians destroyed it in 205 BC and the Romans rebuilt it. Timber, livestock, honey and hides come down here from the mountains, and oil and wine arrive from the south.","The Ligurians","The mountain Ligurians resisted Rome for more than a century. Diodorus says they live off a poor land that has to be broken by force, that the women work like the men and that they are small, lean and extremely tough. Their hillsides are cut into dry-stone terraces.","The Ligurian coast","The Via Aurelia, which leaves Rome along the coast of Etruria, runs on to here and continues towards Gaul along a coast of cliffs. Augustus extended it as the Via Julia Augusta and defeated the last peoples of the Alps: at La Turbie, above the sea, stands his trophy.","In our mountains you don't farm: you tear the soil from the rock, terrace by terrace.","Ligurian timber makes the best ships.","Those of us on the coast are sailors; those in the mountains are as tough as their oaks.","In winter the harbour fills with ships waiting for good weather.","Arena of Verona","Theatre of Verona","Forum of Verona","Capitol of Verona","The arena of Verona","A great amphitheatre of pink Valpolicella stone, built about fifty years ago, outside the walls: it holds some thirty thousand people, more than there are Veronese in the city. People come from all the towns around to watch the gladiator fights and the beast hunts.","The city of Catullus","Here, around 84 BC, was born the poet Catullus, who in Rome fell in love with a woman he called Lesbia and wrote her verses still recited today: \"I hate and I love. Perhaps you ask why I do it. I don't know, but I feel it happening, and I am in torment.\" His family had a villa on Lake Benacus, at Sirmio.","Patavium and Aquileia","To the east lie Patavium, where Livy, the great historian of Rome, was born (Asinius Pollio mocked his Paduan accent), and Aquileia, a colony since 181 BC and the great port of the Adriatic: the amber of the Baltic arrives there. Further on, in Istria, Pola also has its amphitheatre, which is being enlarged.","Veneti","The Veneti","The Veneti, Rome's allies of old against the Gauls, claimed descent from the Eneti of Paphlagonia who came with Antenor after the Trojan War. They were famous horse breeders: a Spartan won at Olympia with Venetic horses, according to Strabo.","The arena holds more Veronese than live in Verona.","Venetic horses won races even at Olympia.","Amber from the north reaches Aquileia and from there all Italy.","Catullus was from here. My grandmother knew his most indecent verses by heart.","Forum of Comum","Temple of Comum","Villa by the lake","Comum and Lake Larius","Novum Comum was founded by Caesar in 59 BC with five thousand colonists, among them five hundred distinguished Greeks. It stands at the tip of Lake Larius, long and narrow between mountains, along which you sail towards the Alpine passes. The town's rich men have villas on its shores.","Here, around AD 23, was born Gaius Plinius Secundus: soldier, lawyer, procurator, admiral and above all a tireless reader. He wrote a Natural History in thirty-seven books about everything known of the world, which he dedicated to Titus three years ago. He died last year in the eruption of Vesuvius, because he wanted to see it up close and help those who were fleeing.","His nephew and heir, Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus, was born here around 61. He is now about eighteen and studies rhetoric in Rome with Quintilian. He will be a lawyer, consul and governor, and will leave ten books of letters, in which he will speak of his villas on the lake: one he will call \"Tragedy\" and the other \"Comedy\".","The Transpadanes","The peoples north of the Po received Latin rights in 89 BC and full Roman citizenship in 49, thanks to Caesar. The great city of the region is Mediolanum, on the plain. To the north, over the Alps, the roads lead to Raetia and Gaul; Augustus defeated the Salassi and founded Augusta Praetoria to guard the passes.","The lake is so long its two shores seem like two countries.","The Plinies are from here: the uncle and the nephew.","From Mediolanum to the Alpine passes is only a few days; from there, Gaul.","In winter a wind comes down from the north that cuts your face.","Temple of Augustus (Tarraco)","Theatre of Tarraco","Forum of the colony","Tarraco, capital of Nearer Hispania","The Scipio brothers landed here in 218 BC, at the start of the war against Hannibal, and made it their base. Today it is a colony and capital of the largest province in the Empire, which stretches from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic. The governor lives here. Augustus spent the winter of 26-25 BC here, ill, during the war against the Cantabri.","The temple of Augustus","In AD 15, shortly after his death, the people of Hispania asked Tiberius for permission to build a temple here to the divine Augustus. It was the first of its kind in the West, as Tacitus says, and served as an example to other provinces. Here the delegates of the province's cities meet every year.","The provincial forum, under construction","The Flavian emperors are turning the upper part of the city into a great terraced complex for the imperial cult and the meetings of the province: at the top, the temple; in the middle, a huge colonnaded square; below, a circus for the races. The work will go on for years yet.","The walls of the Scipios","The walls of the upper town were built during the war against Hannibal and enlarged soon afterwards: at the base there are huge unworked blocks, on which they built with dressed stone. The Romans made them with the labour of the local Iberians.","The governor is back from inspecting the mines in the north. He's in a bad mood.","Delegates come here from every city in the province, from Gallaecia to Carthago Nova.","Tarraco wine is drunk in Rome, even if they boast about their Falernian there.","They say the new forum will be the biggest in Hispania.","Capitol of Carthago","Forum of Carthago","Amphitheatre of Carthago","The Byrsa and the Capitol","The Byrsa was the citadel of Punic Carthage. According to legend, Queen Dido, fleeing from Tyre, asked the local king for as much land as an ox hide could cover; she cut it into very thin strips and surrounded the whole hill with them. The Romans levelled the summit, burying the Punic houses beneath the fill, and built the colony's forum, basilica and Capitol on top.","The harbours of Carthage","Carthage had two connected harbours: a rectangular one for merchant ships and, behind it, a circular one for the war fleet, with an island in the middle where the admiral lived and slipways for some two hundred and twenty ships around it. Today they are used by the grain ships: according to Flavius Josephus, Africa feeds Rome eight months of the year.","Carthage must be destroyed","Cato the Elder ended every speech in the Senate with the same sentence: \"Furthermore, I think Carthage must be destroyed.\" In 146 BC, after a three-year siege, Scipio Aemilianus took the city, burned it and razed it; the survivors were sold as slaves. The idea that the Romans sowed its fields with salt is a modern invention: no ancient author says so.","The tophet","Beside the harbour lies the old sacred precinct of Baal Hammon and Tanit, with thousands of urns and stelae. The urns hold the burned bones of small children and of animals. Greeks and Romans accused the Carthaginians of sacrificing their children; historians today debate whether all of them were sacrifices. The gods have not left: Baal Hammon is now called Saturn, and Tanit, Caelestis.","The colony of Caesar and Augustus","Gaius Gracchus tried to found a colony here in 122 BC, but failed. Julius Caesar planned it and Augustus founded it, with three thousand colonists and many people from the surrounding area. Today it is the capital of the province of Africa, where the proconsul lives, and one of the largest cities in the West.","The Punic people today","The city is Roman, but in homes and in the countryside many still speak the Punic language, the language of their Phoenician forebears. In the towns of the province there are inscriptions in Latin and Punic together, and families with old Phoenician names are Roman citizens today.","My grandmother still prays to Tanit, though she calls her Caelestis now.","In summer a grain ship leaves for Rome almost every day.","They say Hannibal was born in this city. It has walls, a forum and a grid of streets; it has fewer than five thousand inhabitants. It is smaller than Tarraco, but it has a good harbour and plenty of land.","At the top of Mons Taber, the temple of the imperial cult, surrounded by Corinthian columns. Four of them will still be standing twenty centuries later, hidden in a courtyard of the city.","The wine of the Laietani","The fields of the Laietani, the Iberians of this coast, are full of vineyards. Their wine is exported in amphorae to Gaul and to Rome, where it is cheap and plentiful. Now we're all Romans.","Forum of Emporiae","Basilica","Emporion, the Greek town","The Greeks of Phocaea, coming from Massalia, founded a trading post here around 575 BC, an emporion: hence the name. First on an islet and then in this small walled town beside the harbour, next to an Iberian village. For centuries they sold wine, oil and pottery to the Iberians in exchange for grain, metals and flax. Today the Greek town is half empty.","Here Rome landed","In 218 BC the commander Gnaeus Scipio landed here with his army to cut off Hannibal: it was the beginning of six centuries of Roman Hispania. In 195 Cato also landed here, and Livy describes the double town, Greek and Iberian, divided by a wall.","The Asclepius of Emporion","In the sanctuary of the Greek town stands the great statue of Asclepius, the god who heals, carved in Greek marble. The sick come to ask him for health, as at Epidaurus.","The Roman town","On the hill beside the Greek town, around 100 BC, the Romans built a new grid-planned town with a forum, a temple and houses with mosaics. Caesar settled his veterans here, and Augustus joined the two towns into a single municipality, Emporiae.","My family still worships Artemis of Ephesus, like the first settlers.","Hardly anyone lives in the old town now. Their kings, Indibilis and Mandonius, allied sometimes with Carthage and sometimes with Rome, and finally rose against the Romans in 205 BC: Indibilis died in battle and Mandonius was handed over and executed.","In the summer of 49 BC Caesar came here to fight Pompey's generals, Afranius and Petreius. A flood of the Sicoris swept away his bridges and left him cut off and without supplies; he had boats made of wicker and leather, crossed the river and forced the Pompeians to surrender almost without a battle. He tells it himself in The Civil War.","Roman Ilerda","Since Augustus, Ilerda has been a municipality of Roman citizens, with its forum and its magistrates. It lives off the river, its grain and the crossroads between Tarraco, Osca and Caesaraugusta. Well, almost.","From here to Tarraco, three days by cart; from here to Osca, another three.","Forum of Emerita","Theatre of Emerita","Amphitheatre of Emerita","The veterans' city","Augustus founded it in 25 BC for the discharged soldiers, the \"emeriti\", of the Fifth Legion Alaudae and the Tenth Gemina, who had fought against the Cantabri and Astures. An Egyptian-style pylon leads to the temple of Isis; in front opens a long courtyard with red granite obelisks brought from Egypt, sphinxes and statues of animal-headed gods. The priests, with shaven heads and linen garments, open the temple at dawn with water from the Nile, kept in a sacred jar. Vespasian and Titus spent the night here before their triumph of 71. He was the god of Alexandria, a healer and lord of the afterlife. In Alexandria, Tacitus and Suetonius tell us, Vespasian healed a blind man and a lame man on Serapis's advice.","Temple of the Great Mother","The temple of the Great Mother","The Great Mother of the gods, the Cybele of Phrygia, came to Rome in 204 BC, in the middle of the war against Hannibal, because the Sibylline Books so advised: her image was a black stone brought from Pessinus. This temple was dedicated in 191 BC, next to the hut of Romulus, and Augustus rebuilt it after a fire. In April, during the Megalesia, comedies are performed in front of it, with the audience seated on the steps. Her priests, the galli, are Phrygian eunuchs who dance to the sound of drums and cymbals; Roman citizens are not allowed to become one.","Temple of Aesculapius","Porticus Aemilia","Temple of the Divine Claudius","Appia","The Servian Wall","The wall that, according to tradition, King Servius Tullius built. The remains you see date from the 4th century BC, raised after the Gallic sack (390 BC) with large blocks of yellow tuff brought from Veii: about 11 kilometres of wall, with a ditch and an embankment (agger) on the Esquiline plain, where there was no natural defence. Rome has not needed it for centuries and has spilled over it everywhere: houses lean against it or use it as a quarry, and the gates have ended up inside the city, like arches in the middle of the street.","The insulae","Most Romans live in insulae: brick and timber apartment blocks of five or six storeys that fill whole city blocks, separated by narrow alleys. On the ground floor, shops and workshops opening onto the street; above, the flats: the higher up, the smaller, cheaper and more dangerous. They have no running water or latrines, and people cook on braziers, so fires and collapses are frequent. Augustus limited their height to about 70 feet (21 m) and created the vigiles, firefighters and night watchmen. After the fire of 64, Nero required wider streets, open courtyards and porticoes along the façades. Fourth-century catalogues count some 46,600 insulae and 1,790 domus, although they may be counting dwellings rather than buildings.","The fourteen regions","In 7 BC Augustus divided Rome into fourteen regions, which spill beyond the old wall, and these into 265 neighbourhoods (vici), each with its altar of the Lares and its own magistrates. The regions are numbered; the names we know, from later catalogues, come from a monument or place in each one: Porta Capena (I), Caelian (II), Isis and Serapis (III), Temple of Peace (IV), Esquiline (V), Alta Semita (VI), Via Lata (VII), Roman Forum (VIII), Circus Flaminius (IX), Palatine (X), Circus Maximus (XI), Public Pool (XII), Aventine (XIII) and Across the Tiber (XIV). Seven cohorts of vigiles, each in charge of two regions, keep watch for fires.","The gate in the Servian Wall through which the Via Appia leaves for the south. A branch of the Aqua Marcia aqueduct passes over it and drips on those walking through: that is why some call it \"the wet gate\". Journeys to Campania and Brundisium start here, and here people say farewell to those who leave and welcome the generals who return.","Synagogue","A synagogue across the Tiber","A house of prayer (proseucha) of the Jews of Rome, who have lived mostly in this district since Pompey brought prisoners from Judaea in 63 BC. Every Sabbath they gather here to read the Law and the Prophets in Greek; during the week it is a school, a court and a common house. The inscriptions of the catacombs name more than ten synagogues in Rome: that of the Augustesians, that of the Agrippesians, that of the Hebrews… None from this period has been found in the city: this one is modelled on the 1st-century synagogue at Ostia, with its porch and its basin for washing hands. Above the door, the menorah, the seven-branched lampstand.","Warehouses of Galba","Warehouses of Lollius","The warehouses of Galba","The largest warehouses in Rome, built by the family of the Sulpicii Galbae at the end of the 2nd century BC and now the emperor's property. They are huge courtyards surrounded by hundreds of two-storey cells, with a single guarded gate. They store the grain handed out free to some two hundred thousand citizens, as well as oil, wine and marble. Vespasian gave the land back to the people: where the lake was, the amphitheatre now stands, and next to this Oppian wing, the Baths of Titus. Its painted rooms are still in use. Many Latin expressions are still used as they are: these are Latinisms, like ad hoc, status quo, in situ or curriculum vitae. Some come from Roman authors (Horace, Juvenal, Virgil, Julius Caesar) and others were formed much later, in medieval, legal or scientific Latin.","Quiet, children, we have a visitor! Salve, stranger. Two thousand years from now, people we don't know will still be saying ad hoc, status quo or alea iacta est.","What is a Latinism?","A Latin word or expression used within another language, as it is or nearly so. There are two kinds: those taken whole, without changing anything, like in situ or ad hoc, and those adapted to the new language, like deficit, requiem or agenda. They are used a great deal in law, medicine, science and politics, because for centuries Latin will be the language of the learned all over Europe.","Where do they come from?","Some we already say now, here in Rome: the divine Julius said alea iacta est as he crossed the Rubicon, and Augustus put off payments ad Kalendas Graecas. All are about bodies changing shape: Daphne turns into a laurel fleeing Apollo, Narcissus into a flower, Arachne into a spider for challenging Minerva, Icarus falls into the sea when the sun melts the wax of his wings. He worked on it for over forty years. It begins with a famous preface: he says he doesn't know whether it's worth it, but that the best thing about knowing history is having examples of every kind before your eyes, to imitate the good and avoid the shameful. And he confesses that, while writing about the past, he forgets the ills of his own time.","Tell me one of his stories","Hannibal's, which is the best part. Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants, in winter, in the snow, and came down into Italy. He won at Lake Trasimene and at Cannae, where tens of thousands of Romans died in a single day. Livy says Hannibal sent heaps of gold rings from the dead knights to Carthage. And yet Rome didn't give in: when Hannibal camped at the city's gates, the land his camp stood on was sold in Rome, and fetched its full price.","And what was Livy like?","A provincial who never went into politics, rare in a Roman historian. Plautus (c. 254-184 BC) wrote many comedies, of which 21 survive, full of songs, wordplay and cunning slaves. Terence (c. 190-159 BC), a former slave from Carthage, wrote six more refined and realistic comedies. In imperial times audiences preferred mime and pantomime, but the old comedies were still read in schools and sometimes revived.","Ah, a spectator! I'm Ambivius, and I bear the name of Lucius Ambivius Turpio, the great actor who staged Terence's comedies nearly two hundred and fifty years ago. My company is reviving the classics today. It isn't easy: people nowadays prefer mime and pantomime, but a good Plautine slave still makes anyone laugh.","Who was Plautus?","An Umbrian who came to Rome, worked in the theatre, lost his money in business and, they say, had to work in a flour mill, where he wrote his comedies. About a hundred and thirty were attributed to him, and the scholar Varro accepted twenty-one as genuine. He takes Greek comedies and fills them with jokes, songs and witty insults. His great character is the clever slave who tricks his master and fixes everything, like Tranio in The Haunted House.","And Terence?","An African slave, from Carthage, whose master, a senator, educated and freed him. He died young on a journey to Greece. He wrote only six comedies, quieter and more elegant than Plautus', with characters who think and hesitate. His is the line everyone quotes: «I am human, and nothing human is alien to me». In school you learn Latin with him. But even in his lifetime he struggled to fill the theatre: The Mother-in-Law failed twice.","How is a performance put on?","We actors are all men, even those who play women, and nearly all slaves or freedmen. In the first century AD the comedies of Plautus and Terence were rarely staged: audiences preferred mime and pantomime.","The theatre in Rome","Theatre reached Rome from Etruria and from the Greek cities of southern Italy. In 240 BC Livius Andronicus, a Greek from Tarentum, staged the first tragedy and the first comedy in Latin. For two centuries plays were performed on wooden stages taken down after the games: the Senate mistrusted permanent theatres.","The palliata comedy, with Greek characters and settings, adapted Greek New Comedy, especially Menander. Plautus (c. 254-184 BC) filled it with music, wordplay and scheming slaves; 21 of his plays survive. Terence (c. 190-159 BC), a former Carthaginian slave, wrote six more restrained comedies, with careful dialogue and finely shaded characters.","Pompey built the first stone theatre in 55 BC; those of Balbus and Marcellus followed. The comedies of Plautus and Terence were read in schools and only occasionally revived. Quintilian says so: declamation should resemble real lawsuits, not a tragedy.","What is a controversia?","A letter to a friend","A debate between philosophers","It was the most advanced exercise in the rhetorician's school.","What criticism was made of the controversiae?","That they were absurd and didn't prepare for real trials","That they were too short","That they were done in Greek","Quintilian and Petronius complain of it.","The art of memory","To learn a long speech, orators use the method of places: they imagine a building they know well and put in each room an image that recalls a part of the speech. When speaking, they walk through the house in their minds and find each image in turn.","The method was invented, they say, by the poet Simonides of Ceos: at a banquet he stepped out for a moment, the roof fell in and the bodies were unrecognisable; he knew who each one was by remembering where they sat. That's why we Romans say «in the first place», «in the second place».","What does the method of places consist of?","Placing images in the spots of an imagined building","Repeating the speech a hundred times","Writing it on your hand","You walk through the building in your mind as you speak.","Who, according to legend, invented the art of memory?","The poet Simonides of Ceos","King Numa","Cicero and Quintilian tell the story.","Four lessons, like the ones I give the boys every morning. From the age of seven, a boy leaves home with his paidagogos, a slave who escorts and watches him, and goes round three teachers: the grammatistes (letters, sums and poets), the kitharistes (lyre and singing) and the paidotribes (gymnastics in the palaestra).","Girls are educated at home: spinning, weaving, managing the stores and sometimes reading and writing. The poor hardly go to school. From fifteen or sixteen, rich men's sons seek higher teachers: sophists, rhetoricians like Isocrates, philosophers like Plato, who has just founded the Academy. The gymnasia (Academy, Lyceum, Cynosarges) are places of exercise and conversation.","In the game, the school of letters, the music school and the palaestra are together south of the Agora; in each you can attend classes with exercises.","Plato, Protagoras 325c-326e","Aristophanes, Clouds 961-1023","Xenophon, Constitution of the Lacedaemonians 2","Cup by Douris with a school scene (Berlin, F 2285)",null,"D. Hernández de la Fuente and R. López Melero, Civilización griega (2014)","Education in Rome","In Rome teaching is private and organised in three stages. From seven to eleven, the ludi magister teaches reading, writing and arithmetic under a rented pergola. From eleven to fifteen, the grammaticus teaches Greek and Latin language and literature. After that, the rhetor trains young men of good family to speak in public through declamations: suasoriae and controversiae.","Children are escorted by a paidagogus, a slave, often Greek. Some girls go to elementary school; those of rich families have tutors at home. Since Vespasian, some rhetoricians, like Quintilian, draw a state salary. Euripides, Homer.",null,null,null,null,null,null,"The Tyrannicides","Harmodius and Aristogeiton killed Hipparchus, brother of the tyrant Hippias, in 514 during the Panathenaia. They died for it, but the Athenians honour them as founders of freedom: their descendants dine free in the Prytaneion and no one else may have a statue next to theirs. The first bronze group, by Antenor, was carried off to Persia by Xerxes in 480; this is the one made by Critius and Nesiotes in 477.","Statues of Conon and Evagoras","Beside the portico of Zeus the Liberator, the city has recently raised bronze statues of the general Conon and his friend Evagoras, king of Salamis in Cyprus, who with the Persian king's fleet defeated the Spartans at Cnidus (394). With Persian money Conon rebuilt the Long Walls. It's the first time since the Tyrannicides that Athens has honoured a living man this way.",null,null,null,null,null,null,null,"A public fountain (krene): a small portico with a basin into which water falls from bronze lion-head spouts. Athens has no aqueducts like those Rome will have: water comes through underground channels from the hills or is drawn from wells. Going to the fountain is work for slave women and poor women, and one of the few places Athenian women can chat outside the home.",null,"The streets of Athens","Unlike Rome, the streets of Athens aren't paved: they're beaten earth and gravel, dusty in summer and muddy in winter, and many are narrow and crooked, because the city grew without a plan. Stone drains run along one side, carrying rainwater to the great channel of the Agora. A traveller of the time wrote that Athens was dry, badly watered and badly laid out because of its age, though its public buildings were the most beautiful in Greece. At the doors of the houses there are herms and wells.","The market of the Agora","The Agora is also Athens' great market. Each kind of goods has its corner: the «circles» (kykloi) for fish, meat and vegetables, the stalls for perfume, books, pottery, slaves. The market inspectors (agoranomoi) watch over quality, and the metronomoi over weights and measures. «At the hour of the full agora», mid-morning, the whole city is here.","Herms","The Eurotas","Sparta's river. On its banks grow the reeds the boys of the agoge make their beds from: they have to pull them up by hand, without a knife. In myth, Leda was bathing here when Zeus approached her as a swan; from that union Helen and the Dioscuri were born.","Temple of Athena Chalkioikos","Athena Chalkioikos","On the highest hill, which serves as acropolis, stands the temple of Athena «of the Bronze House»: its inner walls are covered with bronze plates with reliefs of the labours of Heracles and other myths, by Gitiadas. The regent Pausanias, victor of Plataea, took refuge here when accused of treason: the ephors walled up the door and let him starve inside.","Persian Stoa","Hall of the common meals","Tomb of Leonidas","The Persian Stoa","The Spartans built this portico with the spoils of the Persian Wars. In place of some columns, marble statues of Persians hold up the roof: among them, they say, Mardonius, the general who died at Plataea, and Artemisia, the queen of Halicarnassus who fought at Salamis. It is the only grand, luxurious building in a city that prides itself on austerity.","The common meals","Every adult Spartan eats each evening with his messmates, about fifteen men, at the syssitia. Each month he contributes flour, wine, cheese, figs and a little money; whoever can't pay loses his citizen rights. The famous dish is black broth, of pork with blood and vinegar. A king of Pontus who tasted it said he now understood why Spartans didn't fear death.","A city without walls","Sparta has no walls: it is a cluster of five villages (Pitane, Mesoa, Limnai, Kynosoura and, further south, Amyklai), with simple houses and no great monuments. The Spartans say their walls are their men. Thucydides already warned that if Sparta were one day deserted, no one would believe from its ruins how powerful it had been.","Temple of Artemis Orthia","Sanctuary of Artemis Orthia","A very ancient sanctuary by the Eurotas, full of votive offerings of lead, ivory and terracotta masks. Here, Xenophon says, boys try to steal cheeses from the altar while others defend it with whips: that's how they learn to bear pain and be cunning. Centuries later, in Roman times, the test will become a brutal flogging in front of an audience of tourists.","The Platanistas","An island of plane trees surrounded by a channel, with two bridges: on one stands a statue of Heracles and on the other, of Lycurgus. Here two teams of boys clash every year: they fight with fists, kicks and bites to throw their rivals into the water. Beforehand they sacrifice a puppy at night to Enyalios, the god of war.","Menelaion","The Menelaion","On the hill of Therapne, across the Eurotas, Menelaus and Helen are worshipped; according to tradition they are buried here. For the Spartans, Helen isn't just the cause of the Trojan War: she is a goddess who protects girls and marriage, with her own cult and festivals.","Speak little, stranger. We don't like long speeches here.","Athenians? Lots of talk and little discipline.","King Agesilaus washes in the river like any of us.","My son entered the agoge at seven. Now I only see him at festivals.","If you want to see a city of marble, go back to Athens.","The Lion Gate","The main entrance to the citadel, from about 1250 BC: two jambs and a lintel of over twenty tonnes, and above it a triangular relief of two lions (or lionesses) resting their paws on an altar either side of a column. Their heads, which faced the visitor, are lost. It is the oldest monumental sculpture in Greece; it was already old when Homer sang of Agamemnon.","The grave circle","Inside the gate, a circle of stone slabs surrounds very ancient graves, marked by stelai with reliefs of chariots and spirals. The Mycenaeans respected it as a sacred place of their ancestors. Almost 2,300 years later, in 1876, Heinrich Schliemann will find gold masks here and believe he has seen the face of Agamemnon.","The palace of the Atreids","At the top, among grass and goats, lie the foundations of the palace and the great throne room, the megaron, with its round hearth and the bases of four columns. Tradition placed here the house of Atreus and his son Agamemnon, the king who led the Greeks against Troy and who, on his return, was murdered by his wife Clytemnestra. Argos razed Mycenae in 468 BC and deported its people.","The Treasury of Atreus","A domed tomb (tholos) of about 1250 BC, cut into the hillside: a 36-metre passage between ashlar walls leads to a doorway over five metres high, with a lintel of some 120 tonnes. Inside, a stone dome 13 metres high, built of courses that gradually close in. The Greeks call it a «treasury» because they believe kings kept their riches here; tradition attributes it to Atreus or Agamemnon.","The Perseia spring","According to myth, Perseus, who killed the Gorgon, founded Mycenae: the name would come from the pommel (mykes) of his sword, which fell off here, or from a mushroom under which he found water. The Mycenaeans brought water from this spring into the citadel by a secret tunnel, to withstand sieges. According to legend, the Cyclopes built the walls, because no man could move those stones.","The Argives let us farm here. They're not interested in the stones.","At night I don't go up to the citadel: they say you can hear Clytemnestra.","The odd traveller comes to see the Lion Gate. The old temple burned in 423, when the priestess Chrysis fell asleep beside a lamp; this new temple, by Eupolemus of Argos, holds a great gold-and-ivory statue of Hera by Polyclitus, seated on a throne, with a pomegranate and a sceptre topped by a cuckoo. Here, according to tradition, the Greeks swore loyalty to Agamemnon before setting out for Troy.","Fountain of Theagenes","At the end of the seventh century the tyrant Theagenes had this fountain built, which Pausanias still admired for its size, its decoration and the number of its columns. Theagenes was the father-in-law of Cylon, the Athenian who tried to make himself tyrant of Athens by seizing the Acropolis around 632: his followers were murdered beside the altars, and from then on the Alcmaeonids bore the curse.","Olympieion of Megara","The temple of Olympian Zeus at Megara. Inside is a statue of the god that was never finished: the sculptor Theocosmus, with help from Phidias, had made the face in gold and ivory, but when the Peloponnesian War broke out the Megarians spent the money on the war, and the rest of the body was left in clay and plaster. Behind the temple you can still see the wooden blocks that were meant to be covered.","Portico of Euclides","The school of Megara","Here teaches Euclides of Megara (not to be confused with the mathematician Euclid of Alexandria, who will be born in half a century), a disciple of Socrates. After Socrates' death in 399, Plato and other disciples took refuge for some days in his house. His pupils, the Megarians, are famous for their arguments and paradoxes.","The Megarian Decree","Around 432 Athens banned the Megarians from its Agora and from the harbours of its empire. For a city that lived by trade it was ruin, and the decree was one of the causes of the Peloponnesian War. Aristophanes mocked the affair in The Acharnians: a starving Megarian tries to sell his daughters disguised as piglets.","The Athenians closed their ports to us and nearly starved us to death. From here you can see the Gulf of Corinth. Seven of its columns will still be standing twenty-four centuries later.","Temple of Aphrodite","Acrocorinth","The mountain that serves as Corinth's acropolis, almost six hundred metres high: from the top you can see both seas. At the summit, a temple of Aphrodite and a spring, the Upper Peirene. According to myth, here Bellerophon tamed Pegasus, the winged horse, with a golden bridle given him by Athena. Much later the geographer Strabo will speak of a thousand servants of the goddess; historians today doubt that figure.","Peirene Fountain","The great fountain of the lower city, with six chambers opening onto a basin. According to myth, Peirene wept so much for her son, killed by Artemis by accident, that she turned into a spring. The Corinthians boast that its water is the best in Greece; Pegasus drank from it.","Market portico","The diolkos","A paved track some six kilometres long crosses the Isthmus, from the harbour on the Gulf of Corinth to the one on the Saronic Gulf. Goods are hauled along it on wagons, and sometimes whole ships, so as not to have to sail around the Peloponnese by the dreaded Cape Malea. Tradition says it was built by the tyrant Periander, around 600. Corinth charges for its use: that is where much of its wealth comes from.","The Corinthian War","For eight years, from 395, Corinth, Athens, Thebes and Argos fought against Sparta, and much of the fighting was here, on the Isthmus. In 392 Corinth and Argos even merged into a single state. The King's Peace, of this very year, forces the union to be dissolved: the exiled supporters of Sparta are coming back, and many fear revenge.","\"Not everyone can go to Corinth,\" the saying goes. The Plataeans were charged with tending the graves and holding a sacrifice for the fallen every year.","The Battle of Plataea","On this plain, in the summer of 479, the Greek army, more than a hundred thousand men according to Herodotus, under the Spartan Pausanias, defeated the Persian army of Mardonius, who died in the fighting. It was the end of Xerxes' invasion. The dead of each city were buried in their own mounds: the Spartans', the Athenians', the Tegeans'.","My father was born in Athens, in exile. First she purifies herself at the Castalian spring and burns laurel leaves. She prophesies only on certain days of the year; the priests put her often ambiguous answers into verse. Much later writers will speak of vapours rising from a cleft; modern science still argues about it.","The Serpent Column","After the victory at Plataea in 479, the Greeks dedicated to Apollo a golden tripod on three intertwined bronze serpents, cast from the weapons of the Persians. The sick come from all over Greece, purify themselves, offer a sacrifice and spend the night in a sacred portico: the god appears to them in dreams and heals them, or tells them what to do. Within the precinct it is forbidden to be born or to die. Here they run the oldest race of the Games, held every four years in honour of Zeus. The last were two years ago, in 388; the next will be in two years' time. During the Games there is a sacred truce throughout Greece. The spectators sit on the earth banks; married women may not attend.","The Zanes","These bronze statues of Zeus are new: at the last Games, in 388, the boxer Eupolus of Thessaly bribed three rivals to let him win. The judges of Elis fined them, and the fine paid for these six statues, with inscriptions warning that at Olympia victory is won with the feet and with strength, not with money.","The speech of Lysias","At the Games of 388 the Athenian orator Lysias gave a speech here: he urged the Greeks to stop fighting among themselves and unite against the king of Persia and against Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse, who had sent an embassy with luxurious tents. Part of the crowd, roused, attacked the tents.","The workshop of Phidias","In this building, the same size as the temple's cella, Phidias and his assistants worked the gold, ivory and glass for the statue of Zeus. The water leaves white crusts on the ground.","The wall of the Phocians","Long ago the Phocians built a wall here to hold back the Thessalians, and diverted the hot water to turn the road into a bog. By 480 the wall was half fallen: Leonidas's Greeks repaired it and took up position behind it. On the last day they went out to fight in front of it, where the pass widened.","The lion of Leonidas","On this small hill the last Greeks held out until the Persians shot them down with arrows. On top they have placed a stone lion in honour of Leonidas, whose name means \"son of a lion\". Beside it, three stelae with epigrams. The most famous, attributed to Simonides, says: \"Stranger, go tell the Lacedaemonians that here we lie, obedient to their laws.\" Leonidas's bones are no longer here: forty years after the battle they were taken to Sparta.","The Anopaea path","Here begins the path that skirts the pass over the mountain. Ephialtes, a man of the region, showed it to the Persians in exchange for a reward. The Immortals took it by night; the thousand Phocians guarding it above withdrew to a peak and let them through. The Amphictyons put a price on Ephialtes's head, and he fled to Thessaly. With the hasta caelibaris, a pin shaped like a spearhead, they part her hair into six braids (seni crines) tied with woollen ribbons: the same hairstyle the Vestals wear. She wears the tunica recta, girded with a woollen belt tied in the knot of Hercules, which only her husband may undo. Over it, the flammeum, the flame-coloured veil that covers her head; on her feet, saffron-coloured sandals, and on her head, a wreath of flowers she gathered herself.","<b>The auspices.</b> In the morning the relatives and friends arrive. First they must find out whether the gods approve of the wedding. In the past people watched the flight of birds; now it is mostly the entrails of a sheep sacrificed on a portable altar in the atrium. The auspex, with his toga drawn over his head, announces that the signs are favourable. Cicero already complained that it was done out of mere habit, but nobody would marry without them.","<b>The wedding tablets.</b> The bride's father and the groom sign the tabulae nuptiales, the contract that sets the dowry Valeria's family gives the husband, which must be returned if there is a divorce. The witnesses seal them with their rings. Like almost all weddings of this period, it is a marriage sine manu: Valeria will remain under her father's authority and keep her own property. Only a few old patrician families still marry by confarreatio, offering Jupiter a cake of spelt before the flamen of Jupiter, the pontifex maximus and ten witnesses.","<b>The joining of hands.</b> This is the central moment. The pronuba, a matron married only once whose husband is alive, joins the right hands of the bride and groom: the dextrarum iunctio, which will be shown for centuries on the reliefs of sarcophagi. There is no priest to marry them and no register to sign: the marriage is the will of the two of them to live together as husband and wife. The guests shout: \"Feliciter!\", \"Good luck!\".","<b>The banquet.</b> Then comes the wedding dinner at the bride's father's house, with relatives and friends reclining on the couches of the triclinium; guests who do not fit eat in the atrium and the peristyle. At the end the mustaceum is handed round, a cake of flour kneaded with must and baked on bay leaves. Some people spend so much on these dinners that a law of Augustus even set a limit for them: a thousand sesterces.","<b>The pretend abduction.</b> At dusk, when the evening star appears in the sky, the procession begins. First there is a little comedy: the bride takes refuge in her mother's arms, and the groom and his friends pretend to tear her away by force. The Romans say it recalls the rape of the Sabine women, when Romulus and the first Romans carried off their wives.","<b>The procession.</b> The procession (deductio) sets off for the groom's house. A boy leads the way with a hawthorn torch lit at the hearth; two other boys, whose fathers and mothers are both alive, hold the bride by the hand. Behind, some slaves carry the distaff and spindle: working wool is the symbol of the good wife. The pipes play and everyone sings Fescennine verses, bold and mocking songs, and shouts \"Talassio!\", a cry so old that nobody really knows what it means any more.","<b>Nuts and coins.</b> The groom throws nuts to the children following the procession: nuts are children's toys, and throwing them away means leaving childhood behind. The bride carries three asses: she will give one to her husband, leave another on the hearth of her new home for the Lares, and the third she rattles now, as she passes, at the altar of the Lares of the crossroads.","<b>The door.</b> The door of the new house is decked with garlands. The bride anoints the doorposts with oil or fat and ties woollen ribbons to them; the Romans believe the word uxor, \"wife\", comes from this, from ungere, \"to anoint\" (it is a mistaken etymology). The groom asks her who she is, and she answers with the old formula: \"Ubi tu Gaius, ego Gaia\": \"Where you are Gaius, I am Gaia\".","<b>The threshold.</b> The bride must not step on the threshold: stumbling on it would be a bad omen, and besides, they say, it is another memory of the Sabine women, who did not enter their husbands' houses of their own free will. So they lift her in their arms and carry her over it. The threshold is sacred to Vesta, the goddess of the hearth.","<b>Water and fire.</b> In the atrium, the husband receives his wife with water and fire (aqua et ignis), the two elements of shared life, of the hearth and of the rites of the house, and she touches them. The boy throws the procession torch to the guests, who scramble for it because it brings good luck. Facing the door stands the marriage bed (lectus genialis), consecrated to the Genius of the family, which will remain in the atrium as a reminder of the wedding.","<b>The bedroom.</b> The pronubae, matrons married only once, accompany the bride to the bedroom and commend her to Juno, protector of wives. Outside, the friends sing the epithalamium, the wedding song, like the one Catullus wrote for the wedding of his friend Manlius Torquatus. The husband will undo the knot of Hercules: married life begins.","<b>The next day.</b> The new bride now dresses as a matron, with the stola and the palla, and offers her first sacrifice to the Lares and Penates of her new home. In the evening, the husband holds a second party for the relatives, the repotia. Valeria is now the mistress of the house: she will manage the slaves, keep the keys and spin the wool. But in Rome, unlike Athens, she will go out into the street, go to the theatre and dine with her husband's guests.","two babies in a basket on the bank of the Tiber, a she-wolf, vultures above two hills, a plough tracing a circle.","Numitor, king of Alba Longa, has been overthrown by his brother Amulius. His daughter, Rhea Silvia, forced to become a Vestal so that she will have no children, gives birth to twins; she says their father is the god Mars. Amulius orders them thrown into the Tiber. But the river is in flood: the basket is left stranded on the bank, beside a fig tree.","A she-wolf coming down from the hills to drink hears them crying and suckles them, so gentle that she licks their faces. There they are found by Faustulus, the king's herdsman, who takes them to his hut and raises them with his wife, Larentia. Livy also gives another explanation: that the shepherds called Larentia «she-wolf», lupa, a Latin word that also meant prostitute.","Grown up, the twins restore the throne to their grandfather Numitor and decide to found a city where they were raised. But since they are twins, age cannot decide who should rule. They ask the gods for a sign through the auspices: Romulus takes his place on the Palatine; Remus, on the Aventine. At dawn, they watch the sky.","Remus sees the birds first: six vultures. His supporters celebrate.","The omen has just been announced when twelve appear to Romulus. Each side hails its own leader as king: one because he saw the birds first, the other because he saw more. Words turn into blows.","According to the best-known version, Romulus founds the city on the Palatine. In the Etruscan manner, he marks its sacred boundary, the pomerium, with a bronze-tipped plough drawn by a white ox and a white cow, so that the earth falls inwards. Where he wants a gate, he lifts the plough and leaves the ground unfurrowed.","The walls are only just rising. Remus, to mock his brother, jumps over them: «Is this what will protect your city?».","Romulus, enraged, kills him and cries: «So perish anyone else who leaps over my walls». Livy also records another version: that Remus fell in the brawl between the two sides after the auspices. Either way, Romulus is left as sole king.","And so the city took its founder's name: Rome. The traditional date, calculated by Varro in the 1st century BC, is 21 April 753 BC, the day of the Parilia, the shepherds' festival. On the Palatine, archaeologists have found 8th-century BC huts and the remains of a wall of the same period, whose interpretation is debated.<p class=\"sub\">Sources: Livy, From the Founding of the City I 3-7; Plutarch, Life of Romulus 3-11; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities I 76-88; Ovid, Fasti IV 807-862.</p>","The death of Romulus","a king before his army, a sudden storm, a cloud, an empty throne and a man who claims to have seen a god.","Thirty-seven years after founding Rome, Romulus is reviewing his army on the Field of Mars, beside the Goat's Marsh. The senators surround him; the soldiers stand in ranks.","Suddenly a storm breaks: thunder, darkness, a violent downpour. The sky closes in as if it were night.","A thick cloud envelops the king and hides him from everyone's sight.","When the light returns, the throne is empty. The senators who stood beside him say that a whirlwind has carried him up to heaven. The people, at first struck dumb with fear, hail him as a god, son of a god.","Livy says that even then another version went round in whispers: that the senators had torn him apart with their own hands.","Days later, Proculus Julius, a respected man, comes before the assembly: at dawn, Romulus came down from heaven and appeared to him, taller and more beautiful than ever.","«Go and tell the Romans that the gods wish my Rome to be the capital of the world. Let them cultivate the art of war, and know, and teach their children, that no human power can resist Roman arms». With these words he rose up to heaven.","Romulus was worshipped as the god Quirinus, with a temple on the Quirinal hill. Modern historians see here a tale of deification that may have shaped the way Julius Caesar's was told: Livy writes under Augustus, who liked to present himself as a new Romulus. Even in antiquity, Livy himself lets his doubts show.<p class=\"sub\">Sources: Livy I 16; Plutarch, Life of Romulus 27-28; Ovid, Fasti II 475-512; Cicero, On the Republic II 17-20.</p>","The Sabine women","two armies facing each other in a marshy valley, and women running between the spears with their children in their arms.","The new Rome has men but few women, and the neighbouring peoples refuse to marry their daughters to these upstarts. Silence. The leaders step forward and make peace: Romans and Sabines will become one people, with Romulus and Titus Tatius as kings. Livy says that, in gratitude, the curiae of Rome were named after those women.<p class=\"sub\">Sources: Livy I 9-13; Plutarch, Life of Romulus 14-19; Ovid, Fasti III 199-234. Many scholars see in the legend the memory of the merging of Latin and Sabine peoples in early Rome.</p>","Horatius Cocles at the bridge","a wooden bridge over the Tiber, an Etruscan army and a single man who will not give way.","Only a few years ago the Romans drove out their last king, Tarquin the Proud. The traditional date is 508 BC.</p>","Athena and Poseidon","a high rock above a plain, a trident striking the stone, a seed and a king looking on.",null,"In the time of Cecrops, the first king of Attica, who was shown as half man, half serpent, the gods were dividing the cities among themselves. The contest is carved on the west pediment of the Parthenon.<p class=\"sub\">Sources: Apollodorus, Library III 14.1; Herodotus VIII 55; Pausanias I 24.5 and 26.5; Saint Augustine, The City of God XVIII 9 (Varro's version).</p>","The trial of Orestes","a man pursued by dark figures, a goddess, two urns and a vote that decides everything.","Agamemnon came home from Troy and his wife, Clytemnestra, killed him. Orestes flees to Athens and clings to the statue of Athena.","Athena does not want to judge so grave a case alone. She gathers the best citizens of Athens and founds a court on the hill of Ares, the Areopagus: the first court to try homicide. So Aeschylus tells it in The Eumenides.","The Erinyes accuse: Orestes spilled his mother's blood, and that blood cannot be washed away. Apollo defends him: he himself ordered him to avenge his father, and Clytemnestra's crime was worse.","The judges drop their pebbles into the urns: one to condemn, the other to acquit. They are counted. It is a tie. Then Athena casts her vote: for acquittal. Ever since, in Athens, a tied vote acquits the accused: they call it «the vote of Athena».","The Erinyes threaten to poison the land. The play ends with a procession with torches and purple robes.<p class=\"sub\">Source: Aeschylus, The Eumenides (first staged in 458 BC). The Areopagus was real: in your day it still tries homicide cases. The cave of the Venerable Goddesses is on its slope.</p>","The Trojan Horse","ships sailing away, a huge wooden horse before the walls and a night of fire.","After ten years of war, one morning the Trojans look out from their walls: the Greek camp is deserted and the ships are sailing away. Xerxes, king of Persia, has crossed the Hellespont with the largest army ever seen: Herodotus speaks of millions of men, although historians today reckon perhaps a hundred or two hundred thousand. To stop him, the Greeks send the Spartan king Leonidas to this pass between the mountain and the sea, with three hundred Spartans and some six or seven thousand allies. They repair the old wall of the Phocians. Meanwhile the Greek fleet waits for the Persian one at Cape Artemisium.","Xerxes sends a horseman to spy. He sees the Spartans in front of the wall: some are exercising and others are combing their long hair. The king does not understand. Demaratus, an exiled Spartan king travelling with Xerxes, explains: \"It is their custom: when they are about to risk their lives, they dress their hair.\" Xerxes waits four days for them to leave.","On the fifth day Xerxes sends in the Medes and then his best troops, the Immortals. In the narrow pass they cannot use their numbers, and their spears are shorter. The Spartans pretend to flee, turn suddenly and cut them down. Xerxes, says Herodotus, leapt from his throne three times, fearing for his army.","On the second day of fighting a man of the region, Ephialtes, comes before Xerxes: for a reward he shows him the Anopaea path, which goes round the pass over the mountain. That same night the Immortals march along it by torchlight, guided by him. At dawn the thousand Phocians guarding the summit hear the oak leaves rustle, but they withdraw and let them pass.","At dawn the lookouts come running down the mountain: the Persians are surrounding them. Leonidas sends most of the allies away to save themselves; he stays with his three hundred, because Spartan law forbids abandoning one's post. With him remain seven hundred Thespians, of their own free will, and four hundred Thebans. An oracle from Delphi had foretold that Sparta would lose either a king or the city.","This time they go out to fight in front of the wall, where the pass widens, to kill as many enemies as they can. The Persian officers drive their men forward with whips; many fall into the sea or are trampled to death. Leonidas falls fighting, and around his body the hardest fight of all takes place: four times the Greeks drive the Persians back. When the Immortals appear behind them, the last of them withdraw to a small hill behind the wall.","On the hill they fight with whatever they have left, with swords, with hands and with teeth, until the Persians bury them under a rain of arrows. The Thebans surrender. The Persians have lost thousands of men, among them two brothers of Xerxes.","The Greeks buried their dead where they fell and placed a stone lion on the hill. The fleet, on hearing the news, withdrew from Artemisium, and Xerxes entered Attica and burned Athens. But weeks later the Greeks won at Salamis, and the following year at Plataea. The epigram of Simonides will be repeated for centuries: \"Stranger, go tell the Lacedaemonians that here we lie, obedient to their laws.\"<p class=\"sub\">Sources: Herodotus 7.175-239; Diodorus 11.4-11; Strabo 9.4.16. The reply \"Come and take them\" (\"Molon labe\") is told by Plutarch five centuries later.</p>","The Battle of Marathon","hundreds of ships beached on a shore, a runner, two lines of men on a plain, a charge at the run and a burial mound.","Summer of 490 BC. Six hundred Persian ships, sent by King Darius and commanded by Datis and Artaphernes, have crossed the Aegean, razed Eretria in Euboea, and are landing in the bay of Marathon.
