Young Bellerophon, grandson of Sisyphus, wanted to tame him, but every time he came near, the horse took flight.","The seer Polyidus advised him to sleep beside the altar of Athena. In a dream the goddess appeared to him with a golden bridle: \"Are you asleep? Take this charm for the horse and offer a white bull to Poseidon the Tamer.\"","When he woke, the bridle lay beside him. He ran to the spring and put it on Pegasus, who let him, tame as can be, and he mounted. Pindar says Athena thus fulfilled a dream that was more than a dream.","Homer tells the rest. Exiled from Corinth, Bellerophon came to Tiryns, and the queen, whom he had rejected, falsely accused him. The king sent him to Lycia with a sealed tablet on which he had written \"baneful signs\": orders to kill him. The king of Lycia sent him against the Chimaera, a fire-breathing monster with a lion's head, a goat's body and a serpent's tail. From the air, on Pegasus's back, Bellerophon killed it.","Victor over the Chimaera, the Amazons and the Solymi, Bellerophon thought himself the equal of the gods and tried to ride Pegasus up to Olympus. Zeus sent a gadfly that stung the horse; Bellerophon fell to earth and wandered alone for the rest of his life. Pegasus kept climbing: ever since, he has carried the thunderbolt of Zeus.","The Corinthians never forgot their hero: Pegasus appears on their silver coins, the \"colts\", which circulate throughout the Greek world, and the spring of Peirene, at the foot of Acrocorinth, is still the pride of the city. Pausanias saw a shrine of Bellerophon beside it.<p class=\"sub\">Sources: Homer, Iliad 6.152-205 (the only mention of writing in Homer); Pindar, Olympian 13.63-92 and Isthmian 7.44-47; Hesiod, Theogony 280-286 and 319-325; Pausanias 2.2.4 and 2.3.5.</p>","The birth of Asclepius","a newborn on a mountain, a goat that suckles him, a dog that guards him, a radiance and a thunderbolt.","This is how they told it at Epidaurus. Coronis, daughter of King Phlegyas, was expecting a child by Apollo. She gave birth in secret on the mountain above the sanctuary and left the baby there, abandoned.","A goat from the flock grazing on the mountain suckled him, and the flock's dog guarded him. That, they say, is why the mountain is called Titthion, the \"nipple\".","Aresthanas, the goatherd, missed the goat and the dog and searched the whole mountain for them. When he found the child he wanted to pick him up, but he saw a radiance coming from him, like a flash of lightning. He understood that it was something divine and turned away.","Pindar tells it differently: Coronis betrayed Apollo, Artemis killed her, and as she was already burning on the pyre, Apollo took the child from his mother's womb and entrusted him to the wise centaur Chiron. Chiron taught him to heal with herbs, with gentle words and with the knife.","Asclepius became the best of all doctors. But one day, for gold, he brought a dead man back to life. Zeus could not allow a mortal to undo the order of the world, and struck him down with his thunderbolt. Apollo, in revenge, killed the Cyclopes who forged the thunderbolts.","But Asclepius became a god. His symbol is the staff with a serpent coiled around it, and sacred snakes live in his sanctuaries. At Epidaurus the sick sleep in the temple's portico waiting for the god to heal them in their dreams, and the cures are written down on stelae. Thirty-four years ago, in 420, the Athenians brought his cult to their city, and the poet Sophocles took the sacred snake into his house while the temple was being built.<p class=\"sub\">Sources: Pausanias 2.26.3-7; Pindar, Pythian 3.1-58; Hesiod, fragment 51; Apollodorus 3.10.3-4; the healing inscriptions of Epidaurus (IG IV² 1, 121-122).</p>","The Third Punic War","fresh figs in the Senate, a city that hands over its weapons, a round harbour, six days of fire and a general who weeps.","Rome, 150 BC. Carthage has lost two wars against Rome, given up its fleet and its colonies, and pays its indemnity every year. But it is rich again. Old Cato, who has visited it, rises in the Senate and lets some fresh figs fall from the folds of his toga: \"They were picked in Carthage three days ago. That is how close the enemy is.\" And he ends every speech, whatever its subject, with the same sentence: \"Furthermore, I think Carthage must be destroyed.\"","In 150 Carthage defends itself, without Rome's permission, against King Masinissa of Numidia, Rome's ally, who has been stealing its land for years. That is the pretext. In 149 a consular army lands at Utica. The terrified Carthaginians hand over three hundred children as hostages and then, because they are ordered to, all their weapons: according to Appian, two hundred thousand suits of armour and two thousand catapults.","Then comes the last order: abandon the city and live ten miles from the sea. For a seafaring people it is a death sentence. The Carthaginians refuse. They shut the gates and make weapons day and night, in the temples and the squares: every day a hundred and forty shields, three hundred swords, a thousand missiles. The women cut off their hair to make ropes for the catapults.","The siege lasts three years. In 147 the Roman people elect as consul, although he is under age, Publius Cornelius Scipio Aemilianus, adoptive grandson of Hannibal's conqueror. Scipio closes the harbour with an enormous stone mole. The Carthaginians secretly dig a new channel to the sea from their circular harbour and bring out a fleet built from the timber of their houses. It comes too late: it is no use.","In the spring of 146 the Romans storm the harbour and break into the city. From the agora they climb towards the citadel, the Byrsa, along three streets of six-storey houses. For six days and six nights they fight house by house, roof by roof; then Scipio orders everything burned to clear a way.","On the seventh day those who have taken refuge on the Byrsa beg for their lives: some fifty thousand men and women come out, to be sold as slaves. Nine hundred Roman deserters, who can hope for no pardon, set fire to the temple of Eshmun and die inside. Their leader, the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal, surrenders at Scipio's feet. His wife, from the top of the temple, calls him a coward and throws herself into the flames with her children.","Polybius, the Greek historian, is beside Scipio as he watches the city burn. Scipio weeps and recites some lines of Homer: \"A day will come when sacred Troy shall perish.\" Polybius asks him what he means, and he answers that he fears the same will one day happen to his own country. Carthage was razed and its ground cursed; its territory became the province of Africa.<p class=\"sub\">Sources: Polybius 38.19-22; Appian, Libyca 74-135; Plutarch, Cato the Elder 26-27; Livy, Periochae 48-51. The idea that the Romans scattered salt on Carthage's land is a modern invention: no ancient author tells it.</p>","Aeneas and the Sibyl of Cumae","a cave with a hundred mouths, a prophetess in a trance, a golden bough, a black lake and a father who shows his son the future of Rome.","After seven years of wandering since Troy, Aeneas's ships at last reach Italy, at the beach of Cumae, the oldest Greek city on this coast. Above stands the temple of Apollo, which legend says Daedalus built when he escaped from Crete.","Beneath the temple opens the cave of the Sibyl, with a hundred mouths from which a hundred voices come. The prophetess falls into a trance, her hair wild, her breast heaving: \"I see wars, terrible wars, and the Tiber foaming with blood.\" And she warns him: going down to the world of the dead is easy; the hard part is coming back.","To enter he needs a golden bough, sacred to Proserpina, hidden in a tree in the forest. Two doves of Venus, his mother, guide him to it. The bough lets itself be plucked: it is the sign that fate is calling him.","Beside Lake Avernus, whose black waters, they said, no bird could fly over, Aeneas sacrifices black cattle to Night and to the gods below. The earth bellows, the hounds of Hecate howl. \"Now you need courage!\" cries the Sibyl, and plunges into the cave. Aeneas follows her.","After crossing the marsh in Charon's boat, seeing the unburied dead and meeting the shade of Dido, who will not answer him, Aeneas reaches the Elysian Fields. There is his father, Anchises. Three times he tries to embrace him, and three times the shade slips from his hands.","Anchises shows him the souls waiting to be born: Romulus, the kings, the heroes of the Republic, Caesar and Augustus. \"You, Roman, remember: your art will be to rule the peoples, to impose peace, to spare the conquered and to cast down the proud.\" Aeneas leaves by the gate of ivory, the gate of false dreams, and returns to his ships.<p class=\"sub\">Source: Virgil, Aeneid 6 (the quotation, 6.851-853). Near Cumae they show the cave of the Sibyl; Lake Avernus is a few miles away. Virgil is buried near Neapolis.</p>","Tages, the child of the earth","a farmer ploughing, a furrow that opens, a child with an old man's face and a book of lightning and entrails.","In the fields of Tarquinii a farmer is ploughing. They say that day he drove the ploughshare deeper than usual.","Suddenly a child sprang up out of the furrow. He had the face and body of a child but the wisdom of an old man, and he began to speak. The terrified farmer shouted so loudly that people came running from all over Etruria.","His name was Tages. Before the lucumones, the lords of the Etruscan cities, gathered in the field, the child dictated a whole science to them: how to read the will of the gods in the entrails of sacrificed animals and in lightning. They wrote it all down.","The liver was divided into regions, each consecrated to a god: if a god's part was healthy or diseased, they knew whether that god was favourable. The sky likewise: depending on which region a bolt of lightning came from and where it fell, it was a warning or a promise. When all had been said, Tages died, or vanished into the earth he had come from.","The books of Tages formed part of the \"Etruscan discipline\", which the Romans respected so much that the Senate sent young men of Etruscan families to learn the craft so that it would not be lost. In the year 80 the emperor and the magistrates still consult the haruspices. In the future, in 1877, an Etruscan bronze liver with the names of the gods engraved in its compartments will be found near Placentia.<p class=\"sub\">Sources: Cicero, On Divination 2.50-51 and 1.92; Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.553-559; Censorinus, On the Birthday 4.13; John Lydus, On Portents 2-3.</p>","Phaethon and the Eridanus","a chariot of fire running wild, a burning earth, a thunderbolt, a wide river, poplars that weep amber.","Phaethon was the son of the Sun. When his friends mocked him, saying his father was no god, he went to the palace of the Sun and asked him for proof. The Sun swore by the river Styx to grant him whatever he wished, and Phaethon asked to drive, for a single day, the chariot that carries the light across the sky.","The horses felt at once that the hands holding the reins were weak. They left the road: they climbed so high that the sky froze, and dropped so low that the earth burned. Ovid tells how the rivers dried up, the ground cracked and the forests and cities burned.","The scorched Earth begged Jupiter for help. And Jupiter, from on high, hurled his thunderbolt at the charioteer. Phaethon fell wrapped in flames, like a shooting star, and his body came down in a distant river: the Eridanus.","The nymphs of Italy buried his body beside the river. His sisters, the Heliades, mourned him for months beside the tomb, until their feet took root, their arms became branches and bark gradually covered their bodies. They turned into poplars.","Their tears, hardened by the sun, fall into the river as amber, which the Eridanus carries along and which Latin women later wear as jewellery. And Cycnus, Phaethon's friend, wept for him so much that he became a swan, the bird that never goes near the fire of the sky.","The poets identified the Eridanus with the Padus, the Po, the great river of this plain. Pliny the Elder mocked the story: amber, he said, does not come from the Po but from the shores of the northern ocean, and reaches Italy overland, through Pannonia, as far as Aquileia, where craftsmen carve it. But on the plain the poplars still stand beside the river.<p class=\"sub\">Sources: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.750-2.380; Apollonius of Rhodes 4.596-626; Pliny the Elder, Natural History 37.31-45; Virgil, Aeneid 10.189-193.</p>","Antenor and the Veneti","a Trojan who escapes with his life, ships sailing up the Adriatic, a people without a king and a city beside a river.","On the night Troy fell, the Greeks spared two Trojans: Aeneas and Antenor. Antenor, an old counsellor, had always urged that Helen be returned to the Greeks, and had welcomed Odysseus and Menelaus into his house. So that no one would plunder it, they hung a leopard skin on his door.","Antenor set out with a people who had lost their king at Troy: the Eneti of Paphlagonia, on the Black Sea, famous for their horses. They sailed up the Adriatic to the head of the gulf, beyond the farthest places, as Virgil says.","They landed with their horses, drove out the Euganei, who lived between the sea and the Alps, and made themselves masters of the land. The Trojans and the Eneti joined into a single people: the Veneti.","Beside a river Antenor founded a city: Patavium. His tomb is still shown there. And the whole region was given the name of that people: Venetia.","The one who told this story best was a son of Patavium: the historian Livy, who put it on the first page of his history of Rome, even before Aeneas. The real Veneti spoke a language of their own, related to Latin, and were allies of Rome from very early on. Patavium is today one of the richest cities in Italy: Strabo says it has five hundred knights, as many as any city except Rome.<p class=\"sub\">Sources: Livy 1.1; Virgil, Aeneid 1.242-249; Homer, Iliad 2.851-852, 3.203-224 and 7.347-353; Strabo 5.1.4 and 5.1.7.</p>","Dream: the palace of Minos","The palace of Minos","You are inside a dream: the palace of Knossos as it may have looked around 1600-1450 BC, twelve hundred years before your journey, following archaeologists' reconstructions. It was a huge complex of about a thousand rooms on several floors around a central court, with storerooms, workshops, shrines and halls, and no walls. Its wooden columns, painted red, taper downwards. Myth made it the palace of King Minos.","Bull-leaping","The frescoes of Knossos show young people grasping a bull by the horns and vaulting over its back: a rite or a sport that may have taken place in this very court. The stone horns crowning the roofs, the «horns of consecration», were a sacred symbol. Some think the myth of the Minotaur arose from the memory of these bull games.","The throne room","A gypsum seat with a wavy back, between stone benches and painted griffins, beasts with a lion's body and an eagle's head. It is the oldest throne in Europe. We do not know whether a king, a queen or a priestess sat on it: Bronze Age Cretans wrote in a script, Linear A, that has still not been deciphered.","The entrance to the labyrinth","According to myth, the architect Daedalus built Minos a labyrinth from which no one could find the way out, to shut up the Minotaur, the monstrous son of Queen Pasiphae and a bull. Every nine years, Athens had to send seven youths and seven maidens to feed it. Theseus came with them to kill it. Ariadne, Minos's daughter, who had fallen in love with him, gave him a ball of thread to find his way back. Go in: the red thread will unwind as you walk. The word «labyrinth» may come from labrys, the double axe, a symbol that recurs throughout the palace.","Touch this stele to wake up beside the ruins of Knossos, in the year 386 BC.","The ruins rise, the columns turn red and the palace of Minos is full of people again.","You are back among tumbled walls and goats.","Knossos was destroyed around 1375 BC; the Greeks of your day see only its ruins.","The archaeologist Arthur Evans will excavate Knossos in 1900 and rebuild part of the palace.","Look for the entrance to the labyrinth, north of the court. Ariadne is waiting there with the ball of thread.","Ariadne puts the ball of thread in your hand: the red thread will mark the way back.","<span class=\"label\">You are out of the labyrinth</span><br>Like Theseus, thanks to Ariadne's thread.","The Minotaur","Asterion, son of Pasiphae · the centre of the labyrinth","<p>In the centre of the labyrinth, among bones, a huge figure rises: the body of a man, the head of a bull. It snorts. Its eyes gleam in the half-light. The Cretans called it Asterion, «the starry one».</p>","Fight with your fists, like Theseus","<p>The fight is short and terrible. According to Apollodorus, Theseus killed the Minotaur with his fists; on Athenian vases he is nearly always shown running it through with a sword. The beast falls.</p><p>Now you must get out. Follow Ariadne's red thread back to the entrance.</p>","<span class=\"n\">1</span><span>Follow the thread</span>","Run away","What is the Tholos?","The round building next to the Council chamber. There we fifty prytaneis eat at the city's expense for the length of our turn, and a third of us sleep there every night: someone must always be awake in case a messenger arrives with news of war. The official weights and measures are kept inside as well.","Who is the epistates?","Every day a chairman, the epistates, is chosen by lot from among the prytaneis. For twenty-four hours he keeps the keys of the temples that hold the treasury and the city's seal. Nobody may serve twice: so almost any citizen can preside over Athens for one day in his life. Socrates presided once, on the day of the trial of the generals of Arginusae.","What does the Council do with money?","We oversee the finances: the magistrates' accounts, the leases of the mines and the taxes, the soldiers' pay. The treasurers of Athena report to us. If a magistrate has spent badly, he can be charged at the end of his year, at the audit, the euthyna.","How is a law prepared?","No proposal reaches the Assembly without going through the Council: that's what we call a probouleuma, a preliminary decree. Sometimes we propose a specific text; other times we just put the matter on the agenda. Recently the fundamental laws are also reviewed by the nomothetai, a special panel, so they aren't changed lightly.","Who can be a councillor?","Any citizen over thirty, chosen by lot in his deme according to its population. Before taking office we go through a scrutiny, the dokimasia: they ask whether we honour our parents, pay our taxes, have done military service. You can only be a councillor twice in your life, so the office goes round everyone.","How do people vote in the Assembly?","Almost always by show of hands: the presiding officers judge by eye who has won, because counting six thousand people would take all day. Only when a decision concerns an individual, as with ostracism or granting citizenship, is there a secret ballot with tokens, and a quorum of six thousand is needed.","What was ostracism?","Once a year the Assembly was asked whether it wished to banish anyone. If it said yes, everyone wrote a name on a potsherd, an ostrakon, and the man with the most votes left for ten years, without losing his property. It was used against Themistocles and Aristides. It hasn't been used for thirty years: the last was Hyperbolus, and it was so ridiculous that it fell out of use.","How does a session begin?","At dawn, with a purification sacrifice: a piglet is carried around the hill. The herald pronounces curses on anyone who deceives the people and then asks: «Who wishes to speak?». The Scythian archers, public slaves, sweep along with a rope dipped in red paint those still chatting in the Agora: anyone who arrives stained red loses his pay.","How often do you meet?","Forty times a year, four in each prytany. One is the principal session: there's a vote on whether the magistrates are doing their jobs well, and grain and the country's defence are discussed. Another is devoted to supplications: anyone can ask the people for whatever he wants, holding an olive branch.","What happens if an orator lies?","If he persuades the people to do something harmful, he can later be charged with deceiving the people. And if he proposes something contrary to the laws, anyone can indict him for illegality. Orators who speak often, the rhetores, run great risks. That's why many citizens like me prefer to vote and keep quiet.","How do you vote at a trial?","At the end, each juror receives two bronze tokens: one with a hollow axle, to condemn, and one with a solid axle, to acquit. We cover the axle with our fingers so nobody can see which one we drop into the bronze urn; the other goes into a wooden urn. That way the vote is secret.","How long does a trial last?","One day at most; small private suits, a few hours. Each side's time is measured with the clepsydra, a water clock: when the water runs out, so does the speech. While documents are being read out, the hole is plugged so no time is lost.","What penalties are there?","In public suits where the law does not fix the penalty, the prosecutor proposes one penalty and the convicted man another, and the jurors choose between them. So it was with Socrates: the prosecutor asked for death, and he proposed that he be fed in the Prytaneion. Then he offered a fine, but it was too late.","And the sycophants?","They're professional accusers: they prosecute rich men to squeeze money out of them for dropping the charge, or to collect a share of the fines. To curb them, anyone who doesn't get even a fifth of the votes pays a thousand drachmas and may not prosecute again. Aristophanes makes great fun of them.","Who can be a juror?","Any citizen over thirty who owes no money to the city. At the start of the year we swear to vote according to the laws and, where there is no law, according to our most just judgement. There are six thousand of us, divided into ten sections. Every morning the lot decides which sections sit and in which court.","Who are the Eleven?","The magistrates in charge of prisons and executions. They're chosen by lot, one per tribe plus a secretary. They receive the condemned, guard prisoners awaiting trial, and can execute without trial certain thieves caught red-handed, if they confess.","What is the prison like?","It isn't for serving long sentences: here people wait for trial, for a fine to be paid, or for execution. There are cells, a courtyard and a room where the condemned bathe. Friends can visit the prisoners and bring them food. Some spend years here because they can't pay a debt to the city.","What is hemlock?","A plant that grows in damp places. Crushed, its seeds paralyse the body from the feet upwards until the cold reaches the heart, without violent pain. It's expensive: a dose costs twelve drachmas. That's why it's given only to citizens; other condemned men are executed in crueller ways.","What did Socrates say at the end?","His belly was already growing cold when he uncovered his face and said to Crito: «We owe a cock to Asclepius; pay it, don't forget». Many take it to mean that death is the cure for life. All I know is that I wept, and that he had told me I was the noblest of all who had passed through here.","What happened to his accusers?","They say the people soon regretted it. They say Meletus was later condemned and Anytus had to leave Athens, though I don't know how much is truth and how much legend. What is certain is that his disciples write about him endlessly: Plato, Xenophon, Antisthenes. Dead, he speaks more than he did alive.","Why did you go to Sicily?","I wanted to see whether a ruler could become a philosopher. In Syracuse I met Dion, brother-in-law of the tyrant Dionysius, an extraordinary young man. But Dionysius didn't want to hear about justice. They say he had me sold as a slave on Aegina, and that a friend from Cyrene, Anniceris, paid my ransom. I came back with more doubts than hopes.","What is dialectic?","The art of asking and answering until you reach what a thing is. It's not enough to give examples of courage: you must find what all courageous acts have in common. Concepts are divided into parts, compared, tested against counterexamples. It's the highest thing one can learn, after mathematics.","Why don't you go into politics?","As a young man I wanted to. But I saw the Thirty, my own relatives, commit crimes, and then I saw the restored democracy condemn Socrates. I understood that cities will be badly governed until philosophers rule or rulers become philosophers. Meanwhile, I educate those who may govern one day.","What is the soul?","What is divine and immortal in us. Before birth it contemplated the Ideas; that's why learning is remembering. It has three parts: reason, spirit and the appetites, like a charioteer driving two horses, one noble and one wild. A good life is one in which reason holds the reins.","Why do you write dialogues?","Because philosophy is conversation. A book can't answer if you question it; it always says the same thing. In a dialogue the reader sees Socrates asking, sees the mistakes and the doubts, and has to think for himself. And I never appear speaking: I let the characters talk.","What is your course like?","Three or four years. My pupils study the speeches of the great orators, write their own and correct them with me again and again. Rules aren't enough: you need natural talent, practice and a good model. I read and comment on their texts sentence by sentence. Some take ten years to finish a speech worth the name.","What is philosophy for you?","Not the geometry or the speculation about the stars at the Academy, which are no use in life. Philosophy is the training that lets you judge well about human affairs, which never have an exact science. A man who knows how to speak well on important matters also learns to think and to live well.","What is panhellenism?","The idea that the Greeks must stop killing each other and unite against the real enemy, the Persian barbarian. I'm writing a speech for the Olympic games, the Panegyricus: Athens and Sparta together should conquer Asia. I've been polishing it for years. It will be read a few years from now.","Who are your pupils?","Sons of good families from all over Greece, future generals and politicians. Timotheus, son of the general Conon, is my favourite pupil. Others come from Sicily, the Pontus, Cyprus. King Evagoras of Cyprus is a friend of mine, and his son Nicocles listens to me attentively: one day I'll write him advice on how to rule.","Why do you charge so much?","Because I teach something worth more than money. But I charge Athenians who can't pay less, and I never charge my fellow citizens more than foreigners. Besides, I don't promise miracles like the sophists: I don't turn anyone into an orator in a week. I just try, for years.","What tax do metics pay?","The metoikion: twelve drachmas a year for a man, six for a woman living alone. We also pay the special war levies like citizens, and we do military service. If you don't pay the metoikion, you can be sold as a slave. And we need a citizen to sponsor us, the prostates.","How do you write a speech for someone else?","The first thing is to know the client: his age, his character, his way of speaking. A farmer can't talk like a sophist; the jurors would be suspicious. I write in simple words and clear sentences, the way people talk. They call it ethopoeia: painting the character. The client learns it by heart and recites it.","Which famous speeches have you written?","I wrote against Eratosthenes, one of the Thirty, who killed my brother Polemarchus: it's the only speech I delivered myself. Also one for a husband who killed his wife's lover, Eratosthenes of Oe, and pleads that the law allowed it. And one for a disabled man they wanted to strip of his pension of one obol a day.","Why aren't you a citizen?","Thrasybulus, who overthrew the Thirty, proposed granting citizenship to all of us who fought for democracy. I gave two thousand drachmas and two hundred shields and paid three hundred mercenaries. But a politician, Archinus, indicted the proposal as illegal and it was annulled. So I'm still a metic, though I pay and serve as much as anyone.","Did you know Socrates?","Of course, he used to come to my father Cephalus' house in Piraeus. Plato sets his conversation about justice there. They say I wrote him a defence speech and he turned it down: «It's beautiful, but it doesn't suit me, like Sicyonian shoes on a man». He preferred to defend himself his own way, and you know how that ended.","Where do slaves come from?","From war and from trade: prisoners sold after a battle and barbarians bought in the markets of the Black Sea, Thrace, Caria and Syria. They're put up for sale in the Agora, in the «circle», with a placard. Greeks shouldn't enslave Greeks, say the philosophers, but in war it's done.","What work do slaves do?","Everything. In houses, cooking, weaving, looking after children. In workshops: Cephalus' shield factory had a hundred and twenty. In the fields. And the worst off, in the silver mines of Laurion: thousands, chained, in narrow galleries. Nobody grows old there.","Can a master kill his slave?","The law doesn't allow it: if a master kills a slave, he must be purified and can be prosecuted. And nobody may strike another man's slave. But the master can flog him, chain him or sell him. In court, our testimony only counts if it's extracted under torture. That's how they see us.","Do you have families?","Sometimes. Some masters let their slaves live together and have children, who will be slaves too. But they can sell us separately whenever they like. I had a wife in Phrygia. I don't know where she is. Here I have friends: we Phrygian slaves get together at festivals and speak our own language.","And festivals for slaves?","At the Anthesteria, the festival of the new wine, we slaves drink too. And at the Kronia, the festival of Cronus, masters and slaves eat together at the same table, as in the golden age. Some slaves are initiated into the Mysteries of Eleusis: the goddess doesn't ask whether you're free.","How do you get that shiny black?","It's not paint but very fine clay, settled out. In the kiln we do three stages: first with plenty of air, and everything turns red; then we close it and throw on green wood, without air, and everything goes black; finally we open up again and the coarse clay turns red again, but the fine stays black and shiny. Get it wrong and you lose the whole firing.","Do you sign the vases?","Some. «Euphronios painted it», «Exekias made me». Some sign as potters and others as painters. Sometimes we write praise of handsome youths: «Leagros is beautiful». And jokes: one painter wrote on a vase that Euphronios had never painted anything like it, to mock his rival.","What shapes of vase are there?","Each for a purpose: the amphora for storing wine and oil, the hydria for water, the krater for mixing wine and water at banquets, the cup or kylix for drinking, the lekythos for the oil left at tombs, the aryballos for athletes, the pelike, the stamnos… A good potter throws them all on the wheel.","And black figure?","It's the old technique: black figures on a red background, with details incised with a point. About a hundred and forty years ago, right here, someone had the idea of turning it round: black background and red figures, with the details painted with a brush. It lets you draw muscles and clothes more freely. Now hardly anyone makes black figure, except for the Panathenaic amphorae.","Where are the vases sold?","All over the sea: to Etruria, Sicily, the Black Sea, Cyprus, Egypt. The Etruscans buy them by the heap for their tombs. A good painted vase isn't that expensive: a few drachmas. What really sells is what goes inside: Attic oil and wine.","How is the priestess chosen?","The priesthood of Athena Polias has always belonged to the Eteoboutadai, descendants of Boutes, brother of Erechtheus. It's for life: the priestess serves until her death and gives her name to the years, like the archon. One of my predecessors, Lysimache, served for sixty-four years.","What is the peplos?","Every four years, at the Great Panathenaia, the old wooden statue of Athena is offered a new saffron-coloured woollen peplos, woven over nine months by the ergastinai, girls from good families. It is embroidered with the battle of the gods against the giants, with Athena in the middle.","Who are the arrephoroi?","Two girls of seven to eleven who live on the Acropolis for a year in Athena's service. One night they go down a secret passage carrying on their heads objects that not even they know the nature of, and come back with others. It's an ancient rite, linked to the myth of the daughters of Cecrops.","What power does a priestess have?","More than men think. A priestess of Athena refused to let the Spartan king Cleomenes into the temple: «Stranger, go back, do not enter the sanctuary». Another, in Xerxes' time, announced that the sacred snake had not eaten its cake: the goddess had abandoned the Acropolis, and the Athenians evacuated the city.","What women's festivals are there?","Many. The Thesmophoria, in autumn, for married women only: three days camping in honour of Demeter, with no men. The Adonia, on the rooftops, mourning Adonis with little gardens that wither. The Skira, the Haloa. Aristophanes wrote a comedy about the Thesmophoria. Men don't know what we do there, and that's how it should be.","What is the parabasis?","In my old comedies, halfway through the play, the chorus took off their cloaks, came forward towards the audience and spoke to them directly on the poet's behalf: complaining about rivals, judges, politicians. It was the freest moment of comedy. Now I hardly use it: times have changed.","What happened with Cleon?","Cleon was the most powerful politician after Pericles' death, a leather-seller with a voice like thunder. In The Babylonians I mocked him in front of foreigners, and he denounced me to the Council. The following year, in The Knights, I put him on stage as a Paphlagonian slave who manipulates his master, old Demos. Nobody dared make his mask: I wore it myself.","Which of your plays do you like best?","Perhaps The Frogs: Dionysus goes down to Hades to fetch a good tragic poet, because Euripides and Sophocles have just died, and holds a contest between Aeschylus and Euripides. It won first prize and was staged a second time, which is very rare. Or The Birds, with their city in the clouds, Cloudcuckooland. Or Lysistrata.","What is Lysistrata about?","The women of all Greece go on a sex strike to force their husbands to make peace, and occupy the Acropolis to control the war treasury. It's a comedy: nobody thought women could really do it. But in the middle of the war, after the Sicilian disaster, the audience laughed and thought.","How is the contest won?","At the Dionysia three or five comic poets compete, one day each. Ten judges, one per tribe, write their verdict on tablets; five are drawn at random and those decide. The audience shouts, applauds, hisses, and the judges take notice. The prize is an ivy crown and glory. And the choregos who paid for the chorus puts up a monument.","What arms does a hoplite carry?","The round shield of wood and bronze, the hoplon, almost a metre across, held on the forearm; a helmet, a corslet of linen or bronze, greaves, a spear two and a half metres long and a short sword. You pay for it all yourself: that's why we hoplites are citizens with a bit of land. It weighs as much as a ten-year-old child.","What is a phalanx battle like?","We form up eight deep, shoulder to shoulder. Each man protects his neighbour's right side with his shield; that's why a phalanx tends to drift to the right. We advance singing the paean, to the sound of the aulos, and clash. Then comes the shoving, the othismos, until one of the two phalanxes breaks and runs.","What happened at the battle of Nemea?","Eight years ago, by the river Nemea, we allies attacked the Spartans. We Athenians were on the left wing, facing the Spartans, and they cut us to pieces. Along the rest of the line we won, but the Spartans rolled up everyone one by one. We lost many men. Since then we haven't dared face them in the open field.","Who trains you?","Nobody, unlike Sparta: here everyone exercises in the gymnasium. Before the war, the young men stand guard in the border forts. That's why the Spartans, who train all their lives, almost always beat us. Now the generals prefer professional mercenaries.","What is a soldier's pay?","On campaign, a drachma a day for the hoplite and another for his attendant, in the good times; now, less. With that you buy your food. If the city doesn't pay, the general has to find money by plundering or asking the allies. Mercenaries earn more and fight better, but only as long as they're paid.","What is a deposit?","You leave money with me and I keep it for you; sometimes without interest, so it's safe, and sometimes I lend it to others and pay you something. I write it all in my books: who, how much, when and to whom it must be paid. A travelling merchant can leave his money here and have someone else collect it in his name with a password.","How much interest do you charge?","The usual is a drachma per mina a month: twelve per cent a year. On maritime loans, much more, up to thirty per cent per voyage, because if the ship sinks nothing is repaid. Some call bankers usurers. But without us, the trade of Piraeus would grind to a halt.","Who is Phormio?","My slave, my right hand. He keeps the accounts better than I do. One day I'll give him his freedom, as mine was given to me, and leave him the bank and perhaps even my widow. My son Apollodorus will say it's a disgrace. But a bank needs someone who knows about banks.","What have you given to the city?","A thousand shields from my factory, when it needed them. A trireme paid for out of my own pocket, five times. That's why the people granted me citizenship. A former slave, imagine! A rich man in Athens has to give: liturgies, choruses, triremes. It's the price of being respected.","How much do you have?","That's not something one asks, stranger. Let's say I have land worth twenty talents, and money out at interest worth more than fifty. The bank makes a talent a year in profit, and the shield factory another. Few citizens of good family have as much. And I started with nothing, with a slave's name.","Who organises a banquet?","The host invites his friends, and sometimes others slip in: some turn up uninvited, like Aristodemus at Agathon's banquet. A symposiarch is chosen to decide how much water goes in the wine and how many kraters are drunk. Drinking unmixed wine is for barbarians: we mix it with two or three parts of water.","What is sung at a banquet?","Skolia, short songs each man sings holding a sprig of myrtle, which he then passes to the next. The most famous is the one about Harmodius and Aristogeiton. Verses of Theognis are recited too, riddles set, witty comparisons made. And sometimes there's talk of philosophy, as at Agathon's banquet.","What instruments do you play?","The aulos, the double pipe, above all. Each pipe has a reed, like a rush, and you play both at once, with a strap over the mouth so you don't tire. I also play the lyre and dance. Flute girls are hired by the night; the law fixes the price at two drachmas, so the rich don't fight over the best ones.","Who are the famous hetairai?","Aspasia, Pericles' companion, who they say taught rhetoric and wrote his speeches. Theodote, whom Socrates visited to talk about how to attract friends. Lais of Corinth, the most beautiful woman in Greece. We're companions, educated, free to choose… as long as we're young and beautiful.","What happens at the end of the night?","The final libation is poured, to Zeus the Saviour. Some go home with a torch and a slave; others set off in a komos, a drunken procession through the streets, with music and torches, to the door of some beloved. That's how Alcibiades came into Agathon's banquet, crowned with violets.","What is autarky?","Being sufficient unto oneself. The wise man needs no luxurious house, no money, no fame: virtue is enough. I sleep where I can, wear a folded cloak and carry a staff. The fewer things you need, the freer you are. The gods need nothing; the wise man is the one who comes closest to them.","Why do you wear your cloak like that?","So as not to need another: folded, it keeps me warm in winter and is easy to carry in summer. Socrates taught me, who always went barefoot in the same cloak. Some laugh. Socrates once said to me: «Antisthenes, through the holes in your cloak I see your vanity». He was right, the old man.","Who were your teachers?","First Gorgias, the great orator from Leontini: I learned to make pretty speeches. Then I met Socrates and walked forty stades every day from Piraeus to hear him. I left my own pupils and told them: «Come with me to find a better teacher». From him I learned that the only thing that matters is virtue.","What do you think of pleasure?","I'd rather go mad than feel pleasure. Pleasure enslaves: whoever seeks it ends up depending on it. Toil, on the other hand, is good, as the example of Heracles teaches, who chose the hard road of virtue. That's why I teach in the gymnasium of Heracles. Labour is a good.","What do you think about names?","That the beginning of education is the study of names. But you can't define what a thing is; you can only say what it's like: silver is like tin. And of each thing you can only state its own name: «man is man». Plato mocks this. I mock his Ideas: «I see a horse, Plato, but I don't see horseness».","What books do you use?","The books of Orpheus and of Musaeus, his disciple: hymns, a theogony, instructions for the rites. We carry them in a pile of scrolls. Plato mocks us, because we go to rich men's doors promising to free them from their own sins and their ancestors' with sacrifices and games.","What is the Orphic life?","A pure life: no eating meat, because animals have souls like ours and killing defiles you; no wool worn in the rites; no burial in wool. Abstaining from certain foods, like beans. Some really follow it; others just pay for the purification and go on eating lamb.","What are the gold tablets?","Small sheets of gold buried with the initiates, with instructions for the journey to Hades: «To the left of the house of Hades there is a spring, beside a white cypress: do not go near it. Say: I am a child of Earth and starry Heaven, I am thirsty: give me to drink from the spring of Memory».","What is the wheel of births?","The soul, punished for an ancient guilt, passes from one body to another, from man to animal, in a painful cycle. Only the rites and the pure life free it for ever. The initiates will say in the afterlife: «I have flown out of the sorrowful, weary circle». The Pythagoreans believe something similar.","Why do the Titans make us guilty?","Because we humans were born from the ashes of the Titans, who had devoured the child Dionysus and whom Zeus struck down with his thunderbolt. That's why we have a Titanic, guilty part and a divine part from Dionysus. Purification removes the Titanic and lets the divine shine.","Who was Prometheus?","A Titan who loved humankind. At a sacrifice he tricked Zeus: he let him choose between bones wrapped in fat and meat hidden in the stomach. Zeus chose the bones, and ever since we burn the bones for the gods. As punishment, Zeus hid fire, and Prometheus stole it in a hollow reed. Zeus chained him in the Caucasus, where an eagle ate his liver.","And Pandora?","For the theft of fire, Zeus had the first woman made, Pandora, adorned by all the gods, and gave her to Prometheus' brother, Epimetheus, who couldn't say no. She opened a jar and all the evils came out. Only hope stayed inside. So says Hesiod. We women say it was a man who opened the jar.","Tell me about Theseus","Theseus is our hero. Son of King Aegeus, as a young man he cleared the road from Troezen to Athens of bandits. Then he went to Crete with the young people of the tribute, killed the Minotaur with Ariadne's help and came back. But he forgot to change the black sails for white, and his father, thinking him dead, threw himself into the sea. That's why it's called the Aegean.","And Heracles?","The strongest of all, son of Zeus and Alcmene. Hera hated him and drove him mad: he killed his own children. To purify himself he performed twelve labours: the Nemean lion, the Lernaean hydra, the stables of Augeas, the hound Cerberus… In the end he died, burned by his wife's poisoned tunic, and rose to Olympus.","Why do you tell children myths?","So they learn what is good and what is bad, what the gods punish and what they reward. So they aren't afraid of the night, or so they're a little afraid: we tell them about Mormo and Lamia, who eat disobedient children. Plato says we should tell only good myths. Children prefer the others.","What is the abaton?","The portico where we sick people sleep, on mats, beside the god's sacred snakes, which do no harm. At night the god appears in dreams, sometimes with his daughters Hygieia and Panacea, and touches you, operates on you or tells you what to do. In the morning the priests interpret what you dreamed.","What cures are told of?","At Epidaurus there are steles with dozens of cures: a blind man who saw, a mute who spoke, a woman who was pregnant for five years and gave birth to a boy who walked off by himself to wash at the fountain. And punishments: one man who mocked the cures was healed but kept the scars. I believe what I see.","What do the doctors say?","The doctors of Hippocrates' school say diseases have natural causes: climate, water, diet, the balance of the humours. One of them wrote that the «sacred disease», epilepsy, is no more sacred than any other. They prescribe diet, exercise and baths. I've tried them. Now I'm trying the god.","What do you offer the god?","Before sleeping, a sacrifice and a honey cake. If you're healed, you pay what you promised and leave a votive: a leg, an eye, breasts, an ear of clay or marble, the part of the body that was cured. Look at the walls: they're covered. The rich leave reliefs showing the god healing them.","What is wrong with you?","My leg has hurt since I was wounded at Corinth. The doctors have cut it and cauterised it, and it's no better. I've been here three nights. The first I dreamed of a dog; the second, of a man offering me an ointment. The priest says I'm on the right path. We'll see.","What is the great procession like?","In autumn, those of us to be initiated purify ourselves in the sea at Phaleron with a piglet, which we then sacrifice. Then we walk thirty kilometres along the Sacred Way to Eleusis, singing «Iacchus, O Iacchus!», with torches. At a bridge, masked men hurl insults at us to make us laugh, as Iambe made Demeter laugh.","What is the Telesterion?","The great initiation hall at Eleusis, square, with tiers of steps along the sides and a forest of columns; thousands fit inside. In the centre is the anaktoron, a small chamber from which a great light shines at the climax. What is seen and heard there cannot be told: it's the secret of the Mysteries.","What is the punishment for revealing it?","Death. Thirty years ago Alcibiades and his friends were accused of parodying the Mysteries in a private house; they were condemned, their property was confiscated and their names were carved on steles. The poet Diagoras of Melos was condemned for mocking them and a price was put on his head. That's why we keep silent.","Who is the hierophant?","The high priest of Eleusis, of the Eumolpidae family, descendants of Eumolpus. He is the one who «shows the sacred things» at the final moment. With him officiates the dadouchos, the torchbearer, of the Kerykes family. His voice must be beautiful, because he sings the hymns.","What is the kykeon?","The drink Demeter took when she ended her fast: barley meal, water and pennyroyal. We fast as she did and then drink the kykeon. We say a formula: «I have fasted, I have drunk the kykeon, I have taken from the chest, I have worked and put it back in the basket». What it means, that I won't tell you.","What is a will in Athens?","Only a man without legitimate sons can make a will; if he has sons, they inherit in equal shares. Since Solon, a man without sons can adopt whomever he likes, during his life or by will, provided he is not mad, ill, or under a woman's influence. That's why many lawsuits argue over whether the deceased was of sound mind.","How do you prove someone is a legitimate son?","With witnesses: that his father presented him to the phratry, enrolled him in the deme, held the tenth-day feast. That he took him to family festivals. If nobody saw it, that's bad. That's why Athenians do everything in front of witnesses: weddings, births, loans.","What is a posthumous adoption?","If a man dies without sons, his family can have one of his relatives adopted into his line to carry on his house, the oikos, and its cult. That an Athenian's hearth not go out is very important. But it brings lawsuits, because several relatives want to be the one adopted and get the estate.","What is an epikleros?","The only daughter who inherits when her father dies without sons. She doesn't really inherit: the estate goes with her, and the closest relative, an uncle or a cousin, has the right to marry her so the property stays in the family. Sometimes the relative divorces his wife to marry the heiress. Their sons will inherit the grandfather's property. They're some of the ugliest lawsuits I know.","How do you write a good inheritance speech?","With a clear family tree: who is whose son, who married whom. Jurors get lost straight away among cousins and uncles. I bring witnesses for every step, read out the laws and, at the end, appeal to the feelings: the dead man's hearth will go out unless my client wins. The other side says the same, of course.","How do you win over the Assembly?","With the voice, the gesture and the moment. You have to know the people's mood: whether they're afraid, sick of the war, short of grain. You need friends who'll applaud at the right moment. And never promise the impossible, because they'll remind you of it later. An orator is a general without an army.","What is an embassy?","When there's negotiating to be done, the Assembly elects ambassadors, sometimes ten, from different factions so they keep an eye on each other. They go with instructions, speak before the foreign people or king and come back to report. If the peace they bring isn't liked, they can end up accused of treason. Andocides went through it recently: he had to flee.","What is the eisphora?","The special war levy. The rich pay it according to their wealth, when the Assembly votes it. It's unpopular with them, of course. So you have to be careful: propose too many wars and the rich hate you; propose too much peace and the people, who get paid on campaign, despise you.","And the liturgies?","The richest citizens pay for public services each year: a chorus for the festivals, a trireme for a year, a tribe's expenses at the games. It's an honour and a burden. If you think someone richer should pay in your place, you can challenge him to an antidosis: either he pays or you swap fortunes with him.","What is your political dream?","A new alliance of free cities, led by Athens, but without the abuses of the old empire: no tribute, no Athenian settlers on other people's land. Against Sparta, if need be. One day it will happen. And I'll be on the platform proposing it. Or perhaps in exile: that's how politicians end up in Athens.","How do you raise a baby?","Wrapped tightly in swaddling bands, so he grows straight, for weeks. He's bathed in warm water and oil, sung to and rocked in a wicker cradle or a swing. I nurse him until he's two, and then he has pap of honey and bread. Some mothers nurse their babies themselves; the rich prefer a wet nurse.","What toys do children have?","Clay rattles with pebbles inside, terracotta dolls with moving arms, little carts, spinning tops, hoops, balls. And knucklebones, the little bones from a lamb's foot, to play with like dice. Before marrying, girls offer their dolls to Artemis. Boys play at war.","What do you do with the children at the Anthesteria?","At the festival of the new wine, three-year-olds are given a little jug, a chous, painted with scenes of children playing. It's their first festival, a bit like joining the community. If a child dies young, he's sometimes buried with his little jug. Many die young, stranger.","What amulets do you wear?","Round the child's neck, beads, wolf's teeth, little bells, to ward off the evil eye and spirits. I spit three times into my bosom when someone praises him too much, so the gods won't be jealous. We Thracian nurses know a lot about such things.","How did you come here?","Pirates sold me when I was young, at the slave market. This family bought me to nurse their first son, and then I stayed. I raised him from birth; now he's a man, and he brings me figs when he visits. We nurses are part of the house. There are tombs that say «good nurse».","What is the dowry?","What the bride's family gives the groom: money, land, a trousseau. But it isn't the husband's: if there's a divorce he must return it, or pay interest of eighteen per cent. That protects the woman. A girl without a dowry hardly ever marries; that's why relatives or the city sometimes help to dower poor orphan girls.","What is the bridal bath?","On the eve of the wedding, the bride bathes in water brought from the Callirrhoe spring in a special tall-necked vessel, the loutrophoros. The groom bathes too. If a girl dies before marrying, a marble loutrophoros is set on her tomb: it's the wedding she never had.","What is the anakalypteria?","The moment when the bride removes her veil before the groom and the guests, at the wedding feast. It's the most important moment: from then on she is his wife. The groom gives her gifts. The women sing the hymenaios, the wedding song, and the friends laugh and joke.","Can a woman get divorced?","Yes, but she has to appear before the archon with a male relative, and that's difficult. The husband has it easier: he just has to send her out of the house and return the dowry. When Alcibiades' wife Hipparete tried to divorce him, he seized her in the middle of the Agora and carried her home in his arms. Nobody did a thing.","What do you hope for your daughter?","That she has healthy children, that her husband is good to her and that she knows how to run her house. That she doesn't have to go to the fountain or the market if she doesn't want to. That her husband doesn't ruin himself. And that one day she has a granddaughter I can tell about this wedding. That's all a mother asks.","What do the children read?","First Homer, always Homer: the Iliad and the Odyssey. Then Hesiod, Theognis with his moral advice, Aesop's fables, lyric poets like Solon or Simonides. They learn whole passages by heart and recite them aloud. That way they also learn to be good and brave, like the heroes.","How are you paid?","Badly. Each family gives me a few obols a month, depending on the days the boy comes. At some festivals, a present. If a month has many festivals, the parents deduct the days without lessons. There's a saying: «He's either dead or teaching his letters», about someone nobody has heard of. That's how they see us.","Are there punishments?","Yes, the cane, when they don't study or misbehave. The parents expect it. In one comedy, a father asks the teacher to thrash his son until his back is more mottled than a snake's skin. I don't beat them much, but I keep the cane in sight. Shame works better.","The boys arrive at dawn with their paidagogos. First reading and writing; mid-morning, reciting the poets. At midday they go home to eat, and in the afternoon some go to the palaestra or the lyre teacher. Solon's laws said schools could not open before sunrise or close after sunset.","What happened at Mycalessus?","Almost thirty years ago, during the war, Thracian mercenaries hired by Athens entered Mycalessus, in Boeotia, and killed everyone. They went into the school, the biggest in the town, and killed all the children. Thucydides tells it. Every time I see my pupils come in, I remember.","How do you carry a full hydria?","On your head, with a cloth pad so it doesn't hurt and to balance it. Full, it weighs as much as a kid goat. You hold it by the side handles to lift it and by the upright one to pour. At first the water spills everywhere; then you learn to walk straight as a column.","Where does the water come from?","From the fountains, from wells in the houses and from channels that bring water from the hills. In summer water is scarce and there are queues. Some houses have cisterns to collect the rain. The rich send their slave women; we poor women go ourselves. That's why the fountain is a place for the poor and for slaves.","What do people talk about at the fountain?","Everything. Who's getting married, who's ill, which husband beats his wife, what oil costs today. In Aristophanes' comedies, the women carrying water up to the Acropolis fight with the old men. Here we hear everything before the men in the Agora do.","What do you do at the loom?","We spin the wool with distaff and spindle and weave on the upright loom, with clay weights to keep the threads taut. A good wife makes the clothes for the whole house: tunics, cloaks, blankets. Fine coloured cloth is bought, but everyday cloth we make at home. Penelope wove and unwove.","What happens when someone dies?","We women of the family wash and dress the body, crown it and lay it out at home, the prothesis. We weep and sing laments and scratch our faces. The next day, before dawn, we carry it to the cemetery. Solon limited the laments and the luxury of funerals: the men didn't like so much noise.","How is the victim chosen?","It must be healthy, without blemish, often white for the gods of the sky and black for those below. We pour water on its head: if it moves its head, it's saying yes, and so it seems to accept its death. Nobody wants to kill an animal against its will. Then we cut a few hairs from it and throw them on the fire.","Which part do the gods eat?","The thigh bones wrapped in fat, burned on the altar, and the smoke rises to the gods. That's because of Prometheus' trick. The innards, heart and liver, are roasted at once and eaten by those taking part, like a communion. The rest is boiled and shared out.","What is a hecatomb?","Originally, a hundred oxen. At the Panathenaia we sacrifice more than a hundred cows at Athena's altar, and the meat is shared out among the whole people, deme by deme, in the Kerameikos. It's almost the only time the poor eat beef. That's why the festivals are so popular.","And libations?","A little wine, milk, oil or honey is poured on the ground or the altar while praying. At every banquet a libation to the gods is made at the start. The dead are given libations at their tombs. The Erinyes never get wine: only water with honey. Each god has his tastes.","How much does a mageiros earn?","I'm hired by the day: a drachma and a piece of the meat, sometimes the hide. I'm butcher, cook and priest of the meat all at once. In comedies, cooks like me are braggarts who boast about their stews. I won't deny it: my lamb broth with onion is famous all over the deme.","What measures do you use?","For liquids, the metretes, about thirty-nine litres, divided into twelve choes. For grain, the medimnos, about fifty litres, divided into forty-eight choinikes; a choinix is what a man eats in a day. The official measures, made of bronze, are kept in the Tholos and at Piraeus.","What is Piraeus to trade?","The great port: there's the Emporion, with its porticoes, where merchants show samples of their goods. There's a grain market, the Long Stoa. Ships from all over the sea pass through. A two per cent tax is charged on everything that comes in and goes out, the pentekoste.","What punishment does a cheat get?","A fine, confiscation of the goods, sometimes a flogging if he's a slave. Grain dealers who hoard to push up the price can be sentenced to death: Lysias wrote a speech against some who had bought more than fifty loads. Grain is sacred in Athens.","Is there counterfeit money?","Yes: copper or lead coins plated with silver. That's why there's a public slave, the tester, sitting in the Agora, who examines coins: he bites them, scratches them, weighs them. Good owls must be accepted; fakes are confiscated. The Athenian owl is good all over the sea.","How is the price of grain set?","There are magistrates, the sitophylakes, who make sure bread is sold at a fair price in line with the price of wheat. When there's a shortage, the Assembly looks for grain wherever it can, in Egypt or on the Black Sea, and some rich men give it away or sell it cheap. A hungry people doesn't vote well.","What is a merchant ship like?","Round, broad, with a square sail and no rowers except for manoeuvring. It carries up to three thousand amphorae. The pilot, the kybernetes, steers with two steering oars at the stern. We sail by day, from cape to cape; at night, close to the coast or by the stars. A good crossing to Egypt takes ten days.","What is brought from the Black Sea?","Wheat, above all: the fields of Scythia and the Bosporus feed Athens. Also salt fish, hides, honey, slaves. In exchange we take wine, oil and pottery. That's why controlling the Hellespont is vital: if the Spartans close it, as they did twenty years ago, Athens starves.","What is jettisoning the cargo?","In a storm, to save the ship, part of the cargo is thrown overboard. The loss is shared among all the owners of goods, not just those who lost theirs. It's an old custom of the sea, respected by every sailor. I hope you never have to see it.","How is a maritime contract signed?","In writing, before witnesses, and it's deposited with a bank or a trusted friend. It states the ship, the route, the cargo, the interest, the date of return and what happens in case of shipwreck. If there's a lawsuit, the written contract is the best evidence before the judges.","Which gods protect sailors?","Poseidon, of course, and the Dioscuri, who appear as fires on the masts in storms. Before sailing we pour a libation, and on returning, we make an offering at the temple. Some get themselves initiated into the mysteries of Samothrace, which protect against shipwreck. I prefer a good pilot.","How do you get into the Academy?","There's no enrolment and no fee: my uncle won't take money, unlike the sophists. All it takes is for someone to introduce you and for you to really want to think. Young men come from all over Greece, and two women too, Axiothea of Phlius and Lasthenia of Mantinea; they say Axiothea came dressed as a man the first time.","Is the story about the sign on the door true?","So they say: «Let no one ignorant of geometry enter». I don't know if anyone has actually carved it, but the idea is right: without mathematics you can't think about what doesn't change. Geometry trains the soul to look beyond what the eyes see.","How do you classify things?","By resemblances, dividing each genus in two. One day we were arguing about what a pumpkin is: a tree, a grass or a vegetable. A Sicilian doctor passing by laughed at us. Plato, without getting angry, told us to keep on dividing. I'm writing a book on the resemblances between plants and animals.","Who will inherit the Academy?","My uncle doesn't talk about it. But someone will have to carry on when he's gone. Plato says Xenocrates needs the spur, and another pupil the bridle.","What do you do when you're not studying?","I walk in the gardens, look after the olive trees of the shrine of Academus and go to the school's banquets, which are sober: little eating and much talking. My uncle has dedicated an altar to the Muses in the garden. Nobody here is rich for being here, but nobody leaves without something.","Who taught you?","Theodorus of Cyrene, a great geometer and a friend of Socrates. It was he who showed that the roots of three, of five and so on up to seventeen cannot be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers. He stopped at seventeen, I don't know why. I tried to understand the general rule, and I found it.","What is a proof?","Starting from things everyone accepts, such as that the whole is greater than the part, and advancing step by step, without leaps, to what you want to prove. If one step fails, everything falls. Sometimes you prove something by assuming the opposite and reaching an absurdity: that's how one shows that the diagonal of a square can't be measured by its side.","Yes, as a boy. He said I looked like him: snub nose and bulging eyes. He asked me what knowledge is, and I couldn't answer. He told me he was like his mother, a midwife, but of souls: he helped ideas to be born and checked whether they were sound or wind-eggs.","And astronomy?","We study it as the geometry of the heavens: the stars move in perfect circles, and the planets, which seem to wander, must follow combinations of circles. Eudoxus of Cnidus, a young man working with us, is looking for a model of spheres to explain it.","Is it dangerous to be a mathematician?","Only if you get called up. I'm Athenian and must serve when summoned: I've been on campaign at Corinth. They say war doesn't need geometers, but siege engines and rations do. I prefer triangles to spears.","What does a choregos do?","He's the rich citizen who pays for a play's chorus: the costumes, the masks, the chorus trainer, the chorus members' food during rehearsals. It's a liturgy. If he wins, he puts up a monument with the prize tripod. Now many rich men find it hard to pay, and choruses are shrinking.","What are comic masks?","Of stiffened, painted linen, with an open mouth so the voice can be heard. Slaves' masks have huge mouths; old men's, beards and raised eyebrows; girls', white skin. The audience recognises the character before he speaks. The actors also wear padded bellies and bottoms.","How many actors are there?","Three speaking actors, all men, who share all the parts by changing masks. If more characters appear, they're silent extras. Women never act; my father would put a man in a woman's mask, and that was enough to get a laugh.","What will become of your father's plays?","Some are copied and read in schools. Nobody will stage The Frogs or The Clouds the same way again, because they're about people who are dead. But the jokes still work. I've presented two of his plays, Cocalus and Aeolosicon, because he wanted people to see me on stage.","Who comes to the theatre?","The whole people: citizens, metics, foreigners, slaves attending their masters and, they say, some women. There are seats of honour for priests and magistrates.","Where are you from?","I'm not from Athens: some say I'm from Smyrna, others from Rhodes, others from Chios. I came here young and stayed. A foreigner can write comedies for the festivals of Dionysus, if the archon grants him a chorus. Types from everyday life. Nobody attacks Cleon by name any more: we laugh at what we're all like.","What is a comic riddle?","People love them: characters set each other riddles at the banquet. «What has no voice yet speaks, and from afar reaches those it wants?» A letter. Women can't hear it, but they read it. I always put riddles in; the audience shouts the answer before the actor does.","How do you work?","In the morning I think up the plot; in the afternoon I write on wax tablets, which I rub out a thousand times; then I copy it onto papyrus. After that you have to teach the text to the actors and the chorus, rehearse for months. The poet is usually the director too. If you win, the glory lasts a night; if you lose, it lasts all year.","What do you think of Euripides?","That we comic poets owe him a great deal: he put ordinary people on stage, maids, farmers, recognitions of long-lost children. Nobody believed light troops could beat Spartans.","What changes have you made to the equipment?","Lighter shields, of wicker and leather, the peltai; longer spears and swords; light boots, which they now call «iphicratids». A well-trained army is like a body: the general is the head, the soldiers the feet.","What does discipline mean to you?","That the soldier fears his general more than the enemy. Every year the ephors declare war on the helots so that killing them isn't impure.
