Then Pericles moved it to Athens for greater safety, he said, and paid for the Parthenon with it. There's no league any more, but the scars remain.","What are the lions?","A row of lions of Naxian marble, seated, gazing at the sacred lake like guardians. The Naxians dedicated them almost two centuries ago, when they were masters of the Aegean. They also dedicated a colossal statue of Apollo carved from a single block of marble, which fell in a strong wind.","What do the Deliades sing?","Hymns to Apollo, Leto and Artemis, and songs of men and women of old. We imitate the voices and dialects of every people that comes, and each thinks it hears its own tongue. Homer, in his hymn, asks that when a stranger asks us who the best singer is, we say: «A blind man from Chios».","What is Naxian marble?","A coarse-grained white marble that sparkles. The first great kouroi, statues of naked youths, were made from it, and the lions of Delos. Our sculptors taught the whole Aegean. And our marble roof tiles are famous: a Naxian, Byzes, invented cutting them thin.","What happened with the tyranny of Lygdamis?","More than a century and a half ago, a nobleman, Lygdamis, made himself tyrant with the help of Peisistratus of Athens. Naxos became rich and powerful: it had eight thousand hoplites and many ships. Then came the revolt against the Persians, and later the first city that tried to leave the Athenian league: it was us, and we were crushed.","What is the temple gateway?","On the islet of Palatia they began a huge temple to Apollo, facing Delos. They only finished the great marble doorway. You can see it from the harbour, like an empty frame looking out to sea. They say you can see Ariadne through it at sunset. I only see fish.","How do you fish?","With nets, with traps, with hooks and, at night, with a torch and a trident: the light draws the fish. Tuna in spring, when they pass in shoals; sardines, octopus, red mullet. Salt fish is sold to Athens. You have to respect Poseidon: nobody fishes on his feast day.","What other famous wine is there?","Naxian, of course, which belongs to Dionysus. But also Chian, the most expensive, and Thasian, which smells of apples. The Athenians mix it with sea water for flavour. Here wine is religion: there are springs that are said to have flowed with wine at the god's festivals.","What laws does Crete have?","Very old ones. They say Minos received them from Zeus every nine years in the cave on Mount Ida. At Gortyn there are laws carved in stone, about inheritance, marriage and slaves, written the way you plough a field: one line left to right and the next right to left. Lycurgus came here to study them.","Who are the Curetes?","Young warriors who danced with shields and spears around the cradle of the newborn Zeus, making noise so his father Cronus wouldn't hear him cry and eat him. That armed dance is still danced at festivals. And in the cave of Dikte people still leave offerings.","Who was Icarus?","The son of Daedalus. Minos shut them both up in the labyrinth for helping Theseus. Daedalus made wings of feathers and wax and told his son to fly neither too high nor too low. Icarus went too near the sun, the wax melted and he fell into the sea, which is now called the Icarian. Daedalus reached Sicily.","What is Talos?","A bronze giant that Hephaestus gave to Minos, or Zeus to Europa, to defend Crete. He walked round the island three times a day and threw rocks at enemy ships. He had a single vein, closed by a nail in his ankle. Medea, with the Argonauts, got him to pull out the nail and he bled to death.","What are the Cretans like now?","Famous archers, who hire themselves out as mercenaries to anyone. The cities fight each other: Knossos, Gortyn, Lyttos. We have common meals like the Spartans and our young are raised in groups. And we have a bad reputation: a poet from here, Epimenides, said all Cretans are liars. Was he lying?","Who was Sappho?","The great poetess of Mytilene, two centuries ago. She wrote about love and desire, about the girls who were leaving to be married, about her daughter Cleis. Plato says she's the tenth Muse. Her poems are sung to the lyre. They say she threw herself into the sea for love from a rock on Leucas, but that's a tale from comedy.","Who was Alcaeus?","Another poet of Mytilene, of the same time. He wrote drinking songs and war songs, against his city's tyrants. He said he lost his shield in a battle and ran, and that the enemy hung it in a temple. He invented a stanza poets still use: the Alcaic.","What happened at Mytilene in the war?","Forty years ago we rebelled against Athens. The Athenian Assembly voted to kill all the men and sell the women and children. They sent a ship with the order. The next day they repented and sent another, which rowed day and night and arrived just as the decree was being read out. They killed only a thousand.","Who is Pittacus?","One of the Seven Sages. He ruled Mytilene for ten years, chosen by the people, and then stepped down. His motto: «Know the right moment». He made a law punishing crimes committed while drunk twice as hard. Alcaeus insulted him in his poems. Pittacus forgave him: «Forgiveness is better than revenge».","What do you write?","Poems about my land and my friends, like Sappho. There are women poets in Greece: Corinna of Tanagra, who they say beat Pindar; Telesilla of Argos, who defended her city with the women; Praxilla of Sicyon. Rarely are we listened to. But poems travel: a verse doesn't ask who wrote it.","What are the musical modes?","Scales with a character of their own. The Dorian is grave and manly, good for education; the Phrygian, passionate, from the ecstatic cults; the Lydian, soft and plaintive. Plato says that in a well-governed city only the Dorian and the Phrygian should be allowed. I teach the little ones the Dorian.","How is a lyre made?","With a tortoise shell for the sound box, an ox hide stretched over it, two horns or wooden arms and a crossbar. Seven strings of sheep gut, tuned by turning pegs. That's how Hermes invented it as a baby. The professionals' kithara is bigger, made of wood, with a much louder sound.","Who was Terpander?","A musician from Lesbos, more than two centuries ago, who fixed the seven strings of the lyre and organised music in Sparta. When there was unrest in Sparta, the oracle ordered them to send for the singer from Lesbos, and his music calmed them. Ever since, at contests, the Lesbians are called first.","What is a paean?","A song to Apollo, of victory or healing. Soldiers sing it as they advance on the enemy, sailors as they set sail, and choruses at festivals. Every child must know how to sing the paean, like the hymns. Music unites the city: when everyone sings together, everyone thinks together.","What happened to Marsyas?","Athena invented the aulos, but she saw herself reflected in the water with puffed-out cheeks and threw it away in anger. The satyr Marsyas picked it up, learned to play it and challenged Apollo, who played the lyre. Apollo won, playing and singing at once, and flayed Marsyas for his daring. The myths of music are cruel.","Which sports make up the pentathlon?","Five: running, the long jump with weights in the hands, discus, javelin and wrestling. The jumper swings himself forward with the weights and lets go at the end, to the rhythm of the aulos. Pentathletes are the most beautiful, say the sculptors: strong and agile at once.","What is wrestling like?","Whoever throws his opponent three times wins: back, shoulder or hip on the ground. No biting or gouging eyes. The pankration is more brutal: anything goes except biting and gouging, and you win when the other gives up by raising a finger. Champions have died in the arena.","What is the strigil?","A curved bronze scraper. Before training we rub ourselves with oil, then with fine dust, and afterwards we scrape ourselves with the strigil to remove the oil, sweat and dust. Then a cold bath. What's scraped off famous athletes, they say, is sold as medicine.","What prizes are there at the games?","At Olympia, a crown of wild olive; at Delphi, of laurel; at the Isthmus, of pine; at Nemea, of celery. But afterwards the city rewards its victors: in Athens, free meals in the Prytaneion for life and five hundred drachmas. At the Panathenaia, amphorae of oil from the sacred olive trees.","Who was Milo of Croton?","The strongest wrestler there ever was: six times victor at Olympia. They say that as a youth he carried a calf every day, which grew into a bull, and he grew with it. He was a Pythagorean. He died devoured by wolves, his hands trapped in a tree trunk he had tried to split with his bare strength.","What did you do in Asia?","I crossed the sea ten years ago to free the Greeks of Asia from the satraps. Before sailing I wanted to sacrifice at Aulis, like Agamemnon, and the Boeotians stopped me: I haven't forgotten. In Asia I defeated the satrap Tissaphernes near Sardis. I was about to march into the heart of the empire when the ephors recalled me: Greece was ablaze with war against us.","What happened at Coronea?","I was coming back from Asia by land, by the same road as Xerxes, in thirty days. At Coronea, in Boeotia, Thebans, Athenians, Argives and Corinthians were waiting for us. We won, but the Thebans broke through our line and charged again. I was wounded many times. Afterwards I let those who had taken refuge in the temple of Athena go free.","How did you become king?","It wasn't my turn: I was the younger son. I was raised in the agoge like any boy, which isn't done with heirs. When my brother Agis died, his son Leotychidas claimed the throne, but they said he was Alcibiades' son. Lysander backed me and the Spartans chose me, lame oracle and all.","Who was Lysander?","The admiral who defeated Athens at Aegospotami and ended the great war. He set up governments of ten of his friends in every city and had himself honoured as a god on Samos. He helped me become king and then tried to rule me. In Asia I humiliated him so he'd learn who the king was. He died at Haliartus, fighting the Thebans.","What advice do you give a young man?","To learn what he'll do when he's a man. To obey before he commands. Not to confuse courage with recklessness. I was once asked which virtue is better, courage or justice, and I said: if we were all just, there'd be no need for courage.","Why did your brother encourage you?","Agesilaus wanted to show that winning at Olympia with horses isn't a personal achievement but a matter of money: if a woman can win, anyone can. He did it to take the rich show-offs down a peg. I did it for myself. And my bronze statue stands at Olympia, with my horses and my charioteer.","What does your inscription say?","«Kings of Sparta were my fathers and brothers. Victorious with a chariot of swift horses, I, Cynisca, set up this statue. I declare that I am the only woman in all Hellas to have won this crown». It isn't modest, I know. We Spartan women aren't modest.","Can women go to Olympia?","Married women may not even watch the games: if they're caught, they're thrown off a mountain. Unmarried girls may. And there are games just for girls, the Heraia, races in honour of Hera, every four years. I wasn't in the race: my horses won. The chariot owners get the crown, not the charioteers.","What land do Spartan women own?","A lot. We inherit like the men, and if there are no brothers, everything. And dowries are large. They say almost two-fifths of the land of Laconia belongs to women. While the men are at war, we run the estates and the helots. The Athenians say Sparta is ruled by its women.","What is Helen to you?","A goddess. She has a shrine at Therapne, across the Eurotas, together with Menelaus. Mothers take their plain daughters there so Helen will make them beautiful. And girls sing and dance in her honour by the river, as Alcman sang centuries ago. Helen was Spartan before she was Trojan.","What do you grow?","Barley, wheat, olives and vines on each Spartan's allotment of land. We give its owner a fixed amount every year: about eighty medimnoi of barley, plus oil and wine. Whatever's left is ours. That's how the Spartans live without working: eating what we sow.","Do you go to war?","Yes. Every Spartan takes helots as attendants, and sometimes the city arms helots as hoplites, promising them freedom. In the great war Brasidas took seven hundred to Thrace. But I also remember that one day they asked the bravest helots to come forward to be freed: two thousand were garlanded… and nobody ever heard of them again.","What are the neodamodeis?","Helots freed for having fought: «the new members of the people». They're free but not citizens; they live on their own land, sometimes on the frontier, and go on fighting for Sparta. It's the highest a helot can hope for. To many of us it seems little.","What happened with the earthquake?","Almost a century ago an earthquake destroyed Sparta: thousands died, and the helots of Messenia seized the chance to revolt. They held out on Mount Ithome for years. In the end they were allowed to leave, and the Athenians settled them at Naupactus. My grandfather used to tell it as the only day the Spartans were afraid.","And the perioikoi?","The «dwellers around»: free people from the towns of Laconia, who are neither Spartans nor helots. They have their towns and their businesses, they make the weapons and fight in the army, but they don't vote in Sparta. They're better off than us, and worse off than their masters. That's Laconia: three peoples, one master.","What is an eiren?","A young man of about twenty who commands a group of boys like me. He sends us to fetch firewood and food, asks us at supper things like «who is the best of the citizens?», and if we answer badly or slowly he bites our thumb. In front of the elders, who judge whether he punishes well or badly.","Why do you steal food?","They give us little on purpose, so we learn to find it and grow tall and lean. If we're caught stealing, we're flogged, not for stealing but for getting caught. There's a story of a boy who stole a fox and hid it under his cloak: he let it gnaw his guts rather than confess.","What games do you have?","Fights between groups on an island in the river, the Platanistas: two sides that have to throw each other into the water, with punches, kicks and bites allowed. And singing and dancing contests at the Gymnopaedia, in summer, naked under the sun. The old men, the men and the boys each sing their own verse.","What happens if you don't get through the agoge?","If you can't take it, you're not a citizen: you don't get into a common mess and you end up an Inferior. Nobody respects you. That's why we endure everything. Foreigners' sons can sometimes go through the agoge with us, like Xenophon's sons. They call it education; we call it becoming a man.","What will you do at twenty?","Join a common mess, by vote of its members: a single black ball is enough to reject you. Then at thirty, full citizenship: marry, attend the assembly. Until sixty, a soldier. Many Spartans visit their wives at night, in secret, because they live in the barracks.","What is the Lion Gate?","The entrance to the citadel. Above the lintel, a triangular stone with two standing lions resting their paws on a column, like guardians. They've lost their heads, which must have been of another stone. They say it's the coat of arms of the Atreids. Nobody has ever made anything like it in Greece.","Who was Perseus?","The founder of Mycenae. Son of Zeus and Danae. He killed Medusa, the gorgon whose gaze turned men to stone, and saved Andromeda from a sea monster. They say he founded this city where the cap of his scabbard, the mykes, fell off; others, that he found a mushroom, also mykes, and drank the water beneath it.","And the curse of the Atreids?","Atreus and Thyestes, brothers, hated each other. Atreus served Thyestes a banquet of his own children's flesh. The sun turned back in horror. Agamemnon, son of Atreus, sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia so the wind would blow towards Troy; his wife Clytemnestra killed him on his return, and his son Orestes killed her. One family, one blood.","Where is Agamemnon's tomb?","They say inside the walls, in a circle of ancient graves, or in the great beehive tomb under the hill, the one they call the Treasury of Atreus, where he kept his riches. Travellers who come always ask the same thing. All I know is that it's cool inside in summer and my goats know it.","What is at the Heraion?","You can see it from here, across the plain: the great sanctuary of Hera, between Mycenae and Argos. That's where Agamemnon gathered the chieftains before setting out for Troy, they say. Now it belongs to Argos. Every year the festival of Hera is held with a procession of white cows.","What is the festival of Hera?","The Heraia, at Argos: a procession from the city to here, with a hecatomb of cows, and the priestess on a cart drawn by white oxen. The young men compete in a race and the prize is a bronze shield: «the bronze of Argos». That's why it's also called the festival of the shield.","Why is Hera the goddess of Argos?","Because it has always been her land. When Hera and Poseidon contended for the Argolid, King Inachus judged in Hera's favour, and Poseidon, angry, dried up the rivers: that's why our rivers only carry water in winter. In the Iliad, Hera says her dearest cities are Argos, Sparta and Mycenae.","How are years counted here?","By the priestesses of Hera: «in such-and-such a year of such-and-such a priestess». There are lists going back centuries, and historians use them to date events. Hellanicus of Lesbos wrote a whole book from them. My name will stay on the list. That's a priestess's immortality.","What are Hera's symbols?","The pomegranate, which her statue holds in its hand, a symbol of fertility and marriage; the sceptre topped with a cuckoo, because Zeus turned himself into a cuckoo to get close to her; the peacock, whose feathers bear the eyes of Argus, the hundred-eyed giant who guarded Io.","Who was Io?","A priestess of Hera, here, in this sanctuary, a very long time ago. Zeus fell in love with her, and to hide her from his wife he turned her into a cow. Hera asked for the cow and put her under the guard of Argus. Hermes killed him, and Hera sent a gadfly that chased Io all over the world, as far as Egypt. The Bosporus, «cow's crossing», bears her name.","How is a fresco painted?","On fresh plaster, just applied: the colour sinks into the wall as it dries and stays for centuries. That's why you must paint fast, each day only the part there's time for, the «giornata». First I make full-size drawings, the cartoons, and transfer the outline to the wall by dusting charcoal through tiny holes. If you make a mistake, you have to chip off the plaster.","What is opposite this fresco?","The Disputation of the Sacrament: theology, heaven and earth gathered around the Eucharist. On the other walls, Parnassus, with Apollo and the poets, and the virtues with justice. Philosophy, theology, poetry and law: all knowledge, in the library of Pope Julius II.","Why do you look like yourself in the painting?","Because I painted myself on the right, in a black cap, looking out at the viewer, next to my friend the painter Sodoma. It's a signature. And on Euclid's collar I put my initials. We painters leave our marks: we want it known that we were among the wise, even if only in a corner.","What architecture is that?","A great basilica inspired by the new St Peter's that my fellow countryman Bramante is designing, with coffered vaults like Roman baths. In the niches I put statues of Apollo, with his lyre, and Athena, with her shield: harmony and wisdom. The space seems to open up to the sky.","What happened with Michelangelo?","While I was painting here, he was painting the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, a few steps away, shut in and letting nobody enter. They say Bramante let me see it in secret. It impressed me so much that at the end I added a solitary figure, leaning on a block, which we think is Heraclitus with Michelangelo's face. A tribute… or a dig.","What is the allegory of the cave?","Imagine men chained since childhood in a cave, facing the wall. Behind them objects pass before a fire, and they see only shadows: they think that is reality. If one breaks free and goes out, at first the sun blinds him; then he sees things as they truly are. If he goes back to tell the others, they laugh at him and perhaps kill him. That's the philosopher.","What would the ideal city be like?","Three classes, like the three parts of the soul: philosopher rulers, guardians who defend it, and producers. The guardians, men and women alike, with no property or families of their own, so they have no private interests. The rulers, educated for fifty years. I know it sounds like a dream; that's why I call it a model.","What is the Timaeus?","My dialogue about the origin of the world: a divine craftsman, the demiurge, ordered matter by looking at the Ideas, as a carpenter looks at a plan. The elements are made of triangles that form perfect solids. That's why in the fresco I carry the Timaeus under my arm, though in Latin and with a title page from Raphael's century.","Did Atlantis exist?","I tell of it in the Timaeus and the Critias: a mighty island beyond the Pillars of Heracles that sought to rule the world and was defeated by primeval Athens, and then sank in a single day and night. Solon told it to me, let's say, having heard it from priests in Egypt. Did it exist? It's a myth that teaches something about pride.","What was your last book?","The Laws, a long dialogue in Crete between three old men who design the laws for a new city. More realistic than the Republic: no philosopher kings, but written laws, magistrates and education. It was still on wax tablets when I died, at eighty, and my disciple Philip of Opus wrote out a fair copy.","Why did you found the Lyceum?","I spent twenty years at the Academy. When Plato died, they didn't choose me but his nephew Speusippus. I went to Asia, to Lesbos, to Macedon to educate the young Alexander. When I came back to Athens I founded my own school in the gymnasium of the Lyceum. We taught while walking: that's why they call us Peripatetics.","What is logic?","The instrument of all the sciences. The syllogism: if all men are mortal and Socrates is a man, Socrates is mortal. From two true premises, properly joined, a necessarily true conclusion follows. I studied it in every detail, as no one had before, and for centuries almost nothing could be added.","What did you study about animals?","Everything I could: more than five hundred species. I dissected fish and octopuses on Lesbos, watched day by day how the chick forms in the egg, described how the octopus changes colour and how dolphins breathe air and suckle their young. Alexander sent me specimens from Asia, they say.","What are the four causes?","To understand something, ask: what is it made of? (the matter), what is it? (the form), who made it? (the efficient cause), what is it for? (the purpose). A statue: bronze, the figure of Hermes, the sculptor, to adorn a temple. Nature has purpose too: the eye is for seeing.","What is a human being for you?","A political animal: by nature he lives in the city, and whoever lives alone is either a beast or a god. And he is the only animal with speech, to talk about what is just and unjust. Virtue lies in the mean: courage, between cowardice and recklessness. And happiness, in living according to reason.","What is your daimon?","A divine voice that has been with me since childhood. It never tells me what to do, only warns me when I'm about to do something wrong. It kept me out of politics, and on the day of the trial it gave no warning: that's how I knew that what was happening to me was good. My accusers said these were new gods.","What did the oracle of Delphi say?","My friend Chaerephon asked whether anyone was wiser than me, and the Pythia said no. I was puzzled, because I know that I know nothing. I went and questioned politicians, poets and craftsmen, and found that they thought they knew and didn't. My wisdom is knowing that I don't know.","What was your life as a soldier like?","I fought as a hoplite at Potidaea, Delium and Amphipolis. At Potidaea I saved Alcibiades' life and gave up the prize for valour in his favour. I bore the cold barefoot on the ice. Once I stood a whole day and night thinking, and the soldiers brought out their mats to see whether I'd move.","Why did you write nothing?","Because philosophy is living dialogue, and a book doesn't answer back. What you know of me was written by Plato, Xenophon and others. Each made me his own way: Plato's is deeper; Xenophon's, more practical; Aristophanes', a windbag hanging in a basket. None of them is entirely me.","What is virtue?","Knowledge. Nobody does wrong knowingly: whoever acts badly does so because he thinks it good. If he truly knew what is good, he would do it. That's why virtue can be taught, though I never found anyone who knew how to teach it. And it is better to suffer injustice than to commit it.","What happened with the herms?","The night before we sailed for Sicily, someone mutilated the statues of Hermes all over Athens. They accused me, and of parodying the Eleusinian Mysteries as well. I asked to be tried before leaving, but my enemies waited until I'd gone. When they sent the ship to bring me back, I escaped. They condemned me to death in my absence.","How was your return to Athens?","I came back in style, after winning battles in the Hellespont for Athens. I sailed into Piraeus with ships decked out with enemy shields. The whole people came down to welcome me. They gave me back my property and made me general with full powers. It didn't last: one defeat suffered by my lieutenant and they threw me out again.","Why did you cut off your dog's tail?","I had a magnificent dog that cost me seventy minas, and I cut off its tail, its finest feature. Everyone talked about it. I told my friends: «Let them talk about that, and they won't say worse things about me». People need something to talk about; better to give it to them yourself.","How many chariots did you take to Olympia?","Seven four-horse chariots, more than any private man or king. I won first, second and fourth prize. Euripides wrote an ode in my honour. I told the Assembly it would show the Greeks that Athens was not ruined by the war. And also to show them who I was.","How did you die?","In Phrygia, in a village, with my companion Timandra. The satrap Pharnabazus, pressed by Lysander, sent men who set fire to the house. I came out with a dagger and they didn't dare come near: they shot me with arrows from a distance. Timandra wrapped me in her own clothes and buried me. Not a bad end for someone like me.","What is the music of the spheres?","The planets revolve at distances proportioned like the strings of a lyre, and produce a harmonious sound, the most beautiful of all. We don't hear it because we've heard it since birth, as the smith no longer hears his hammers. I did hear it, my disciples said.","How did you discover harmony?","Passing a smithy I heard the hammers ringing in harmony. I weighed them: those sounding an octave apart weighed twice as much; a fifth, three to two; a fourth, four to three. I tried it with strings on the monochord: the same. Numbers govern the beauty of sound! That's why music heals the soul.","What is the tetractys?","The triangle of ten dots: one, two, three and four. In it lie the ratios of harmony: two to one, three to two, four to three. My disciples swore by it: «By him who gave us the tetractys, source of everlasting nature». Ten is the perfect number.","Did you remember your previous lives?","Yes: Hermes granted me to keep my memory from one life to the next. I was Aethalides, son of Hermes; then Euphorbus, the Trojan who wounded Patroclus; then Hermotimus, who recognised Euphorbus' shield hanging in a temple at Branchidae; then Pyrrhus, a fisherman of Delos. And then Pythagoras.","What was your community like?","The disciples shared their property and lived together. Beginners listened in silence for five years, behind a curtain, without seeing me. Each day began with a solitary walk, music and an examination of conscience: what have I done today? what have I left undone? And there were women among us.","What is the logos?","The common reason that governs all things, the law of the world. Everyone could understand it, but most people live as if they had a private understanding, asleep even when awake. «Listening not to me but to the logos, it is wise to agree that all things are one».","Why fire?","Because the world is an ever-living fire, kindling in measures and going out in measures. All things are exchanged for fire, and fire for all things, as goods for gold. Nothing stays; only change stays. Fire is the element most like that.","Why do they call you the Obscure?","Because I write in short sentences, like an oracle, that need a lot of thought. Socrates said of my book that what he understood was excellent, and what he didn't probably was too, but it would take a Delian diver to reach the bottom of it. I left it in the temple of Artemis at Ephesus so that not just anyone would read it.","What do you think of the other sages?","That learning many things doesn't teach understanding: otherwise it would have taught Hesiod, Pythagoras and Xenophanes. Homer deserves to be thrown out of the contests and flogged. The Ephesians should all go and hang themselves for having exiled my friend Hermodorus, the best of them.","Why are you weeping?","Raphael painted me alone, leaning on a block, writing, lost in thought. They called me «the weeping philosopher», as against Democritus, who laughs. I weep for the folly of men. I died, they say, covered in dung, trying to cure my dropsy. The gods have a sense of humour too.","What did you say to Alexander?","He came to see me in Corinth, when all the Greeks were flattering him. I was sunbathing. He said: «Ask me for whatever you like». I answered: «Stand aside, you're blocking my sun». His friends laughed, but he said: «If I weren't Alexander, I'd want to be Diogenes».","Why did you look for a man with a lamp?","I walked through the Agora in broad daylight with a lit lamp, saying: «I'm looking for a man». Real men, who live according to nature and reason, not slaves of opinion and luxury. I didn't find one. In Sparta there were boys; in Athens, not even that.","Why did you live in a jar?","A big clay jar, the kind for storing grain, beside the temple of the Mother of the Gods. What do I need a house for? One day I saw a child drinking water from his hands and threw away my bowl: that child had beaten me at simplicity. The less you have, the less has you.","What does it mean to be a cosmopolitan?","They asked me where I was from and I said: «A citizen of the world», kosmopolites. I don't belong to a city or its laws, but to nature. I'd been exiled from Sinope, for debasing the coinage, they say. Since then I've devoted myself to debasing the currency of custom.","How were you sold as a slave?","Pirates captured me and put me up for sale in Crete. The auctioneer asked what I could do. I said: «Govern men. Sell me to that one, he needs a master». A Corinthian, Xeniades, bought me and put me in charge of educating his sons. I educated them well.","What are the Elements?","Thirteen books in which I gather all known geometry in order: definitions, postulates, common notions and then propositions, each proved from those before it. The first theorem constructs an equilateral triangle. The last, the five regular solids. It will be used as a textbook for more than two thousand years.","What is the fifth postulate?","That through a point outside a line only one parallel passes, to put it my way. It's less obvious than the others, and many tried to prove it for centuries without success. Much later it was found that consistent geometries can be built without it. I suspected something: that's why I made it a postulate.","Are there infinitely many prime numbers?","Yes, and I proved it. Suppose there is a finite number of primes. Multiply them all together and add one. That number isn't divisible by any of them. So either it is prime or it has a new prime factor. Either way, there was another one. So they never run out.","What is the Museum of Alexandria?","An institution founded by King Ptolemy: scholars from all over the world, supported by the king, with an enormous library and gardens to walk in. I taught there. Medicine, astronomy, poetry and geometry were studied. A man asked what he'd gain by learning geometry, and I gave him three obols: «He needs to make a profit from what he learns».","Why am I bending down in the fresco?","Because I'm teaching some pupils with a pair of compasses on a slate. Raphael gave me the face of Bramante, his architect friend. It makes sense: an architect is a geometer too. And on the collar of my tunic Raphael hid his signature. You have to look at paintings carefully, like geometric figures.","What is the Almagest?","My great treatise on astronomy, the «Mathematical Syntaxis». The Arabs called it «the greatest», al-Majisti. I calculate the motion of the sun, moon and planets with tables, and there's a catalogue of over a thousand stars. For fourteen centuries it was the world's astronomy, until Copernicus.","What are epicycles?","The planets sometimes seem to go backwards in the sky. To explain it, I imagined each planet turning on a small circle, the epicycle, whose centre moves on a large circle around the Earth. And I added the equant, a point from which the motion appears uniform. It worked very well for prediction.","What is the Geography?","A book with the coordinates of some eight thousand places in the known world, in latitude and longitude, so maps can be drawn. I explained how to project the sphere of the Earth onto a plane. I got the size of Asia wrong, too big; centuries later, that encouraged Columbus to sail west.","Did you believe in astrology?","Yes, I wrote a book of astrology, the Tetrabiblos. In my day they weren't separate: if the sun changes the seasons and the moon the tides, why shouldn't the stars influence men? But I said it was a conjectural art, not exact like astronomy.","Why are you wearing a crown in the fresco?","Raphael confused me with the Ptolemaic kings of Egypt, who ruled Alexandria, and painted me with a crown. I wasn't a king: I was a scholar living in Alexandria in the time of the Roman emperors, some four centuries after Plato. I hold a celestial globe, facing Zoroaster.","What are good and evil?","Two twin spirits: the holy spirit and the destructive spirit. Every human being must choose between them in thought, word and deed. At the end of time good will triumph. The world is a battlefield, and we choose sides every day.","What are the Gathas?","Seventeen hymns I composed to Ahura Mazda, the Wise Lord, in a very ancient language of eastern Iran. They're the oldest part of the Avesta, the sacred book. For centuries they were handed down by memory, until they were written down. They're difficult even for those who recite them.","Why is fire sacred?","Because it is the image of Ahura Mazda's truth and purity. In the temples it is kept burning always. My faithful pray facing a light: fire, the sun. We don't worship fire but what it stands for. That's why it must not be defiled by corpses; we leave them in towers in the open air.","Who are the magi?","The priests of my religion in Persia. The Greeks admired and feared them: astronomers, interpreters of dreams. The word magic comes from their name. The Gospels tell of magi from the East who followed a star to Bethlehem. Plato, they say, wanted to meet them.","When did you live?","Nobody knows. The Greeks said six thousand years before Plato; scholars today think around 1000 BC, or somewhat later. The Achaemenid Persians, those of Darius and Xerxes, already honoured Ahura Mazda. My religion is still alive today: the Parsis of India and the Zoroastrians of Iran.","Who was your father?","Theon of Alexandria, mathematician and astronomer, the last known member of the Museum. He educated me himself, in mathematics, astronomy and philosophy, as he would a son. Together we prepared editions of Euclid and Ptolemy. Soon I surpassed him, his own pupils said.","What did you invent?","I improved instruments or taught how to build them: the plane astrolabe, for measuring the altitude of the stars; the hydroscope, for measuring the density of liquids. We know this from the letters of my pupil Synesius, who became a bishop and wrote asking for help with his instruments.","What did you teach in philosophy?","The Neoplatonism of Plotinus: that everything proceeds from the One and that the soul can rise towards it through reason. I walked about the city in the philosopher's cloak and explained Plato and Aristotle to anyone who would listen. My pupils were Christians and pagans alike.","Did you marry?","No. They say a pupil fell in love with me and, to cure him, I showed him a cloth stained with my menstrual blood: «This is what you love, and there is nothing beautiful about it». It's an oft-told story, perhaps invented. What is certain is that I devoted my life to study and teaching.","Why are you in the fresco?","It's not clear that I am. Many point to a figure dressed in white, standing and looking out at the viewer, between Parmenides and Pythagoras. Others say it's the young Duke of Urbino, Francesco Maria della Rovere. I, who come from the dream, stay in doubt, like a good philosopher.","What is the Garden?","My school in Athens, in a house with a kitchen garden on the outskirts. Friends lived there, men and women, even slaves, simply: bread, water and, on feast days, a little cheese. Over the gate it said: «Stranger, here you will do well to stay; here the highest good is pleasure».","What are atoms?","Invisible, indivisible particles moving in the void. Everything is made of them, the soul included. At death, they scatter. I took them from Democritus, but I added that sometimes they swerve a little at random: that swerve saves human freedom from blind fate.","Do the gods exist?","Yes, but they live happily in the spaces between the worlds and pay us no attention. A perfect being neither gets angry nor rewards. So there's no need to fear them. You can honour them by admiring their happiness, not by buying them with sacrifices.","What is friendship?","Of all the things wisdom provides for happiness, the greatest is friendship. More important than what you eat is whom you eat it with. A friend is not someone who always helps you, nor someone who never does: it's the confidence that he will.","What is the fourfold remedy?","Four sentences to heal the soul: the gods are not to be feared; death is not to be feared; the good is easy to obtain; evil is easy to bear. My disciples repeated it like a medicine. I died in terrible pain, and wrote to a friend that it was a happy day, remembering our conversations.","What is an epigram?","Originally, an inscription on a tomb or an offering: a few lines, because stone is expensive. I use it for everything: praising, mocking, asking for money, saying thank you for a dinner. The key is the ending, the point, the punch that makes you laugh. If an epigram is long, it's no longer an epigram.","Whom do you make fun of?","Vices, not people: I change the names. The man who dyes his hair, the doctor who was an undertaker yesterday, the poet who forces his verses on you, the stingy rich man, the old woman who marries for money. «My page is lewd, my life is clean», I say. As for the powerful, better to praise them.","What is Bilbilis like?","A town in Hispania, in Celtiberia, on a hill by the river Salo. They work iron there, tempered in the river's icy water, and it comes out the best in the world. Everything is cheap there and the people are simple. Here in Rome I miss it every winter, and every winter I stay.","Who are your friends?","Other Spaniards, mostly: Quintilian, from Calagurris; Lucan and Seneca, from Corduba, though they're dead now, Nero killed them. Also young Pliny, who is generous. A poet needs rich friends to invite him to dinner. Otherwise he dines at home: a leek and an onion.","What do you think of Rome?","That it's impossible to sleep: the bakers at night, the schoolmasters at dawn, the coppersmiths' hammers all day. That everything is expensive. That you have to go and greet your patron in a toga, which weighs a ton. And yet everyone is here. Books are published here. Here you become famous.","What is rhetoric?","The art of speaking well. It has five parts: finding the arguments, arranging them, choosing the words, memorising it all and delivering it with the right voice and gesture. A good speech has an introduction, a narration, proofs, a refutation and a conclusion. But above all: the orator must be a good man skilled in speaking.","How do you memorise a speech?","With the memory palace: you picture a house you know well and place each part of the speech in a room, with a striking image: an anchor to talk about the fleet, a spear for war. Then, as you speak, you walk through the house in your mind. Simonides invented the method.","Who pays you?","The emperor Vespasian appointed me the first professor of rhetoric paid by the state: a hundred thousand sesterces a year. Before that each teacher charged his pupils. It's an honour and a responsibility. Some say it's to keep the orators happy with the emperor. I just teach.","What should young people read?","First, Homer and Virgil, to elevate the spirit. Then tragedies, for gravity; Menander's comedies, for everyday life; historians, like Livy, for their elegance; and above all Cicero, the perfect model. Whoever enjoys reading Cicero knows he has made progress.","How should children be raised?","You must start early, as soon as they speak: the nurse must speak well, because what we hear first sticks to us. School is better than a tutor at home, so the child learns alongside others. And let him learn through play: with ivory letters. A good teacher praises more than he punishes.","How did you survive at Jotapata?","I commanded the Jewish forces in Galilee. After a forty-seven-day siege the city fell and I hid in a cave with forty men who preferred death to surrender. We drew lots to kill one another. In the end two of us were left, another man and I, and we surrendered. Luck or the providence of God? Let the reader judge.","What did you prophesy to Vespasian?","When they brought me before him, I told him he would be emperor, he and his son after him. Two years later the army of the East proclaimed him. He freed me and I took his family name: Flavius. Now I live in his old house and receive a pension. My people call me a traitor. I believe I saved what could be saved.","What is Masada?","A fortress on top of a rock by the Dead Sea, built by Herod. The last rebels, the Sicarii, held out there three years after Jerusalem fell. The Romans built an enormous ramp. When they got in, everyone was dead: they had killed themselves rather than be slaves. Almost a thousand people.","The history of the Jewish War, first in Aramaic for the Jews of the East, now in Greek, with assistants who correct me. Vespasian and Titus have read it and approved it. One day I want to write the whole history of my people, from the creation of the world, so that the Greeks and Romans will know us.","What is the arch they're building?","At the end of the Forum an arch will be raised in Titus' honour, with reliefs of the triumph: the soldiers carrying the seven-branched candlestick from the Temple, the silver trumpets, the table of the showbread. For the Romans it's a victory. For me, the picture of what we lost.","Who is your master?","Epaphroditus, a freedman who was Nero's secretary and helped him to die. He's rich and powerful. He lets me go and listen to Musonius Rufus, the philosopher. They say he'll free me one day. But I'm already free in what matters. He, on the other hand, is a slave to his fear of the new emperor.","What is up to us?","Our opinions, desires and aversions: everything that is our own doing. Not up to us are the body, wealth, reputation, office: everything that is not our own doing. If you desire what is not up to you, you'll be miserable. If you desire only what is up to you, nobody can stop you.","What makes us suffer?","Not things, but our opinions about things. Death is not terrible: if it were, it would have seemed so to Socrates. What is terrible is the opinion that it is terrible. When you get angry or sad, don't blame others, but your own opinion.","How should we treat others?","If someone insults you, think: he does it because he thinks he's right. If he's wrong, the harm is his. Be like an actor in a play: the author decides whether you play a king or a beggar. Your job is to play well the part you've been given. Choosing it belongs to another.","What would you do if they exiled you?","I'd go. Can they stop me going with a smile? Can they chain me? My leg, yes; my will, not even Zeus can conquer. If they exiled me, I'd teach philosophy wherever I was. Perhaps one day, if the emperor expels the philosophers, I'll open a school at Nicopolis, in Epirus.","What should one eat?","Simple food, prepared without fire if possible: fruit, vegetables, milk, cheese, honey. Meat is more fit for wild beasts and dulls the mind. Eating isn't for pleasure but for living. Whoever lives to eat is a slave to his stomach, the worst of masters.","What is marriage?","A partnership of life and of bodies, for having children but above all for caring for each other, in health and in sickness. Husband and wife should compete in who loves more. And fidelity applies to both: if a husband may sleep with a slave woman, then a wife may with a slave man; and that seems unacceptable to us. So, neither of them.","Must children always obey?","A father must be obeyed in what is just. If the father orders something wrong, the son obeys the common father of all, Zeus, who commands us to do good. If a father forbids his son to study philosophy, the son should study it anyway, for that is how he truly honours his father.","What happened with Nero?","He exiled me to Gyaros, a desert island in the Cyclades, without water. Then they put me to work on the Corinth canal, in chains, digging. There a philosopher recognised me and I said to him: «Does it grieve you to see me digging the Isthmus? Bearing cold and heat, hunger and thirst, sleeping on the ground; that way the body toughens and the soul learns it doesn't need luxuries. A philosophy lesson that doesn't change your life is like a doctor who explains the medicine to you but doesn't give it to you.","What did you do in Britain?","I was governor for three years. Now Agricola governs there, pushing north towards Caledonia. He's the father-in-law of my young friend Tacitus.","What are stratagems?","I'm compiling a book of the great generals' tricks of war: how to hide your plans, how to panic the enemy, how to deceive during a siege. Hannibal tied torches to the horns of oxen so the Romans would think his army was escaping another way. A general reads so he doesn't have to invent.","How is water measured?","By the mouths of the bronze pipes that leave the reservoirs, the calices, with official sizes: the quinaria, the smallest. Whoever has the right to water at home pays according to the bore. But there's cheating: pipes bigger than authorised, illegal connections. The plumbers, bribed, turn a blind eye.","What is the Aqua Marcia?","The most prized aqueduct: it brings cold, pure water from the mountains, more than ninety kilometres. The praetor Quintus Marcius Rex built it over two centuries ago, with money from the spoils of Carthage and Corinth. It's the water the rich drink. Other aqueducts, like the Anio Vetus, bring muddy water, good only for irrigation.","Why are aqueducts better than the pyramids?","Because they're useful. The pyramids of Egypt and the famous works of the Greeks are idle: they serve no purpose. Our aqueducts, with their arches striding across the valleys, give water to a million people: fountains, baths, houses, gardens. That is the greatness of Rome.","What did your uncle write?","The Natural History, thirty-seven books with everything he knew about the world: astronomy, geography, animals, plants, medicines, metals, stones, painting and sculpture. He read or had someone read to him at all times, even in the bath, and took notes. He used to say no book is so bad that it hasn't something good in it.","What was your uncle like?","He slept little, worked at night, always had a secretary with tablets at hand. He adopted me in his will: that's why I bear his name.","What do you study?","Rhetoric with Quintilian. I want to be an advocate and a senator, as my uncle wished. I also write verse, bad verse, and letters, lots of letters.","How did you and your mother escape?","We were at Misenum, across the bay. The day after the eruption, the earth shook so much that we left the town with a crowd. The sea was drawing back from the shore. A black cloud came down over the water and covered everything. It was night in broad daylight. My mother begged me to flee alone; I refused. Then the ash thinned out.","What is the pine-tree cloud?","The cloud from Vesuvius rose high like a trunk and then spread into branches, like one of the pines we have here. Sometimes white, sometimes dirty, depending on whether it carried earth or ash. One day I'll describe it in a letter to a historian friend, Tacitus, if he asks me. Scientists will name that kind of eruption after it.","What is Germania?","The land beyond the Rhine, of forests and marshes, where free peoples live, tall, blue-eyed and red-haired. One day I want to write about them.","Who is Agricola?","My father-in-law, the governor of Britain, a man of integrity. He's conquering the north of the island. I married his daughter three years ago. When he dies, if he dies before me, I'll write his life, so that people know a man can be good even under bad emperors.","What do you think of the emperors?","That Augustus took all power little by little, on the pretext of peace, and the Romans, weary of civil wars, gave it to him. Since then there's been little freedom. Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero are no good examples. Vespasian was better. Titus shows promise. We'll see.","What happened in the year of the four emperors?","Eleven years ago, after Nero died, four emperors followed one another in a single year: Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian. The legions discovered a secret: that an emperor can be made outside Rome. There was fighting in the streets and the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol burned.","How should history be written?","«Without anger and without partiality», though it isn't always achieved. You must tell the facts and seek the causes, but also judge: so that good deeds are not forgotten and bad ones fear the infamy of posterity. And briefly: a sentence should say a great deal.","What is Prusa?","My city, in Bithynia, at the foot of the Mysian Mount Olympus, in Asia. It has hot springs, good wine and a great deal of local politics: everyone wants to be first. My family is rich and has served the city. Here in Rome I have powerful friends, but sometimes I miss Prusa.","What is the Second Sophistic?","That's what they'll call our age. Greek orators are in fashion again: we give lectures in the theatres, improvise speeches on any subject, imitate the language of the ancient Athenians. The public applauds us like actors. Some get rich. I'd rather be called a philosopher.","What is the Euboean Discourse?","One I want to write: a shipwreck on Euboea and some poor hunters who take me in up in the hills. They live happily, without money, on what the land gives. I want to show that the poor can live with dignity, and that cities should care for honest work, not for the rich and their luxuries.","What do you think of the Romans?","That they govern the world well and their own city badly. They've brought peace, roads, law. But many are coarse and love gladiatorial combats, which we Greeks learned only from them. In Athens they're now held in the theatre of Dionysus. A philosopher criticised them and was answered with stones.","What is a good king?","One who governs as a shepherd tends his flock, not as a butcher. Who works harder than anyone, doesn't let himself be flattered, has true friends and is loved, not feared. The bad king is a tyrant enslaved to his passions. Not like the poets' mistresses, who never existed: real love, married love, fifteen years together. I speak frankly, without shame, and that scandalises some. Martial praises me: he says no woman should read anything else, nor any man.","Who was the other Sulpicia?","A noble girl of Augustus' time, niece of Messalla, the patron of poets. I bear her name with pride.","How are girls educated?","Girls from well-off families go to primary school with the boys, sometimes for longer. Then, with a grammarian, they read the poets. Many learn Greek, music and dance. Then, at twelve or fourteen, they marry. Those of us who keep studying do so at home, with books and tutors.","What is a matrona?","The married woman, mother of a family, respected. She wears the long stola and covers her hair in public. Today many matronae have fortunes and businesses of their own.","Which deities do women honour?","Juno, who protects marriage and childbirth; the Bona Dea, whose rites are for women only, held at night in a magistrate's house: almost a century and a half ago Clodius sneaked in disguised and there was a scandal; Vesta, at the hearth; and the Fortune of women, Fortuna Muliebris, whose temple was founded by the matronae who persuaded Coriolanus not to attack Rome.","What is opus caementicium?","Concrete: lime, water and stones, and the secret, the volcanic sand of Puteoli, the pulvis puteolana, which sets even under water. It's poured between two walls of brick or stone, which act as formwork. That's how harbours, vaults and domes are built. The Greeks didn't know it.","How was the Amphitheatre built?","In under ten years, on top of the lake of Nero's Golden House, which was drained. I have ideas: huge vaulted halls, courtyards with fountains, a private stadium.","Who is Vitruvius?","An architect of Augustus' time who wrote ten books on architecture. He says every building needs three things: firmness, usefulness and beauty. He talks about the orders, the proportions of the human body, machines, water clocks. All architects read him.","What is a codex?","A book of parchment leaves folded and sewn together, like wax tablets, instead of a roll. It fits in one hand, you can take it on a journey, you can open it at any page. Martial sells his epigrams that way, for travellers. They say it's a fad. I think one day it will replace the roll.","A book of Martial's epigrams, well turned out, the roll smoothed with pumice and dyed purple, five denarii. A plain one, less. Copying a long book takes days: I have slave copyists who write at the dictation of a reader, several at once. That way dozens of copies come out.","Does the author earn anything from his books?","Little or nothing. The bookseller pays the author for the first copy or pays him nothing; after that anyone can copy it. The author gains fame, and fame brings rich patrons who give him presents. Martial complains that his books are read even in Britain and he's still poor.","What is a recitatio?","A public reading: the author gathers his friends in a hall or in the forum and reads his new work. It's like publishing. Pliny the Younger goes to a lot of them. Sometimes the audience gets bored, leaves halfway through or stays outside chatting until the end. Some pay a claque to applaud them.","What is the Argiletum?","The booksellers' street, between the Forum and the Subura. The shops have the columns at their doors covered in notices listing the titles for sale. Poets drop by to see whether their books are on display. Some spend hours reading without buying. Those I throw out.","What types of gladiator are there?","The murmillo, with a fish-shaped helmet, a large shield and a short sword; the thraex, with a small shield and a curved sword; the retiarius, with net and trident and no helmet; the secutor, who chases the retiarius in a smooth helmet; the hoplomachus, like a Greek hoplite. They're paired so the fight is evenly matched.","What is the ludus?","The gladiator school. Next to the amphitheatre is the Ludus Magnus, with its own training arena. There we live, eat and train with wooden weapons against a post. A lanista buys us and hires us out to the organisers. We eat a lot: barley and beans. They call us the barley-eaters.","What do gladiators swear?","On entering the ludus we swear to let ourselves be burned, chained, flogged and killed by the sword. It's the most terrible oath. In return, if you survive and win, you can become famous, rich and, in the end, free. Some free men hire themselves out as gladiators of their own will: for money or for glory.","What is the munus?","Originally, the fights were a gift to a dead man: they were held at the funerals of great men, to honour their spirit with blood. The first were more than three centuries ago. Then they became a political show. Today the emperor pays for them, and he decides who lives.","What do you do now that you're free?","I received the rudis, the wooden sword. I could train others as an instructor, a doctor, or go back to fighting for a lot of money. Women look at me, children draw my face on the walls of Pompeii… well, not in Pompeii any more. I don't know. The arena is the only thing I know how to do.","What is the fire of Vesta?","The hearth fire of Rome, which must never go out. If it goes out, it's a terrible omen, and the guilty Vestal is flogged by the pontifex maximus. It's relit from the sun, with a mirror. Every year, on the first of March, the sacred fire is renewed.","What does the temple keep?","Sacred objects nobody may see except us: they say the Palladium, the statue of Athena that Aeneas brought from Troy. If it falls into enemy hands, Rome falls. The temple is round, like the huts of the first Romans. Next to it is our house, the Atrium Vestae.","How is a Vestal chosen?","The pontifex maximus, now the emperor, chooses girls of six to ten, from noble families, with both parents living and without blemish. He takes them by the hand and says: «I take you, beloved». We serve thirty years: ten learning, ten serving, ten teaching. After that we may marry. Few do.","What is the mola salsa?","A flour of roasted spelt mixed with salt that we prepare ourselves from the grain of the first ears, gathered in May. It's sprinkled on the heads of sacrificial animals: that's where the word immolate comes from. We also prepare the brine, the muries, and the sacred water, which must not touch the ground.","Which wills do you keep?","The most important in Rome: Julius Caesar and Augustus left their wills with the Vestals. We're trustworthy: if a Vestal crosses paths with a condemned man on his way to execution, he is pardoned. We have a lictor, seats of honour in the theatre, and we can give evidence without taking an oath.","What is an Augustalis?","We rich freedmen can't be magistrates, but we can belong to the Augustales, who organise the emperor's cult in each town. We pay for games, banquets, statues. In return we sit in places of honour and wear insignia. It's our way of being somebody.","What about freedmen's children?","They're born free, full citizens. They can have careers, become knights and even senators. I can't; my son can. The poet Horace was a freedman's son. That's why I spend on my son's education: a Greek tutor, a rhetorician. So nobody can tell where he comes from.","How do you dress?","At festivals I wear a gold ring, which the emperor granted me, and a white toga like any citizen's. At home, coloured clothes, yes, perhaps too many. The nobles laugh at rich freedmen: they say we overdo the luxury, that we count our money out loud. Let them laugh. They eat at my dinners.","What did you do when you were a slave?","I came from Asia as a boy. I was handsome and clever, and my master put me to keeping the accounts. For fourteen years I was his favourite. With my peculium, the money a master lets a slave keep, I bought my freedom. Then I inherited part of his fortune. Talented slaves are worth more free.","What will you put on your tomb?","A relief with my ships, my coins and my family. And an inscription: «Gaius Pompeius Hermeros, freedman, Augustalis. He started with nothing and left thirty million. He never listened to a philosopher». Let it be known that he lived well. We freedmen fill the roads of Rome with big tombs.","What is the sportula?","A little basket of food or money that the patron gives his clients every morning. Now it's nearly always money: six and a quarter sesterces. You can barely eat on that. That's why some clients greet three or four patrons every morning, running from house to house all over the Esquiline.","What does your patron ask of you?","To escort him to the Forum, so people see he has a big following. To applaud him in court and at readings. To vote for whoever he says, back when there were real elections. In return he defends me in lawsuits, lends me money, invites me to dinner now and then. At the bottom of the table, with the worst wine.","What is the toga?","The citizens' garment: a great semicircle of white wool almost six metres long, wrapped around the body without pins. It's heavy and hot, and you need help to put it on properly. It's compulsory for the salutatio. Senators wear it with a purple stripe. Mine is worn thin from so much washing.","Where do you live?","On the third floor of an insula in the Subura, with my wife and children, in two rooms. No water, no kitchen, no latrine: we buy cooked food at the taverns. The rent goes up every year. The rich have houses with gardens on the Palatine or the Esquiline. We have windows looking onto the neighbour.","What was Rome like in the days of the Republic?","They say patron and client were like father and son: they defended each other to the death, and betraying a client was as serious as betraying your parents. The Twelve Tables curse the patron who cheats his client. Today it's all money. My grandfather voted in the assemblies; I only applaud.","How much does a praetorian earn?","Much more than a legionary: about three thousand sesterces a year, three times as much. We serve sixteen years instead of twenty-five and live in Rome, not on the frontier. When we retire, a good lump sum. And when a new emperor takes the throne, he gives us a present, the donativum. That's why everyone envies us.","What is the camp?","The Castra Praetoria, on the north-eastern edge of the city: a huge rectangular camp with brick walls. There live the nine thousand of us in the praetorian cohorts. Sejanus built it for Tiberius. From there we control Rome. Whoever controls the camp controls the emperor.","What does a legionary carry?","Helmet, armour of iron strips, a curved rectangular shield, the scutum; two javelins, the pila, which bend on impact so the enemy can't throw them back; a short sword, the gladius; a dagger. Plus tools, a cooking pot, food for three days. That's why they call us Marius' mules.","What happened with Caligula?","Officers of our guard killed him in a corridor on the Palatine, after the games. Then we found his uncle Claudius hiding behind a curtain, trembling, and made him emperor. The Senate didn't dare say a word. That shows who really rules in Rome.","Who commands you now?","Titus himself was our prefect during his father's reign, and he was hard: he had suspects killed without trial. Now he's emperor and seems a different man: he says he hasn't wasted a single day without doing someone some good. We'll see how long it lasts.","What is the Circus Maximus like?","The biggest building in Rome: more than six hundred metres long, between the Palatine and the Aventine. It holds a hundred and fifty thousand people, perhaps more. In the middle, the spina, with obelisks, statues and the lap counters: seven eggs and seven dolphins that are turned one by one. Seven laps per race.","What are the metae?","The conical posts at each end of the spina, where you turn. It's the most dangerous moment: you have to hug them as tightly as you can without crashing. Many chariots overturn there; we call it a naufragium, a shipwreck. I wear the reins tied round my waist and carry a knife to cut them if I fall, or the horses drag me.","Which horses are the best?","Those from Hispania and Africa, fast and hardy. The most important is the left-hand horse, the one hugging the turning post: he has to be the cleverest. Famous horses have names and fans, like the charioteers. Some say Caligula wanted to make his horse Incitatus consul. Exaggerations… or not.","Are charioteers famous?","More than the consuls. The best win thousands of races and millions of sesterces, more than a senator. There are statues of them. But most die young. A charioteer who reaches thirty-five with all his bones intact is a wise old man.","What are curse tablets?","Sheets of lead with curses against rival charioteers and horses: «Bind the horses of the Blues, may they not run, may they fall at the turn». They're buried near the circus or in tombs. Fans buy them from magicians. I wear amulets. You never know.","What is Ostia?","Rome's port, at the mouth of the Tiber. The big grain ships unload at Claudius' new harbour, which has a lighthouse built on top of the ship that brought the Vatican obelisk, sunk and filled with concrete. From there the cargo goes up the river in barges towed by oxen to the Emporium.","What are the horrea?","The warehouses. Huge brick buildings around a courtyard, with rooms for storing grain, oil, wine and spices. The Horrea Galbana, behind the Emporium, are the biggest. Grain is stored on raised floors so it won't get damp. There are watchmen day and night.","What are the risks of trade?","Shipwrecks, pirates, storms, grain rotting. That's why the emperor Claudius offered insurance: if the ship sinks, the state pays. And privileges for shipowners who build big ships for the annona. Even so, one bad winter can ruin you. We sail from spring to autumn.","What other goods arrive?","Oil from Baetica, in Hispania: it comes in round amphorae, the Dressel 20, which are smashed afterwards on Monte Testaccio. Wine from Gaul and Italy, garum from Hispania and Mauretania, marble from Greece and Egypt, spices from India, silk from China, which arrives through a thousand hands.","What is garum?","A sauce of fermented fish: mackerel or tuna innards with salt, left in the sun for months. It smells awful and tastes divine. It goes on almost everything. The best, from Carthago Nova in Hispania, sells at a fortune: the garum sociorum. The Jews have a special one, without unclean fish.","What rooms do the baths have?","The changing room, apodyterium; the tepidarium, warm; the caldarium, hot, with a hot pool and a cold-water basin to cool off; sometimes the laconicum, with dry heat, like a sauna; and the frigidarium, with a cold pool. Plus an open-air exercise ground, the palaestra, and gardens.","What do people do at the baths?","Everything: bathing, exercising with balls or weights, getting oil massages, having hair removed, eating a snack, chatting, reading in the library, doing business. Seneca, who lived above a bathhouse, complained of the noise: shouting, the slap of massage, sausage-sellers and hair-pluckers crying out for customers.","How much does it cost to get in?","A quadrans, the smallest coin: practically free. Children don't pay. Sometimes a rich man or the emperor pays everyone's entry for a day. That's why everyone, rich and poor, bathes here. Titus sometimes comes to bathe with the people: it's his way of winning them over.","Is it hygienic?","More or less. The water is changed, but not as often as it should be, and sick people with wounds go in to bathe. Doctors prescribe baths for everything. Martial mocks people who bathe with wounds. There are public latrines next to the baths, of marble, with running water underneath: there you chat with your neighbour.","What baths are there in Rome?","Agrippa's, next to the Pantheon, the first great ones; Nero's, in the Campus Martius, of which Martial says: «What's worse than Nero? And now these, Titus', next to the amphitheatre, built in a rush for the opening.","How do you put out a fire?","With chains of esparto buckets coated in pitch, passing water hand to hand from the fountains; with piston water pumps, the siphones; with blankets soaked in vinegar and hooks to pull down the neighbouring houses and make a firebreak. Sometimes a whole block has to be knocked down to save the neighbourhood.","Why do the insulae burn so easily?","They're tall, six or seven storeys, of wood and poor brick, with braziers and oil lamps in every room. The streets are narrow. Augustus limited the height to seventy feet; Nero, after the great fire, ordered more stone and porticoes. Builders still cheat.","What other duties do you have?","We patrol at night: we're also the night police. We arrest thieves and watch the baths, where clothes get stolen. We remind people to keep water at home. The prefect of the vigiles tries petty crimes. There are seven cohorts, one for every two districts of Rome.","Who founded the vigiles?","Augustus, almost ninety years ago, after many fires. Before that there were only public slaves, and a certain Crassus, the rich one, had his own brigade: when a house was burning, he bought it cheap before putting the fire out. We vigiles are mostly freedmen. After six years' service we're given full citizenship.","What burned this year?","A few months ago, while Titus was in Campania because of Vesuvius, the Campus Martius burned for three days: the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol, just rebuilt, the Pantheon, the Baths of Agrippa, the Theatre of Pompey. We fought it for days on end. Titus is now paying for the rebuilding out of his own pocket.","What is the lituus?","My curved staff, without knots. With it I mark out in the sky the sacred space, the templum, where I watch the birds. Romulus had one; they say it was found unharmed after a fire. It's our symbol: it appears on the coins of emperors who are augurs.","What are the sacred chickens?","Armies carry them in cages. Before a battle they're fed: if they eat eagerly and food drops from their beaks, it's a good omen. An admiral, Claudius Pulcher, seeing they wouldn't eat, threw them into the sea: «Let them drink, if they won't eat». He lost the battle and the fleet.","Who are the haruspices?","Etruscan seers who read the entrails of sacrificed animals, especially the liver, divided into regions belonging to the gods. They also interpret lightning and portents. There's a bronze model of a liver at Placentia with the gods' names on it. We augurs are Roman; they're Etruscan.","What are the Sibylline Books?","Books of prophecy that the Sibyl of Cumae sold to King Tarquin. She asked a price and he refused; she burned three and asked the same for the remaining six; she burned another three, and he paid for the last three the price of all nine. They're consulted in times of disaster. Fifteen priests keep them.","What is religion for a Roman?","More than believing, it's doing: performing the rites exactly, in the right order, with the right words. If there's a mistake, everything must be repeated. It's a pact: we give, the gods give. Do ut des. Every house has its Lares and Penates, and every place its genius. There are gods for everything.","What do you do at your meetings?","We meet in houses, on the first day of the week, before dawn, because many of us are slaves and have to work. We sing hymns to Christ, read letters from the apostles, share a meal and the bread and wine in memory of Jesus. We help widows and orphans.","Who were Peter and Paul?","Two apostles of Jesus who died here in Rome under Nero. Peter, a fisherman from Galilee, crucified on the Vatican hill. Paul, a Roman citizen from Tarsus, beheaded on the road to Ostia. Paul wrote a letter to our community in Rome; in it he greets a Junia, who was an apostle.","Why do they hate you?","Because we don't worship the gods of Rome or the emperor, and they think that brings misfortune. They call us atheists. They say we eat human flesh because we speak of the body and blood of Christ, and that we do terrible things at night. Many educated Romans call us a superstition.","Who becomes a Christian?","Mostly humble people: slaves, freedmen, craftsmen, women. But also some from important families. Women are given a place: there are deaconesses and women who host the community in their homes, like Priscilla with her husband Aquila.","Where do you bury your dead?","The Romans burn their dead; we, like the Jews, bury them, because we await the resurrection. That's why we buy plots outside the walls, along the roads. One day galleries will be dug underground to bury thousands of our brothers and sisters.","Who was Asclepiades of Bithynia?","My namesake, who a century and a half ago brought Greek medicine to Rome with success: he prescribed baths, walks, wine and massage instead of purges and bleeding. He said healing should be safe, swift and pleasant.","What do the Romans think of doctors?","Cato the Elder hated Greek doctors: he said they had sworn to kill all barbarians with their medicines, and that to them we Romans were barbarians. He cured himself with cabbage. Pliny the Elder was suspicious too. Today almost all the doctors in Rome are Greeks, and many are freedmen.","How do you operate?","With bronze and iron instruments: scalpels, forceps, probes, hooks, bone saws, specula. You operate fast, because the pain is terrible; wine or poppy is given. Celsus says a surgeon should be young, with steady hands, and unmoved by screams. Cataracts are operated on with a needle.","What are the humours?","According to Hippocrates, the body has four humours: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. Health is their balance. If there's too much of one, it must be drawn off: bleeding, purges, vomiting. Diet and the seasons affect them. A melancholic has too much black bile.","What is a military doctor?","Every legion has doctors and a hospital, the valetudinarium, with well-ventilated rooms for the wounded. Dioscorides, who wrote about medicinal plants, travelled with the army.","What is the Art of Love?","Three books by Ovid with advice on seduction: where to find a partner in Rome (the theatre, the circus), how to make someone fall in love, how to keep love alive. But Augustus, who was passing laws on morality, didn't find it funny at all.","What are the Heroides?","Imaginary letters from heroines to their absent lovers: Penelope to Ulysses, Dido to Aeneas, Ariadne to Theseus, Medea to Jason, Sappho to Phaon. Ovid gives a voice to the women of myth, abandoned or waiting. Some read like real laments. It's what I like most about him.","What are the Fasti?","A poetic calendar of Rome's festivals, month by month, with their myths and origins. Ovid wrote only six books, January to June; exile cut off the rest. If you want to know why the city is purified in February or what happens at the Lupercalia, read it.","What is your favourite metamorphosis?","Pyramus and Thisbe, two young people in Babylon who talk through a crack in the wall. They arrange to meet by a mulberry tree; she arrives first, flees from a lioness and drops her veil. He finds it stained with blood and kills himself. She comes back and kills herself too. The mulberries, once white, turn red for ever.","How does Ovid end the Metamorphoses?","With a challenge: «I have finished a work that neither the wrath of Jupiter, nor fire, nor iron, nor time can destroy. Hannibal, with fewer men, let the Romans push back the centre of his army, then surrounded them with his wings and his cavalry. Fifty thousand Romans died in a single day. Livy says Hannibal sent to Carthage a bushel of gold rings taken from the dead knights.","Why did Livy write?","So that the Romans would see in their past examples of virtue: the courage, piety and simplicity of the ancients. Livy taught history to the young Claudius.","What is Patavium?","My city and Livy's, in northern Italy, near the Alps: rich, with a reputation for strict morals. Envy!","Who was Ambivius Turpio?","My namesake and model, the great troupe manager of Terence's day. He staged all of his comedies and rescued two of them when the audience booed: The Mother-in-Law failed twice, because people left to watch tightrope walkers and gladiators. He persisted, and the third time it was a triumph.","What were theatres like before?","Wooden ones, put up for each festival and taken down afterwards. Pompey built the first stone one, a hundred and thirty years ago, and put a temple of Venus on top of the seating so it would look like a shrine.","What is pantomime?","What the public loves today: a single masked dancer who acts out every character of a myth with gestures, while a chorus sings and pipes and cymbals play. Famous pantomimes are stars, adored by the ladies. Plautus' comedies are performed less and less.","What are the ludi?","The public games, religious festivals with shows: the Roman Games in September, the Plebeian in November, the Apollinarian, the Megalensian in April, in honour of the Great Mother. Many of Plautus' and Terence's comedies premiered at them. The aediles organise them, paying out of their own pockets to win votes.","Why were actors looked down on?","Actors were nearly always slaves or freedmen, and the law stripped them of rights: a citizen who acted lost his honour. They could be flogged. Today some are rich and famous, friends of emperors, like the pantomime Paris. But a senator who sets foot on stage is still a scandal, like Nero.","What is Vulgar Latin?","The Latin people speak in the street, different from Cicero's.
