From this street Latin, centuries from now, Spanish, Catalan, French, Italian will come…","What is grammar?","The art of reading and writing correctly and explaining the poets. The grammarian teaches the parts of speech, declensions and conjugations, metre, and comments on Virgil line by line. Remmius Palaemon, a freedman, was the great grammarian of a few years ago. He earned a fortune.","Who was Verrius Flaccus?","My namesake, a grammarian of Augustus' time, who educated the emperor's grandsons and wrote a great dictionary, On the Meaning of Words, explaining old and rare words. He also made a stone calendar at Praeneste. He was as famous for rewarding his pupils with books as for punishing them.","What are abbreviations?","On inscriptions everything is abbreviated to save stone: SPQR, the Senate and People of Rome; DM, to the spirits of the dead, on tombs; STTL, may the earth lie light on you. And in letters, SVBEEV: if you are well, good; I am well. You have to learn them to read any wall in Rome.","How do you tell the time?","The day has twelve hours, from sunrise to sunset, so in summer they're long and in winter short. The sixth hour is noon: that's where the Spanish word siesta comes from. The night is divided into four watches, like soldiers' guard duties. Sundials and water clocks mark the hours. Nobody agrees.","What materials do you use?","Wooden tablets coated with wax, written on with a point, the stilus, and rubbed out with its flat end to write again. For practice, also pebbles and abacuses for counting. Papyrus is expensive: only for the older ones. The youngest children learn their letters by tracing grooves carved in wood.","How do you count?","On the fingers, with a system that lets you count into the thousands, and on the abacus: pebbles, calculi, in columns of units, tens and hundreds. That's where the word calculation comes from. Numbers are written with letters: I, V, X, L, C, D, M. Adding is easy; for multiplying, better use the abacus.","What is the paedagogus?","A slave, often Greek, who takes the child to school, carries his books and watches over him. He teaches him manners and sometimes Greek. Little Pliny, Quintilian, all had one. Some paedagogi are so loved that the children, once grown, give them tombs with affectionate inscriptions.","Are there holidays?","Yes: the festival days, which are many, especially the Saturnalia in December and the Quinquatria in March, the feast of Minerva, patroness of teachers. Copy and recite, copy and recite. Those who scribble on the walls write other things I won't repeat to you.","Aristeas of Metapontum","Claims to be Pythagoras reborn","Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans","By the entrance to the Academy","Pythagoras of Samos (c. 570-c. 495 BC) emigrated around 530 to Croton, in southern Italy, where he founded a philosophical and religious community with political influence. He taught the immortality and transmigration of souls, a life of purity with ritual prohibitions, and the idea that number and proportion explain the order of the world and musical harmony. He wrote nothing; what we know comes from disciples and much later biographers, full of legends. Around 450 the Pythagorean communities were attacked in Croton and other cities; survivors like Philolaus and Lysis scattered across Greece. In 386, Archytas of Tarentum, Pythagorean, mathematician and statesman, was a friend of Plato's.","At last someone who looks me in the eye! They call me Aristaeus of Metapontum, but that's only the name of this body. I was Pythagoras, son of Mnesarchus, of Samos. I died more than a hundred years ago, and here I am again. Don't look at me like that: Pythagoras himself remembered having been Euphorbus, at Troy. Why shouldn't I remember having been Pythagoras?","Are you really Pythagoras?","That's what I say, and I say it slowly so they won't laugh. Souls don't die: they pass from one body to another, from man to animal and animal to man. Pythagoras remembered his lives because Hermes granted it to him. I remember a golden thigh, a city in Italy, a fire. Though, if you want the truth, what matters isn't whether I was him, but whether I live as he taught.","Who was Pythagoras?","I was born on Samos, son of a ring engraver, Mnesarchus. I travelled to Egypt and perhaps to Babylon to learn from the priests. When the tyrant Polycrates seized Samos, I left for Italy, for Croton, a hundred and fifty years ago. There I spoke to the young men in the gymnasium, to the elders in the council, to the women in the temple of Hera. And many followed me.","What did the Pythagoreans teach?","Three things, above all. That the soul is immortal and is reborn. That one must live purely so it is reborn better: not eating animals, not swearing falsely, examining oneself every night. And that the world is ordered by number: the notes of the lyre, the movements of the stars, the figures of geometry. To know numbers is to know the order of the cosmos.","What happened to the community?","We had so much influence in Croton and other cities that many hated us. They say I fled to Metapontum and starved to death there in a temple of the Muses. Perhaps that's why I've been reborn in Metapontum: the soul returns to where it left.","What did the Pythagoreans believe about the soul?","That it is immortal and reborn in other bodies, even animals'","That it dies with the body","That only philosophers have one","No. The Pythagoreans believed in transmigration: the soul is immortal and passes from one body to another, animals' included. Almost everything told about Pythagoras comes from biographies written centuries later and mixes legend and tradition; the game points this out where needed.","And the theorem?","The square built on the longest side of a right-angled triangle equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. The truth is the Babylonians already knew those numbers (three, four and five), but we look for the proof: why it is always so.","What are numbers to a Pythagorean?","They aren't only for counting: they have shape and character. One is the principle; two, the feminine; three, the masculine; four, justice, because it is equal times equal; five, marriage; ten, perfection. Numbers are drawn with pebbles: triangular, square, oblong. The even is unlimited; the odd, limited. The world is a mixture of limit and unlimited.","What are the akousmata?","The maxims that were heard and obeyed without question: don't eat beans, don't pick up what falls from the table, don't stir the fire with a knife, don't step over a balance, don't speak without a light, put on the right shoe first. Some disciples, the akousmatikoi, simply obeyed them. Others, the mathematikoi, looked for the reason behind them. Each side said the other weren't true Pythagoreans.","What legends are told about Pythagoras?","That he had a golden thigh and showed it to the sage Abaris, who travelled riding on an arrow; that he was seen on the same day in Croton and in Metapontum; that a river greeted him aloud as he crossed it; that he ordered a she-bear never to eat men again. Philolaus of Croton wrote the first Pythagorean book; he said there is a fire at the centre of the cosmos, and the Earth revolves around it. Lysis teaches young Epaminondas in Thebes. And in Tarentum Archytas governs, a great mathematician, who has solved the doubling of the cube and built a wooden dove that flew. He's a friend of Plato, who listens to us more than he admits. The walls were mud brick on a stone footing, with few windows onto the street. The andron, with its off-centre door and the floor edge prepared for couches, was the room where the master received his guests; the women had their rooms (gynaikeion), sometimes upstairs. The oikos was also the family and its property, slaves included. Sophists often gave their lessons in rich men's houses, like that of Callias described by Plato in the Protagoras.","Welcome home, master! I'm Xanthias. Callias, your host, has told me to serve you while you're in Athens: I sweep, shop at the market, mind the door and keep the accounts. If you'd like me to bring a sophist to teach here, in the andron, you only have to say so.","Is this house mine?","While you're in Athens, yes. But really it's Callias's. A foreigner can't own houses or land in Attica unless the Assembly grants him that privilege, which they call enktesis; even the richest metics rent. That's why Callias lends it to you. He's very fond of wise men: years ago, at his other house, Protagoras, Hippias and Prodicus all gathered at once, and half of Athens went to hear them.","What is an Athenian house like?","Like this one: from outside, an almost blind wall, with a door and the odd high window, so the women can't be seen and thieves can't get in. Inside, everything opens onto the courtyard: the portico at the back, where you work in the shade; the andron, for banquets; the storeroom and the kitchen; and upstairs, by a wooden staircase, the bedrooms and the women's quarters. The walls are mud brick: a thief can make a hole with a pick. He became famous for the «correctness of names»: precisely distinguishing words that seem synonymous, like disputing and quarrelling, or rejoicing and enjoying. He charged one drachma for a short lecture and fifty for the full one. His fable of Heracles at the crossroads, between Vice and Virtue, is known to us through Xenophon (Memorabilia II 1). Socrates thought well of him and sent him pupils.","Greetings, young host, and thank you for the warm wine; I have a delicate throat, you know. I am Prodicus, of Ceos. These boys come to hear me speak about the exactness of words. Listening is not the same as hearing, nor speaking the same as saying: you'll see.","How much do you charge?","It depends. For one drachma I give a sample: half an hour of what I know. For fifty drachmas, the complete course on the correctness of names, which leaves anyone speaking properly. Socrates says, laughing, that he could only afford the one-drachma lecture, and that's why he doesn't know the truth about names. He says it to annoy me, but he sends me pupils.","What is the use of distinguishing words?","To think clearly. If in the Assembly one man says «courage» and another understands «rashness», they argue without knowing about what. If a judge confuses «wanting» with «desiring», he condemns wrongly. Words are like coins: if you don't know which is silver and which is copper, you get cheated. Before arguing, you must agree on the names.","What do you think of the gods?","I think, and I say it quietly, that the first men called gods the things that were useful to them: the sun, the rivers, the springs. Yet Gorgias defends her, and wins.» That was how pupils trained: praising someone everyone criticises, or criticising someone everyone admires.","The argument has four cases. Helen went to Troy either by the will of the gods and of fate, and no one can resist the gods; or carried off by force, and then she is a victim; or persuaded by speech, and speech rules the soul as drugs rule the body; or in love, and love is a god or an illness. In all four cases she is innocent.","Gorgias ends by saying he wrote the speech «as praise of Helen and as a game for myself». Another: «Who learns, the wise or the ignorant?». Learning can mean «acquiring knowledge» or «understanding what you're told»: the sophist jumps from one sense to the other.","And the boldest: «No one can lie, because whoever speaks says something, and what is something exists; so he says what is, that is, the truth». Plato and, later, Aristotle will turn these games into the beginning of logic.","«Your dog is a father and it's yours: so it's your father». Each neighbourhood, the <b>vicus</b>, looks after it with its own magistrates, the <b>vicomagistri</b>, who are usually freedmen. Augustus reorganised Rome into 265 neighbourhoods and had his own Genius placed on these altars beside the Lares: so every neighbour honoured the emperor on his own corner.</p><p>In winter the <b>Compitalia</b> are celebrated, the festival of the crossroads, when even slaves have a holiday.</p><p class=\"sub\">Sources: Suetonius, Augustus 30-31; Ovid, Fasti V 129-148."," <b>It is Ianuarius: the Compitalia are on.</b>","<p>A pillar with three female figures standing back to back: <b>Hecate</b>, who watches all three roads of a crossroads at once. The sculptor Alcamenes made a famous one, with three bodies, at the entrance to the Acropolis: look for it beside the temple of Athena Nike.</p><p class=\"sub\">Sources: Pausanias II 30, 2; Aristophanes, Wasps 804 and Wealth 594-597. He dreams of one day writing the history of his time, “without anger and without partiality”. For that he needs witnesses. And you have a boat, and a wish to see the world.","Talk to Tacitus, by the Curia","You have shown that you know how to find the truth among papers and lies. I have a job for you. I want to write the history of these years: the Judaean war, the Rhine rebellion, Britain… and Vesuvius. But I don't trust what is told at banquets.","Find four witnesses: a survivor of Pompeii, a veteran of Jerusalem, someone from Colonia who lived through the revolt of Civilis, and a soldier of my father-in-law's in Britain. Ask them what they saw. I will pay for the journey.","Why does Tacitus want to talk to witnesses instead of copying what people say?","Because a historian must look for reliable sources, not rumours","Because that way he is paid more","Because the witnesses write better than he does","Exactly. Thucydides already said it: you must ask those who were there, and even then compare what they say.","No: a good historian looks for reliable sources and compares them. Banquet gossip is useless.","Look in Pompeii for Herennius, the survivor","A historian? Tell him it was not just the ash. First light stones fell all afternoon and all night; the roofs caved in. Many stayed at home, waiting. What killed them came in the morning: a burning cloud that came rushing down the mountain.","And tell him too that the emperor sent help. You have to give Titus that.","You write his words on your wax tablets. First testimony.","Look in Jerusalem for Lucius Antonius, the veteran","Let him write what it was: a terrible siege for both sides. Hunger inside the city, crucifixions outside. When the temple burned, nobody could tell me who gave the order.","And don't let him write that the Jews are cowards: they fought to the end. I know because I was facing them.","Many years later, Tacitus will write about the Jews with contempt and many errors. Historians do not always listen to their witnesses.","Look in Colonia for Ennius, the glassblower","The revolt of Civilis… The Germans from the other bank asked us to kill all the Romans in the city and pull down the walls. We said no: here we live mixed together, our children have Roman mothers.","We had to pretend to be with the rebels to survive. When the legions came back, they accused us of treason. That is war on a frontier.","Look in Agricola's camp for Titus Flavius","The general's son-in-law sent you? I will write it, even if it takes years.","And I will. I will write my father-in-law's life, then the Histories, then the Annals. And I will put into the mouth of a British chieftain what you have brought me from Britain: “Where they make a desert, they call it peace.”","Tacitus will write the Life of Agricola in 98, the Histories around 105 and the Annals around 115. Only part of his works survives.","You have travelled the empire from end to end looking for witnesses: Pompeii under the ash, Jerusalem in ruins, Colonia on the Rhine frontier and Agricola's camp in the north of Britain.","History is written with sources. Ancient historians, like Thucydides or Tacitus, looked for witnesses and documents, but they also had their prejudices and interests. See it in the menu (Tab) › Learn › What have I learned?"," touches your forehead…","A history lesson, with scenes imagined from what we know.","A myth, as the ancients told it.","Back to ","The Minoans","Crete, the island of palaces","Long ago, in the Bronze Age (around 3000-1450 BC), Crete was home to a people you do not remember by name. Around 1900 BC they built great palaces at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia: courtyards, storerooms, red columns that taper downwards, coloured frescoes. We call them «Minoans» after Minos, the king of your legends; we do not know what they called themselves.","Masters of the sea","They lived from the sea. Their ships carried oil, wine and textiles to Egypt, Cyprus and the Cyclades. Egyptian tombs show foreigners bringing gifts, the <i>keftiu</i>, whom almost everyone identifies with the Cretans. Thucydides says Minos was the first to have a fleet and clear the sea of pirates: that is a tradition, not a proven fact.","A script nobody can read","Scribes recorded on clay tablets what went in and out of the storerooms: grain, oil, sheep. They used a script we call <b>Linear A</b>. Even today nobody has managed to read it: we know they are accounts, but not what language they spoke.","Bulls and goddesses","In the frescoes of Knossos, young people leap over a bull by grabbing its horns. Figurines show women holding snakes, perhaps goddesses or priestesses. Many scholars think a great goddess played a central role, but their religion remains largely a mystery.","Around 1600 BC the volcano of Thera (Santorini) erupted and buried the town of Akrotiri; Crete suffered but stood. Around 1450 BC many palaces burned. Soon afterwards, at Knossos, scribes were writing in <b>Linear B</b>, which is Greek: the Mycenaeans of the mainland had taken the island.","Thucydides I 4; frescoes and tablets of Knossos (excavations by A. Evans from 1900); J. L. Fitton, <i>Minoans</i>.","The Mycenaeans","Citadels of stone","Between 1600 and 1200 BC, on the mainland, some Greeks built citadels: Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos, Thebes… and right here, on this Acropolis. Their walls are so huge that you say the Cyclopes built them. At the entrance to Mycenae, two stone lions have guarded the gate for almost nine hundred years.","The wanax and his scribes","A king ruled, the <i>wanax</i> (your <i>ánax</i>), from a palace that collected and redistributed goods. His scribes used Linear B, a very old form of your language. The tablets already name gods: Zeus, Hera, Poseidon… and a «lady of Atana».","Tombs of gold","They buried the great in domed tombs, the <i>tholoi</i>, or in shaft graves full of gold: masks, cups, inlaid swords. Centuries later someone will say one of those masks is «Agamemnon's»; in fact it is older than any Trojan War.","Warriors and the memory of Troy","They were warriors: chariots, boar's-tusk helmets, enormous shields. Around 1200 BC a city in Asia, Troy, was destroyed. Singers turned those times into the Iliad; the «Catalogue of Ships» preserves names of real Mycenaean cities. But Homer is not a chronicler: he mixes periods.","The collapse","Around 1200 BC the palaces burned one after another. Why? It is still debated: droughts, earthquakes, revolts, the «Sea Peoples» who attacked Egypt… probably all at once. With the palaces, writing disappeared.","Homer, <i>Iliad</i> II (Catalogue of Ships); tablets from Pylos and Knossos (Linear B, deciphered by M. Ventris in 1952); J. Chadwick, <i>The Mycenaean World</i>.","The Dark Age","No palaces, no letters","After the collapse (around 1100-800 BC) Greece had fewer people, small villages and houses of mud and straw. Nobody wrote: that is why historians call it the «Dark Age», not because nothing happened, but because we know little.","Iron","You learned to work iron, which is found in more places than the copper and tin of bronze. Hesiod will call his own time the «age of iron», the worst of all, full of toil and weariness.","Not so dark","At Lefkandi, on Euboea, around 950 BC, a man and a woman were buried with gold and horses inside a building almost fifty metres long. There were contacts with Cyprus and the East. The darkness was not total.","The bards","What was not written was sung. Bards recited from memory, with fixed formulas («swift-footed Achilles»), stories of heroes and gods. That is how the poems we know as Homer's reached the 8th century BC.","Letters return","Around 800 BC, trading with the Phoenicians, you took their alphabet and added vowels. Herodotus tells it: you call them «Phoenician letters». With them a new age begins.","Hesiod, <i>Works and Days</i> 174-201; Herodotus V 58; excavations at Lefkandi (Toumba); I. Morris, <i>Archaeology as Cultural History</i>.","The Archaic period","The polis is born","Between 800 and 480 BC villages joined into city-states, the <i>poleis</i>: an acropolis with temples, an agora to meet in and a territory of fields. Each polis with its own laws and gods. It is the way of life you know.","Colonies all over the sea","Land was short, and many cities sent out colonists: Syracuse (733 BC, according to Thucydides), Massalia (around 600), Byzantium, cities on the Black Sea and in Italy. Plato will say you live around the sea «like ants or frogs around a pond».","The phalanx","Citizens who could afford shield, helmet and spear fought shoulder to shoulder in the hoplite phalanx. Those who defend the city want a say in it: many see here a root of citizen politics.","According to tradition, the first Olympic Games were held in 776 BC. Every four years a sacred truce let Greeks from everywhere travel to Olympia. You count the years by Olympiads.","Laws and tyrants in Athens","In Athens, Draco wrote very harsh laws (621 BC). Solon (594) banned enslavement for debt and shared out rights according to wealth. Then the tyrant Pisistratus and his sons ruled. In 508/507 Cleisthenes reorganised the citizens into ten tribes: the democracy you have today.","The wars against Persia","The Persian Empire reached the Aegean. Athens won at Marathon (490 BC) and, ten years later, the Greek fleet defeated Xerxes at Salamis (480). That ends the Archaic period and begins your grandparents' age.","Aristotle, <i>Constitution of the Athenians</i> 2-22; Herodotus VI-VIII; Thucydides VI 3; Plato, <i>Phaedo</i> 109b.","The future: Hellenism and Rome","What has not yet happened","I will show you what has not happened yet. In the north, Macedonia will grow. Its king Philip II will defeat Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea (338 BC). You may see it in your old age. <i>(In the game it is 386 BC: this is the future.)</i>","Alexander","His son Alexander (336-323 BC) will cross into Asia, defeat the Persian king and reach India. He will die in Babylon aged thirty-two. His teacher will be Aristotle, who is not yet born: he will be born in Stagira in two years. <i>(In this game you will already see him as a child: anachronism noted.)</i>","The kingdoms of the successors","His generals, the Diadochi, will divide the empire: the Ptolemies in Egypt, the Seleucids in Asia, the Antigonids in Macedonia. The Greek cities, Athens too, will no longer decide their fate alone.","A world that speaks Greek","Common Greek, the <i>koine</i>, will be spoken from Egypt to the Indus. Alexandria will have a gigantic lighthouse and a Library that will try to gather every book. This age will be called <b>Hellenistic</b> (323-31 BC).","Rome arrives","A city in Italy, Rome, will defeat Macedonia (Cynoscephalae, 197; Pydna, 168), raze Corinth (146), and its general Sulla will sack Athens (86 BC). In 31 BC, after the battle of Actium, the last kingdom will fall, Cleopatra's Egypt.","Greece conquers its conqueror","But Rome will learn from you: its young men will come to study in Athens, its houses will fill with Greek statues. A Roman poet, Horace, will put it like this: «Greece, conquered, conquered her fierce victor».","Arrian, <i>Anabasis</i>; Polybius; Plutarch, <i>Sulla</i> 12-14; Horace, <i>Epistles</i> II 1, 156.","My birth","Metis, cunning","My mother was Metis, the wisest of the gods. Gaia and Uranus warned Zeus: Metis would bear him a son stronger than he. So Zeus, with sweet words, swallowed her.","The headache","Soon after, Zeus had a headache like never before. Hephaestus (others say Prometheus) took a double axe and split his head open with one blow.","I am born armed","And out I came, already grown, with helmet, spear and shield, giving a war cry. That is why I am the goddess of wisdom: I carry my mother's cunning within me.","Olympus astonished","Olympus shook, the earth cried out and the sea was stirred, the hymn says, until I took off my armour. You will see it carved on the east pediment of the Parthenon, above your head as you enter.","Hesiod, <i>Theogony</i> 886-900 and 924-926; <i>Homeric Hymn</i> 28; Pindar, <i>Olympian</i> 7, 35-38.","The olive tree and Poseidon","Two gods for one city","When Cecrops, half man and half serpent, ruled this land, Poseidon and I both wanted to be the city's patron. Each would give a gift.","The trident","Poseidon struck the rock with his trident and a spring gushed out… of salt water. You can still see the mark and the «sea» in the Erechtheion.","The olive tree","I planted an olive tree: oil for food, for light and for athletes. The sacred olive is still on the Acropolis; Herodotus says that when the Persians burned it, the next day it had already put out a shoot.","The verdict","The judges gave me victory and the city took my name. A late version says everyone voted, men and women, and the women won by one vote; Poseidon, furious, flooded the land and women lost the vote. That is what Varro told, according to Saint Augustine. Look for the scene on the west pediment of the Parthenon.","Herodotus VIII 55; Apollodorus, <i>Library</i> III 14, 1; Augustine, <i>City of God</i> XVIII 9 (quoting Varro).","Erichthonius, child of the earth","Hephaestus pursued me, but I am a virgin, <i>parthénos</i>: hence the name of my temple. From that encounter seed fell to the earth, and Earth gave birth to a child, Erichthonius.","The closed basket","I hid him in a basket and entrusted it to the daughters of Cecrops, with one order: not to open it. Curiosity won.","The serpent","Inside was a child… and a coiled serpent. The girls, terrified, threw themselves from the Acropolis. That is why a sacred snake lives in my temple, and my statue, right here, has another beside the shield.","King of Athens","Erichthonius grew up in my temple, became king of Athens and, they say, founded the Panathenaea, the great festival in my honour. You Athenians call yourselves children of the earth, <i>autochthonous</i>, because of him.","Apollodorus, <i>Library</i> III 14, 6; Euripides, <i>Ion</i> 20-26 and 267-274; Pausanias I 24, 7.","The proud weaver","In Lydia lived Arachne, the best weaver in the world. When people said I had taught her, she grew angry: nobody had taught her anything.","The old woman","I disguised myself as an old woman and advised her to ask the goddess's pardon. She challenged me. Then I threw off the disguise.","The contest","I wove the gods in majesty and the punishments of the proud. She wove the tricks and loves of the gods, without a single flaw. I could find no fault in it, and that enraged me.","The spider","I tore her web; she, in despair, tried to hang herself. I turned her into a spider: she would go on hanging and weaving forever. This myth is told by the Roman poet Ovid, centuries after your time.","Ovid, <i>Metamorphoses</i> VI 5-145 (a Roman source, 1st century BC-1st century AD: anachronism noted).","Perseus and the Gorgon","An impossible task","Young Perseus promised to bring the head of Medusa, one of the three Gorgons: whoever looked her in the eye turned to stone. Hermes and I helped him.","The shield as a mirror","I gave him advice: never look at her directly, only at her reflection in the polished bronze shield. With winged sandals and a helmet that made him invisible, he reached them while they slept.","The Gorgons","He cut off the head of Medusa, who was mortal; her immortal sisters woke and chased him, but could not see him.","The aegis","Perseus gave me the head and I set it on my aegis, the skin I wear over my breast. Look at it on Phidias' statue: Medusa's face in the centre.","Hesiod, <i>Theogony</i> 274-283; Apollodorus, <i>Library</i> II 4, 2-3; Pausanias I 24, 7.","The household: the oîkos","A house is more than walls","The <i>oîkos</i> is the whole household: family, slaves, property and land. At its head is the <i>kýrios</i>, the man who represents it before the city.","The women","The woman of a good family runs the house from within: the stores, the slaves, the weaving. Xenophon, Socrates' pupil, describes it so in the <i>Oeconomicus</i>. But poor women work outside: they sell in the market, they are wet nurses, spinners.","Children and inheritance","The most important thing is that the household should not die out: sons inherit equal shares, and if there is only a daughter, the <i>epíkleros</i>, she must marry a relative so the property stays in the family.","The household slaves","Almost every household has at least one slave. They are property, but also part of the oîkos: on arrival they are welcomed with dried fruit and nuts at the hearth.","Xenophon, <i>Oeconomicus</i> VII-X; Isaeus, speeches on inheritance; S. Pomeroy, <i>Goddesses, Whores, Wives and Slaves</i>.","Citizens and Assembly","The Pnyx","About forty times a year the adult male citizens climb the hill of the Pnyx. There they vote on war and peace, taxes and laws, by show of hands.","Who wishes to speak?","The herald asks: «Who wishes to speak?». Any citizen may, though in practice the usual orators speak. For some years now attendance has been paid, so the poor do not lose a day's wage.","The Council of Five Hundred","Five hundred citizens chosen by lot, fifty from each tribe, prepare the Assembly's business in the Bouleuterion. Nobody may be a councillor more than twice in a lifetime.","The lot","Almost all offices are filled by lot: you believe it is the most democratic, because anyone can govern. Only the generals, the strategoi, are elected by vote, because war needs experts.","Aristotle, <i>Constitution of the Athenians</i> 41-44 and 62; Aristophanes, <i>Assemblywomen</i> (392 BC); M. H. Hansen, <i>The Athenian Democracy in the Age of Demosthenes</i>.","Courts and ostracism","The people are the judges","Each year six thousand jurors are drawn by lot, the heliasts. An important trial may have five hundred and one: an odd number so there can be no tie.","Speaking against the clock","There are no lawyers or prosecutors: each party speaks for itself, though it may pay a logographer to write its speech. Time is measured with a water clock, the <i>klepsydra</i>.","Voting with tokens","Jurors vote in secret with bronze tokens: with a hollow axle to condemn, a solid one to acquit. That is how Socrates was condemned thirteen years ago.","Ostracism","In the past, if a politician seemed too powerful, citizens wrote his name on pieces of pottery, <i>ostraka</i>. With six thousand votes, he went into exile for ten years, without losing his property. The last ostracism was some thirty years ago, around 417.","Aristotle, <i>Constitution of the Athenians</i> 22 and 63-69; Plutarch, <i>Aristides</i> 7; ostraka from the Agora and the Kerameikos.","Those who do not vote","Most do not vote","Citizens with political rights number some thirty thousand adult men. But many more people live in Attica: women, children, foreigners and slaves.","Athenian women are citizens: they pass citizenship to their children and play a huge role in religion (priestesses of Athena Polias, the festivals). But they do not vote or speak in the Assembly or the courts.","The metics","Foreigners who live here, the metics, pay a tax of twelve drachmas a year, serve in the army and do much of the trade. Pasion, the richest banker in Athens, was a slave and then a metic.","The slaves","There are tens of thousands of slaves: in houses, workshops and, in the worst conditions, in the silver mines of Laurion. Athenian democracy also rested on their labour.","Aristotle, <i>Politics</i> I and III; Xenophon, <i>Ways and Means</i> II and IV; Demosthenes XXXVI (on Pasion).","School and gymnasium","Three teachers","There is no public school: families pay. The boy goes to the <i>grammatistes</i> to read and write, to the <i>kitharistes</i> for the lyre and Homer's poems, and to the <i>paidotribes</i> for physical training.","A slave goes with him, the <i>paidagogos</i>, «the one who leads the boy»: he carries his books and makes sure he behaves. The word «pedagogue» comes from this.","Girls learn at home to spin, weave and run the household. Some learn to read. They do not go to the palaestra.","Philosophers and sophists","Rich young men pay sophists to learn public speaking. And right now, around 387, Plato has opened his school at the Academy. The ephebeia, two years of compulsory military training, will be organised later, around 335.","Plato, <i>Protagoras</i> 325c-326c; Aristophanes, <i>Clouds</i> 961-1023; Aristotle, <i>Constitution of the Athenians</i> 42.","Origins and kings","Villages by the Tiber","In the 8th century BC there were huts of wood and straw on the Palatine, beside a ford of the Tiber. Archaeologists have found their post holes. Tradition dates Romulus' founding of Rome to 21 April 753 BC.","Seven kings","According to Livy, seven kings reigned: Romulus, Numa (who ordered religion), Tullus Hostilius, Ancus Marcius, Tarquinius Priscus, Servius Tullius and Tarquinius Superbus. The last three are linked to the Etruscans, the neighbouring people who taught Rome many things.","My temple on the Capitol","The Tarquins built the temple where you stand: three cellas, for Jupiter, Juno and me, Minerva. It was dedicated in the first year of the Republic, 509 BC. This year, AD 80, it burned in a fire; Domitian will rebuild it.","Farewell to the kings","In 509 BC, after Sextus Tarquinius' crime against Lucretia, the Romans expelled the last king. From then on the word «king», <i>rex</i>, was cursed in Rome.","Livy I; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, <i>Roman Antiquities</i> III-IV; Tacitus, <i>Histories</i> III 72; excavations of the Palatine huts.","The Republic and the conquest of Italy","Consuls and Senate","Instead of a king, two consuls elected each year, who keep watch on each other. The Senate, made up of former magistrates, advises, and its advice is almost always followed.","Patricians against plebeians","The plebeians withdrew from the city (the secession of 494 BC) until they won their tribunes. They demanded written laws: the Twelve Tables (451-450). In 367 a plebeian could be consul for the first time.","Around 390 BC the Gauls won at the river Allia and sacked Rome. Livy says Juno's geese, on my hill, woke the defenders of the Capitol.","Roman Italy","Through wars and alliances, Rome defeated Latins, Etruscans, Samnites and the Greek cities of the south. In 272 BC Tarentum fell: Italy was Roman.","Livy II-X; Polybius VI (the Roman constitution).","Carthage and the Mediterranean","The First Punic War","In 264 BC Rome and Carthage clashed over Sicily. Rome, which had no fleet, learned to build ships by copying a stranded Carthaginian one, Polybius says. It won in 241.","In 218 Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants and crushed the Romans at Cannae (216). But Rome did not give in: Scipio took the war to Africa and won at Zama (202).","In the same year, 146 BC, Rome destroyed Carthage and Corinth. The Mediterranean began to be «our sea», <i>mare nostrum</i>.","The price of victory","Riches and slaves poured in. Great landowners bought up land and many farmers, who had fought for years far from home, lost everything.","Polybius I 20-21 and III; Livy XXI-XXX; Appian, <i>Libyca</i>.","From Republic to Empire","The Gracchi","Tiberius Gracchus (133 BC) and his brother Gaius (123) wanted to share out land to the poor. Both died violently. Roman politics filled with blood.","Generals with their own armies","Marius opened the legions to the poor, who became loyal to their general. Sulla marched on Rome with his army. Then came Caesar and Pompey.","In 49 BC Caesar crossed the Rubicon with his army and won the civil war. He became dictator for life and was murdered in the Senate on the Ides of March, 44.","Augustus and the emperors","Octavian, his heir, defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium (31 BC) and in 27 received the name Augustus. He kept the forms of the Republic, but he was in charge. Then: Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius, Nero… and in 69, four emperors in one year. Vespasian won; today his son Titus reigns, who has just opened the Flavian Amphitheatre.","Plutarch, <i>Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus</i>, <i>Caesar</i>; Suetonius, <i>Lives of the Twelve Caesars</i>; <i>Res gestae divi Augusti</i>.","The future of Rome","I will show you what has not yet happened. Under Trajan (AD 117) the Empire will reach its greatest size, from Britain to Mesopotamia. <i>(In the game it is AD 80: this is the future.)</i>","Everyone a citizen","In 212 the emperor Caracalla will give Roman citizenship to almost every free inhabitant of the Empire.","The crisis","The 3rd century will bring civil wars, invasions, plague and inflation: some fifty years with more than twenty emperors. Aurelian will surround Rome with a new wall.","A new religion","The Christians, today a small persecuted sect, will grow. Constantine will protect them (313) and found Constantinople (330); Theodosius will make Christianity the official religion (380). My temple will be closed.","The end of the West","In 476 a Germanic chieftain will depose the last emperor of the West. In the East the Empire, with its capital at Constantinople, will last until 1453. And Latin will live on in the languages your descendants will speak.","Cassius Dio; <i>Historia Augusta</i>; Eusebius, <i>Life of Constantine</i>; <i>Theodosian Code</i> XVI 1, 2.","My birth and the Triad","Born from Jupiter's head","The Greeks call me Athena and tell that I sprang armed from Zeus' head. In Rome you kept the story: I was born from Jupiter's head.","Menrva","But I was in Italy before that: the Etruscans called me Menrva. My name may come from <i>mens</i>, «mind». I am the goddess of intelligence, of crafts and of well-planned war.","The Capitoline Triad","Three of us live in this temple: Jupiter in the centre, Juno on one side and I on the other. Every Roman colony builds its own Capitol for the three of us.","The god who would not leave","When Tarquin cleared the hill to build the temple, all the gods there agreed to leave except Terminus, the god of boundaries. He stayed inside the temple: Rome would never retreat, said the augurs.","Livy I 55; Ovid, <i>Fasti</i> II 667-678 and III 835-848; Vitruvius I 7, 1.","The Palladium","The statue fallen from heaven","In Troy there was a small wooden statue of me, the Palladium, which had fallen from the sky. As long as it stayed in the city, Troy would not fall.","The theft","That is why, the Greeks say, Diomedes and Odysseus entered Troy by night and stole it. Soon afterwards the city fell.","The Romans tell another story: that Aeneas saved the true Palladium from the fire and brought it to Italy.","In the temple of Vesta","Today it is hidden in the temple of Vesta, in the Forum, and only the Vestals see it. When the temple burned in 241 BC, the pontiff Metellus went into the flames to save it and was blinded.","Dionysius of Halicarnassus, <i>Roman Antiquities</i> I 68-69; Ovid, <i>Fasti</i> VI 417-454; Virgil, <i>Aeneid</i> II 162-170.","Your poet Ovid tells it: in Lydia lived Arachne, the best weaver in the world, and she denied that I had taught her.","I disguised myself as an old woman and asked her for humility. She challenged me to a contest. I threw off the disguise.","I wove the gods in majesty; she, the tricks of the gods, without a flaw. It was perfect, and I could not bear it.","I tore her web and turned her into a spider. That is why spiders weave while hanging: it is Arachne. A warning against pride… and also against a goddess who cannot lose.","Ovid, <i>Metamorphoses</i> VI 5-145.","The flute and Marsyas","I invent the tibia","I invented the <i>tibia</i>, the double pipe, by boring holes in boxwood. The music was beautiful. That is why pipers honour me at my festivals.","My reflection","But as I played I saw my reflection in the water: puffed cheeks, a distorted face. I threw it far away.","The satyr Marsyas picked it up, learned to play it and thought himself so good that he challenged Apollo, the lyre player.","The punishment","Apollo won and cruelly punished Marsyas for his pride. In the Forum there is a statue of Marsyas: they say it is a symbol of the city's liberty.","Ovid, <i>Fasti</i> VI 693-710 and <i>Metamorphoses</i> VI 382-400; Pliny, <i>Natural History</i> XXI 9.","The Quinquatrus, my festival","Five days in March","From 19 to 23 March you celebrate my Quinquatrus. The first day was my birthday, Ovid says, and the temple on the Aventine was dedicated that day.","The craftsmen","All the crafts honour me: weavers, fullers, shoemakers, carpenters, doctors, painters, sculptors… and teachers. I am the goddess of skilled hands.","The schoolchildren","Children have a holiday and bring the teacher his fee, the <i>minerval</i>. Juvenal, a poet who will write in a few years' time, will speak of the boy who at my festival prays for Cicero's eloquence.","The trumpets","On the last day, the <i>tubilustrium</i>, the sacred trumpets are purified. You see: between school and war, everything that needs a head is mine.","Ovid, <i>Fasti</i> III 809-848; Juvenal X 114-117; Varro, <i>On the Latin Language</i> VI 14 and 17.","The family and the paterfamilias","The paterfamilias","The Roman <i>familia</i> is everything under the power of the <i>paterfamilias</i>: wife (depending on the type of marriage), children, grandchildren and slaves. While he lives, not even his adult sons own property.","The matrona","The matrona runs the house, receives guests and goes out freely, more than an Athenian woman. Epitaphs praise her who «kept the house and spun wool».","The children","In theory the father could decide over his children's lives. In practice, today it is frowned upon. At fourteen the boy leaves the purple-bordered toga and puts on the toga of manhood.","In the atrium of noble families the wax masks of the ancestors are kept, and they come out at funerals. To be Roman is to live up to one's elders: the <i>mos maiorum</i>.","Gaius, <i>Institutes</i> I 48-55; Polybius VI 53; epitaph of Claudia (<i>CIL</i> I² 1211); J. Carcopino, <i>Daily Life in Ancient Rome</i>.","The salutatio","At dawn, before every powerful man's door there is a queue of clients in togas: they come to greet their patron, the <i>salutatio</i>.","What the patron gives","The patron protects: he helps in lawsuits, lends money, gives a small daily sum, the <i>sportula</i> (six and a quarter sesterces: Martial, who is just starting to publish, will complain about it in his epigrams).","What the client gives","The client escorts his patron through the Forum, applauds when he speaks and votes for him. The more clients, the more important you look.","A web of favours","All of Rome runs on favours and loyalties. A freed slave becomes the client of his former master.","Martial III 7 and X 70; Juvenal I 95-126; Seneca, <i>On the Shortness of Life</i> 14.","Senators, knights and plebs","The senators","About six hundred senators, with at least a million sesterces and the broad-striped tunic. They may not engage in trade: their wealth must be in land.","The knights","The equestrian order: four hundred thousand sesterces and a narrow stripe. They are bankers, tax collectors and senior officials of the emperor.","The plebs","The vast majority of Rome's citizens are plebeians: craftsmen, shopkeepers, day labourers. About two hundred thousand receive free grain every month.","Bread and games","The emperor looks after the plebs with grain, baths and shows. In a few years the poet Juvenal will sum it up with contempt: the people ask only for «bread and games».","Suetonius, <i>Augustus</i> 40-41; Pliny, <i>Natural History</i> XXXIII 32; Juvenal X 77-81.","Millions of slaves","Prisoners of war, abandoned children, children of slave women: in Italy perhaps one inhabitant in five is a slave. They work in houses, workshops, mines and on huge estates.","Without rights","Before the law a slave is a thing: he can be sold, punished, separated from his family. His fate depends on his master.","Freedom","But in Rome slaves are often freed, by manumission. The freedman becomes a citizen, and his children fully Roman.","Rich freedmen","Some freedmen grow very rich through trade. Petronius mocks one, Trimalchio, in his novel. And the emperor's freedmen have come to govern the Empire from the palace.","Gaius, <i>Institutes</i> I 9-17; Petronius, <i>Satyricon</i> 26-78; Pliny the Younger, <i>Letters</i> III 14.","The ludi magister","From the age of seven, many boys (and some girls) go to the school of the <i>ludi magister</i>, sometimes under an awning in a portico, to read, write and count. They start before dawn.","The grammarian","Around eleven, the <i>grammaticus</i> teaches them to read the poets well: Virgil and Homer, in Latin and Greek.","The rhetor","Around fifteen, the <i>rhetor</i> teaches public speaking through exercises on invented speeches. It is preparation for the Forum and politics.","The cane","Discipline is harsh: Horace remembers his teacher Orbilius as «the flogger». In the niche the two Lares and the emperor's genius are painted or carved. Augustus divided the city into neighbourhoods (vici), and each one chooses its magistri every year to look after the altar (Pliny, Natural History 3.66, counts 265 crossroads with their altar in the city). At the Compitalia, in early January, the neighbours hang woollen dolls here for each free person in the household and balls for each slave (Festus, s.v. pilae).","A public fountain.","A lacus: a stone basin into which water from the aqueducts pours ceaselessly through a spout. The people of the tenement blocks, who have no water at home, fetch it here. Agrippa, as aedile in 33 BC, built seven hundred (Pliny, Natural History 36.121); Frontinus, in charge of the waters from AD 97 (seventeen years from now), will count 591 (On the Aqueducts 78).","Wooden balcony","A wooden balcony jutting out over the street.","A wooden balcony jutting out over the street (maenianum). The name comes from Gaius Maenius who, according to Festus, was the first to build platforms over the columns of the Forum to watch the shows (s.v. Maeniana). With so much wood, fires leap from house to house: after the fire of 64, Nero ordered porticoes built in front of the tenement blocks so that fires could be fought from their flat roofs (Suetonius, Nero 16; Tacitus, Annals 15.43).","Vomitorium","An entrance to the stands.","One of the openings through which the audience enters and leaves the stands. Macrobius explains that they are called vomitoria because they «spew» people out (Saturnalia 6.4.3). Each spectator carries a token with the number of their arch, section and row, and so finds their seat without getting lost.","Awning mast","A mast for an awning.","One of the wooden masts which, set in stone brackets at the top of the façade, hold the ropes of the velarium, the great awning that shades the stands. It is worked by sailors of the fleet at Misenum, who have their barracks next to the amphitheatre (Historia Augusta, Commodus 15.6).","Travertine marker","A stone marker.","One of the stone markers that ring the amphitheatre at some distance. Nobody knows for sure what they were for: perhaps to tie the awning ropes, perhaps to close off the way and control the crowd on games days.","Pots at the window","potted plants","Flowers and herbs in pots.","People who live in a tenement block have no garden: they keep flowers and herbs in pots at the window. Pliny the Elder describes it as a custom of the common people of Rome, who make themselves a picture of a garden at their windows (Natural History 19.59).","Shop sign","A shop sign.","The sign of a shop, painted on a board. Many shops also advertise with a picture of what they sell, because not everyone can read, like the painted signs preserved on the façades of Pompeii.","Audience","Athenians spend whole days in the theatre during the festivals of Dionysus, watching one play after another from dawn. The seats of honour in the front row (proedria) are for priests, magistrates and benefactors of the city.","Everyone sits according to who they are: senators at the bottom; knights in the rows behind; soldiers apart; women right at the top. Augustus ordered it so (Suetonius, Augustus 44).","Dry-stone wall","field boundary","Stones without mortar, piled up when clearing the field: they mark the edge of each plot and, on slopes, hold up terraces. In Attica the soil is stony and these walls are everywhere.","Stones without mortar that separate the plots. Roman surveyors measure the land and divide it into lots, and the markers and walls show who owns each one.","Wall tower","A tower of the wall of Athens. The Spartans had it pulled down at the end of the war (404 BC), and only seven years ago Conon raised it again with Persian money, together with the Long Walls to the Piraeus (Xenophon, Hellenica 4.8.9-10). Above a stone base, the rest is mud brick. Thucydides says the first wall, Themistocles', was built in such haste that even gravestones were put into it (1.93).","A wall tower.","Column drums in the wall","remains of the burnt temple","Look at the north wall of the Acropolis: column drums and pieces of cornice are built into it. They come from the temples the Persians burned in 480 BC; the Athenians put them here, in sight of the whole city, so that no one would forget that destruction. They can still be seen from the Agora today.","Column drums built into a wall.","Grave stele","tomb by the road","Athenians bury their dead outside the walls, along the roads, and set a stele over them with the name of the dead person and sometimes a farewell relief. Someone writing <b>at the time</b> could have seen it or spoken to someone who did; someone writing <b>later</b> tells what was remembered or what they read, sometimes centuries later, and may get it wrong or embellish it. That is why, in the game, what comes from a later source is marked.</p>","<p class=\"sub\">A question to think about: why might a historian writing three hundred years later know something no one at the time tells us? First a little unmixed wine is poured for the «good spirit» (Agathos Daimon); then the one presiding, the symposiarch, decides how much water goes into each krater. Drinking wine unmixed is for barbarians: they say the Spartan king Cleomenes went mad from drinking it neat, like the Scythians (Herodotus 6.84).</p><p>In Plato's Symposium the guests agree to drink in moderation so they can talk about love all night (176a-e); in Xenophon's there is music, riddles and a dancer. It is the largest and tallest room, and the coolest in summer.","You have bathed like a Roman.","A complete bath","<p>You have done the round of a Roman bath: changing room, warm room, hot room and, to finish, the cold water. People went almost every day, in the afternoon, for very little money: a quarter of an as (Horace, Satires 1.3.137), and free on days when a magistrate or the emperor paid.</p><p>Vitruvius explains how the rooms are heated with the hypocaust and why the hot room faces the afternoon sun (On Architecture 5.10). Seneca, who lived above a bath-house, complains of the noise: men grunting as they lift weights, the hair-plucker shouting to advertise himself, the sellers of cakes and sausages (Letters 56.1-2).</p><p class=\"sub\">The Baths of Titus were opened this year, next to the amphitheatre (Suetonius, Titus 7.3).
